title: Writing argumentative essays: should school start later?
summary: Eighth graders learn to write a five-paragraph argumentative essay on whether school should start later. They read and mark up one article for and one against, then build a claim, reasons, cited evidence, explanation, and a counterclaim with rebuttal. The essay grows through a planning organizer, model paragraphs, drafting in class, peer review and revision.
brief: Writing argumentative essays for grade 8 English language arts: a three-week unit of fifteen 45-minute lessons. Students learn to state a clear claim, support it with reasons and evidence from two short articles, explain how the evidence supports the claim, answer a counterclaim, and organize a five-paragraph essay with an introduction and a conclusion. The topic is one they care about: should school start later? Use the two attached opinion articles, one for and one against, as the evidence students read, mark up and cite. Build the essay in steps across the unit: a planning organizer, model paragraphs, drafting in class, a peer review session and revision. Grading: the final essay 60% with a rubric, the organizer and drafts 25%, and short quizzes on the terms of argument 15%.
policies:
Bring your writing folder to every class: the organizer, drafts and peer review sheets all stay in it until the final essay is handed in.

Drafts are due on the day set in class. A late draft can still earn full credit if it is finished before peer review, so that your partner has something to read.

Essays use evidence only from the two unit articles, with the article named each time. Copying sentences without quotation marks, from the articles or anywhere else, is plagiarism.

segments.title: Should our school start later?
segments.description:
Every student writes yes, no or not sure on a scrap of paper, with a reason in a few words.
Students tell a partner their answer in one sentence.
The teacher hears two answers, one “yes” and one “no” if possible.

segments.title: Claim, fact or feeling?
segments.description:
The teacher shows three statements about school start times. Each student writes a label for each one: fact, feeling or claim.
Students compare labels with a partner and explain one choice.
The teacher then reveals the table and defines each type.
The teacher stresses that a claim takes a side and must be supported, and that a fact can serve as evidence for a claim.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected labels: A feeling, B fact, C claim. Common mistake: thinking a claim is just an opinion. A claim is an opinion that must be backed up. Students also think a fact cannot belong in an argument; show that it can become evidence.

B: The American Academy of Pediatrics recommended in 2014 that middle and high schools start at 8:30 a.m. or later.

segments.title: Sort six statements
segments.description:
Working alone, students write one letter for each of six statements: F for fact, L for feeling or C for claim. They do not explain their choices in writing.
Students compare letters with a partner and settle a difference with one question: can it be checked, is it just how someone feels, or does it take a side?
The teacher hears two disputed items.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and answers:
1. Seattle’s public high schools moved their start time from 7:50 a.m. to 8:45 a.m. in 2016. Fact
2. I hate early mornings. Feeling
3. Schools should start later because teenagers’ body clocks shift later during puberty. Claim
4. California passed a law in 2019 requiring most public high schools to start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. Fact
5. Mornings are the worst part of the day. Feeling
6. Our school should not change its start time until it studies the cost of buses. Claim
Keep the pace brisk: about 40 seconds an item.

segments.title: Find and fix the mistake
segments.description:
The teacher shows a note from a fictional student, Sam, who calls a fact a claim.
Each student writes whether Sam is right and why.
Then each student rewrites Sam’s sentence so it becomes a real claim about school start times, using the fact as a reason.
Students read their rewrite to a partner, and the teacher hears two or three.
segments.teacherNotes: Sam is wrong: the sentence is a fact, since it can be checked and no one takes a side. A fix: “Our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later, because teenagers need 8 to 10 hours of sleep a night.” Check that the rewrite includes should and a because.

segments.title: Meet the two sides
segments.description:
The teacher explains that students will read two opinion articles written for this unit, one for a later start and one against. The writers are fictional but the facts are real.
The teacher reads aloud the opening claim of each article from the screen.
For each writer, each student writes one short line: the side taken and the hope or worry behind it, in a few words.
Students compare lines with a partner, and the teacher hears two answers, one for each writer.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: Torres hopes for more sleep, better learning and better health. Okafor worries a later start would create new problems for families and communities. Point out that both writers agree students need sleep; they disagree on the solution. Keep the written lines to a few words each.

segments.title: Take a first stand
segments.description:
Each student completes two sentences: a position on later start times and one thing they still want to find out.
Students underline the part of their first sentence that is the claim.
Partners swap papers and check that the first sentence takes a side and gives a because.
segments.teacherNotes: Tell students a first position can change after reading; the goal now is a clear side. Common mistake: writing a feeling (“I’m tired”) instead of a claim with should. Students keep this page in the writing folder.

The teacher tells students that next time they will read and mark up Maya Torres’s article, “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later”, to find her claim, her three main reasons and the evidence behind each.
The teacher reminds students to bring their writing folder next time.

keyIdeas: A claim is a statement that takes a side. Reasonable people could disagree with it, so it needs reasons and evidence.
A fact can be checked as true or false. A feeling is personal. Facts and feelings are not claims, but facts can become evidence for a claim.
The start-time question has two sides: Maya Torres argues for a later start and Daniel Okafor urges caution.
A first position is a starting point. It can change as you read and weigh evidence.
The essay will use evidence only from the two unit articles, with the article named each time.

study.overview: A claim is a statement that takes a side on a question people can disagree about. This guide shows how to tell a claim from a fact and from a feeling, how a fact can become evidence, what the two sides of the start-time debate are, and how to write a first position that is clear.

points.heading: Claim, fact or feeling: three questions to ask
points.explanation: Ask three questions about any statement. Can it be checked as true or false? Then it is a fact. Is it only how one person feels? Then it is a feeling. Does it take a side that reasonable people could disagree with? Then it is a claim, and it needs reasons and evidence. Example: “The American Academy of Pediatrics recommended in 2014 that middle and high schools start at 8:30 a.m. or later” is a fact, because you can look it up. “Waking up at 6:00 a.m. feels terrible” is a feeling, because it is true or false only for the person who says it. “Our school should keep its current start time” is a claim, because someone could answer “No, it should change.” A claim is not just an opinion. It is an opinion that you must back up.

points.heading: A fact is not a claim, but it can become evidence
points.explanation: A fact on its own does not take a side, so it is not a claim. But a fact can work as evidence once it is attached to a claim. Example: the statement that days are shorter in fall and winter is a fact. It takes no side. Put it behind a claim and it does a job: “Our school should not end later in the day, because sports teams would have less daylight for practice in the fall and winter.” The claim takes a side. The word “because” brings in the reason, and the fact about daylight supports it. When you find a fact, ask what claim it could help prove.

points.heading: The start-time question has two sides
points.explanation: In this unit you will read two opinion articles. The writers are fictional, but the facts in the articles are real. Maya Torres, in “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later,” argues for a later start. She hopes students will get more sleep, learn better and stay healthier. Daniel Okafor, in “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems,” urges caution. He worries that a later start would create new problems for families and communities. Notice that both writers agree that teenagers need sleep. They disagree about the solution. Your essay will use evidence only from these two articles, and you must name the article each time you use evidence. Copying sentences without quotation marks is plagiarism.

points.heading: Writing a first position you can build on
points.explanation: A strong first position names a side, uses the word “should” or “should not,” and gives a reason with “because.” A feeling such as “Early mornings are hard for me” is not enough, because it takes no side on what the school should do. Here is a model on a different topic from the start time itself: “Our school should keep a single bell schedule for every grade, because it is easier for families with several children to plan.” Check it: it takes a side, it has a because, and someone could disagree. Your first position is a starting point. It can change as you read both articles and weigh the evidence. Next time you will mark up Maya Torres’s article to find her claim, her three main reasons and the evidence behind each. Bring your writing folder.

Circled answer: Accept yes, no, or not sure.

blocks.caption: Statements about school start times

blocks.text: If you and your partner disagree, ask one question

items: Can it be checked?
Is it just how someone feels?
Does it take a side?

handouts.key:
1. F. The date and start times can be checked. Source: Maya Torres, Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later.
2. L. This expresses a personal feeling about mornings.
3. C. This takes a side in favor of later starts and gives a biological reason. A factual reason can support a claim; it does not make the whole statement a fact.
4. F. The law’s date and high school start-time requirement can be checked. Source: Maya Torres, Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later.
5. L. This expresses a personal judgment about mornings. Stating a feeling broadly does not make it a fact, and it is not a claim: it asks no one to do anything, and no evidence could settle it.
6. C. This argues against changing the start time before studying bus costs. A claim can take a conditional position.
Partner discussion: There is no additional written answer. Look for students to use whether the statement can be checked, expresses a feeling, or takes a side to resolve a disagreement.

handouts.title: Find and fix the mistake

blocks.text: Sam is a fictional student. Sam was asked to write a claim about school start times and wrote the note below. Read it, then answer the two questions.

blocks.label: Sam's note: my claim
blocks.value: Teenagers need 8 to 10 hours of sleep a night.

items: Is Sam right that this is a claim? Say yes or no and explain why.

blocks.hint: Yes or no, and why

items: Rewrite Sam's sentence so it becomes a real claim about school start times. Use Sam's fact as the reason.

blocks.hint: Your rewritten claim. You will read it to your partner.

handouts.key:
Yes or no, and why: No. Sam gives a checkable fact about sleep needs. The sentence does not take a side on whether school should start later. A common slip is calling it a claim simply because it could support an argument.
Your rewritten claim: Accept a clear position about school start times that uses the sleep fact as its reason. Example: Our school should start later because teenagers need 8 to 10 hours of sleep each night. The sleep information appears in both unit articles. Look for should or should not, a position on start times, and because linking that position to Sam’s fact. Merely adding because without taking a side is insufficient.

handouts.title: Meet the two sides

blocks.text: Your teacher will read the opening claim of each article aloud. For each writer, write one short line in a few words: the side the writer takes, and the hope or worry behind it.
Maya Torres, Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later

blocks.hint: Side taken, and the hope or worry behind it

blocks.text: Daniel Okafor, A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems

blocks.hint: Side taken, and the hope or worry behind it

handouts.key:
Maya Torres—side taken, and the hope or worry behind it: Supports starting at 8:30 a.m. or later; hopes students will get enough sleep, learn better, and stay healthier. Accept a few words naming the side and at least one of these hopes.
Daniel Okafor—side taken, and the hope or worry behind it: Opposes moving the school day later as a simple solution; worries about new problems for families and communities. Accept a few words naming the side and this concern.
Common slip: Saying Okafor thinks sleep does not matter. Both writers value students’ sleep; they disagree about changing the schedule.

handouts.title: My first stand

blocks.text: Complete both sentences. Then underline the part of your first sentence that is your claim. Swap papers with your partner. Your partner checks that your first sentence takes a side and gives a because. Keep this page in your writing folder. Your position can change after you read the articles.

items: Our school should / should not start later because ...

blocks.hint: Write the whole sentence, with your position and your reason

items: One thing I still want to find out is ...

blocks.hint: Write the whole sentence

handouts.key:
Position and reason: Accept either side with a relevant reason linked by because. Examples: Our school should start later because students need enough sleep to pay attention in class. Our school should not start later because a later dismissal could interfere with caring for younger siblings. Look for a clear position, not only a feeling such as being tired.
Underlining: Students should underline the part stating that their school should or should not start later. Underlining the whole sentence is also acceptable because it includes the position and its reason. Underlining only the reason misses the position.
One thing I still want to find out: Accept a specific, relevant question or uncertainty. Examples: One thing I still want to find out is how much more sleep students get when school starts later. One thing I still want to find out is how a later start would affect bus schedules.
Partner check: The position sentence takes a side and includes because followed by a reason. Students do not need to agree with their partner’s position.

segments.teacherNotes: Reason 1: teenagers need more sleep than most of them get. The American Academy of Sleep Medicine gives the recommended sleep amount; the body-clock explanation helps show why early schedules can limit sleep. The bus example illustrates the problem but leaves the student’s wake-up time unstated. The AAP recommendation supports the claim, while the CDC finding gives background about school schedules. Prepare a copy of the article for every student. Students use pencil or pen, one color.
shown: Table: Mark | What you do | What it finds / Underline | Draw one line under the sentence | The claim / Number | Circle 1, 2 or 3 beside the reason sentence | The three reasons / Label | Write E in the margin and box the fact | The evidence and its source
Steps: Find the claim → Number the reasons → Label the evidence

segments.title: Mark the second and third reasons
segments.description:
Working alone, students reread the “Second” and “Third” paragraphs and number each reason.
They put one E beside the Seattle findings and write the source’s name in the margin.
They put one E beside the statements about attention, moods, safe choices, illness and recovery and write “source not named”.
Students compare reason numbers with a partner and fix any difference by going back to the text. Students bracket the paragraph beginning “Some people say” as the other side and leave it unnumbered.
segments.teacherNotes: Reason 2: when schools do start later, students really do sleep more. Evidence: Seattle 2016, 7:50 to 8:45 a.m., University of Washington researchers, a little over half an hour more sleep, grades up in biology classes, fewer late or absent at one school. One E beside the whole group is enough. Reason 3: sleep is about more than grades. Explain that the health statements are harder to check because Torres does not identify their sources. Bracket the “Some people say” paragraph as the other side, unnumbered. Later in the course, students judge strong evidence.

segments.title: Build the argument map
segments.description:
The teacher draws a three-row map on the board with the headings Reason, Evidence and Source named.
Students copy it into their writing folder and fill it from their marked article.
Three volunteers each report one reason and its support while everyone else checks their own map.
Students correct their own markup where it differs.
segments.teacherNotes: Timing: about 5 minutes to fill, 3 to hear three reasons, 1 to correct. Row 1 source: American Academy of Sleep Medicine; source not named for the body-clock explanation. Keep the AAP recommendation labeled as support for the claim and the CDC finding labeled as background on the article. Row 2 source: University of Washington researchers. Row 3 source: none named. Accept short phrases, not full sentences. Maps stay in the writing folder.

segments.title: Which way of marking is better?
segments.description:
Give out the sheet “Which way of marking is better?”.
Two ways of marking Reason 2 are on the sheet.
Each student chooses the better way and writes two sentences saying why.
Students read their choice to a partner and fix their own map if it matches the weaker way.
The teacher hears three students.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: Way 2. Way 1 treats a checkable fact as the reason and leaves nothing backing it. Way 2 states the general reason and puts the Seattle findings underneath as evidence. Ask: does this statement explain why schools should start later, or does it give a specific fact supporting that explanation? Common mistake: choosing Way 1 because it has dates and numbers.

segments.title: Exit ticket, homework and what comes next
segments.description:
Each student completes the sheet Exit ticket: claim and evidence, using Maya Torres’s article. They write her claim in their own words, then one piece of evidence from the article with its source named, and keep the sheet in the writing folder.
The teacher sets the Torres markup and map as a short ungraded step toward Organizer and drafts (25%), due at the start of next time.
The teacher writes on the board the article students read before next time: Daniel Okafor, “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems”.
Next time students annotate his article on buses, after-school activities and family schedules, then compare his reasons with Torres’s.
The short practice quiz on today’s lesson is taken after class and counts toward no grade.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected answers. Claim: the school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later so students sleep more, learn better and stay healthier. Evidence: one of the American Academy of Pediatrics recommendation, the Seattle study or the American Academy of Sleep Medicine sleep recommendation, with its source named. Remind students to bring the writing folder. The step stays in the writing folder.

keyIdeas: A claim is the sentence that takes a side. In Maya Torres’s article it is the sentence in the opening paragraph that says our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later.
A reason answers the question “why?” Torres gives three main reasons, and the words First, Second and Third help a reader find them.
Evidence is a checkable fact that backs up a reason. Torres’s evidence includes the American Academy of Pediatrics recommendation and the Seattle study.
A reason and a piece of evidence are different things. A reason is a statement that needs support, and evidence is the checkable fact that gives the support.
Marking up an article with underlines, numbers and labels shows the shape of an argument: claim, then reasons, then evidence under each reason.

vocabulary.definition: To mark a text with underlines, numbers and short notes in the margin so its parts are easy to find.
A word such as First, Second or Third that tells the reader a new reason is starting.
The person, group or publication that a fact comes from, such as the American Academy of Pediatrics.
Official advice from a group of experts about what should be done.
Research in which people collect and compare information, such as sleep before and after a school’s start time changed.
A simple chart that lists each reason and the evidence and source that back it up.

slides.title: Marking up the for article: claim, reasons, evidence
bullets: Maya Torres, “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later”
Underline the claim. Number the reasons. Label the evidence.
slides.notes: Welcome students. Today they annotate Maya Torres’s article, which they read at home. By the end they should be able to underline her claim, number each reason, and label evidence such as the American Academy of Pediatrics recommendation and the Seattle study. Remind them that their writing folders stay on the desk. Hand a spare copy of the article to anyone who did not bring one.

slides.title: What does Torres want, and why?
bullets: Write two things from memory.
1. One short sentence: what does Maya Torres want our school to do, and why?
2. A few words for one fact from her article that you remember.
slides.notes: Students take out their writing folders and the article. Give a spare copy to anyone without one. They write from memory, without looking at the text. Then they tell a partner what they wrote. Hear two. Expected: she wants school to start at 8:30 a.m. or later, because of sleep, learning and health. Common mistake: recalling a feeling (“teenagers are tired”) instead of a checkable fact. Ask: could we check it? Students may add their first-position page from last time.

slides.title: How to mark up an argument
slides.notes: Introduce the marking key. Students have the same key on their handout, “Marking key for an argument”, and keep it in the writing folder. Explain each mark in a sentence. The kinds of evidence are expert, study, statistic and example. On the handout they are written E, S, N and X. Tell students they will mark their own copies as you model on the next slide.

rows: R1, R2, R3 in the margin
[ ] bracket, then E, S, N or X
a piece of evidence, with its kind written beside it (expert, study, statistic, example)

slides.title: Torres’s first two paragraphs
bullets: Paragraph 1: “Every school morning, millions of teenagers drag themselves out of bed before the sun is up. Many of them are not lazy. They are tired, and science can explain why. Our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later, because later start times help students sleep enough, learn better and stay healthier.”

Paragraph 2: “First, teenagers need more sleep than most of them get. Sleep experts at the American Academy of Sleep Medicine say that people from 13 to 18 years old need 8 to 10 hours of sleep every night. A student who must catch a bus at 6:45 a.m. would have to fall asleep by about 9:30 p.m. to get even eight hours. For most teenagers, that is not realistic.”
Before we read on: which word do you expect to start the second reason?
slides.notes: Model paragraph 1. Underline the last sentence and say aloud how you know it takes a side: it says “should” and gives a because. Common mistake: underlining “Every school morning...” as the claim. It only sets the scene. Point out that the claim previews the benefits she will argue (sleep, learning, health); her numbered reasons come next. Model paragraph 2. Write R1 beside the first sentence. Bracket the American Academy of Sleep Medicine sentence and write E, expert beside it. Students mark the same on their own copies as you go. Before moving on, each student writes the word they expect to start the second reason and tells a partner. Hear two or three. Expected prediction: Second.

slides.title: Mark up the rest of the article
bullets: Alone: re-read paragraphs 3 to 6 and mark them.
Bracket each piece of evidence and write its kind.
Write R2 and R3 beside the second and third reasons.
Label the American Academy of Pediatrics and Seattle evidence.
Then compare marks with a partner. Go back to the text.
slides.notes: Students work alone with the same key. Circulate and check that every bracket has a kind written beside it. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommendation and the Seattle study must each be labeled. Partners then compare marks for a few minutes. Where they differ, they go back to the text and decide. Expected for Reason 1: 8 to 10 hours, the 6:45 a.m. bus example, the melatonin shift, the AAP recommendation in 2014, and the CDC report. Expected for Reason 2: Seattle 2016, 7:50 to 8:45, a little over half an hour more sleep, grades, fewer late. For Reason 3: attention, moods, driving, illness and athletic recovery are benefits Torres names. Explain that this paragraph does not provide a specific study, statistic or expert source to support those statements. Common mistake: mixing up the Sleep Medicine and Pediatrics academies.

slides.title: Two labels: which is better?
bullets: Choose A or B for each sentence.
Ask: does it take a stand, or can it be checked and does it back up a reason?
slides.notes: Students use the worksheet and write A or B for each sentence. Partners compare choices for a short time. When they disagree, they ask the question on the slide. Hear two or three disagreements, and ask students to explain their choices only for those. Answers for you: 1. B, it gives another answer to why school should start later, and the Seattle study then supports it. 2. B, a checkable fact that backs Reason 2. 3. A, it reports what doctors said. The claim is about our school. 4. A, it opens Reason 3. The American Academy of Pediatrics number matches the claim’s 8:30, which tempts students to pick the claim.

rows: 1. “Second, when schools do start later, students really do sleep more.”
2. “They found that students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights.”
3. “In 2014, the American Academy of Pediatrics, an organization of tens of thousands of children’s doctors, recommended that middle and high schools start at 8:30 a.m. or later.”
4. “Third, sleep is about more than grades.”

slides.title: Build the argument map
bullets: Tell your partner the three reasons, one sentence each.
slides.notes: Each student looks at their marked copy and tells a partner the three reasons in their own words. Hear one reason from each of three pairs and fill in the table. For each reason, that pair also names its strongest piece of evidence, or explains that Torres gives no specific study, statistic or expert source. Likely strongest evidence: Reason 1, the American Academy of Pediatrics recommendation; Reason 2, the Seattle study. For Reason 3, students should notice that Torres names benefits but supplies no specific study, statistic or expert source. Accept reasoned alternatives. Students fix their own marks where the class map differs. Paragraph 7 (“Some people say...”) answers worries. That is a different job, and the class will look at it later in the course.

slides.title: Exit ticket
bullets: Work from the sheet “Exit ticket: Torres’s argument”.
slides.notes:
Give out the sheet “Exit ticket: Torres's argument”.
Each student writes their name on the half sheet and answers the prompt on the sheet alone, in one sentence.
Students put the sheet in their writing folder when finished.

slides.title: Before you leave
bullets: Before next time: read Daniel Okafor, “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems”.
Short ungraded step toward Organizer and drafts: due at the start of next time.
Bring your writing folder.
slides.notes: Students put their marked-up article in the writing folder. Set the short ungraded step, naming it Preparing to compare the articles. It is a step toward Organizer and drafts (25%), and it is due at the start of next time. Give each student a copy of Daniel Okafor’s article and tell them to read it before then, with a pen. Preview next time: students will annotate Okafor’s article on buses, after-school activities and family schedules, then compare his reasons with Torres’s. Remind them to bring the writing folder.

study.overview: Marking up an argument means finding out what the writer wants and how each part of the text helps get it. Last time you read Maya Torres’s article. This guide shows the steps for marking it up: find the claim, number the reasons, then bracket and label the evidence. Keep your marked copy and the marking key in your writing folder. You will use the same marks on the other article next time.

points.heading: Find the claim first
points.explanation: The claim is the sentence that takes a side. It usually says what should happen and gives a because. Sentences that set the scene do not take a side, so they are not the claim. Here is a made-up example. Suppose a writer opens with: “Lunch is the loudest, most crowded part of the day. Many students gulp their food and run. Our school should give students 40 minutes for lunch, because they need time to eat and rest.” The first two sentences describe a scene. The third says “should” and gives a because, so it is the claim. Underline it once. In Torres’s article the claim comes at the end of the first paragraph, after the sentences that set the scene.

points.heading: Number the reasons
points.explanation: A reason answers the question why. Writers often signal reasons with words like First, Second and Third, and you can use those words to find them. Write R1, R2 and R3 in the margin beside the sentence that gives each reason. Torres’s first reason is that teenagers need more sleep than most of them get. Her second is that when schools start later, students really do sleep more. A reason is a general statement that the writer still has to back up, and the next step is to find what backs it up.

points.heading: Bracket the evidence and write its kind
points.explanation: Evidence backs up a reason. Bracket the words, then write the kind beside the bracket: expert, study, number or example. Two pieces from Torres show how this works. (1) She writes that the American Academy of Sleep Medicine says people from 13 to 18 years old need 8 to 10 hours of sleep every night. That is E, expert, and it backs R1. (2) She writes that in 2016 the public high schools in Seattle moved their start time from 7:50 a.m. to 8:45 a.m., and researchers found that students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights. That is S, study, and it backs R2. Then check each piece. Can it be checked? Which reason does it back up? Is the source’s name right? Be careful here, because the American Academy of Sleep Medicine and the American Academy of Pediatrics are two different groups.

points.heading: A reason and its evidence do different jobs
points.explanation: Do not mix up the claim, the reasons and the evidence. The claim is the side the writer takes. A reason says why. Evidence is a fact that can be checked and that backs a reason. Torres reports that in 2014 the American Academy of Pediatrics recommended that middle and high schools start at 8:30 a.m. or later. This sounds a lot like her claim, but it reports what doctors said, so it is evidence. Her claim is about our school. Here is a quick test for any sentence. Ask whether it takes a stand about what should happen, whether it tells why, or whether it is a fact you could look up. Use that test every time you mark a sentence.

handouts.title: Which way of marking is better?
handouts.usedIn: Which way of marking is better?

blocks.text: Two students marked Reason 2 in Maya Torres's article, "Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later." Read both ways. Then choose the better way.

rows: In 2016, the public high schools in Seattle moved their start time from 7:50 a.m. to 8:45 a.m.
Second, when schools do start later, students really do sleep more.
The Seattle findings: students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights, grades went up in the biology classes studied, and fewer students were late or absent at one school
blocks.caption: Two ways of marking Reason 2

blocks.label: The better way is (write Way 1 or Way 2)

blocks.hint: Write two sentences that say why this way is better.

handouts.key:
Choice: Way 2.

Sample two-sentence answer: Way 2 identifies the general reason: later school starts help students get more sleep. It marks the specific Seattle findings as evidence and names the University of Washington researchers as the source.

Look for: A distinction between a reason and the facts supporting it, with the Seattle findings placed under evidence. Naming the researchers helps readers identify the evidence’s source.

Common slip: Choosing Way 1 because its sentence includes a date and times. Those details describe the schedule change; they do not state Torres’s general reason or show its results.

handouts.title: Exit ticket: claim and evidence
handouts.usedIn: Exit ticket, homework and what comes next

blocks.text: Use Maya Torres's article, "Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later." Keep this ticket in your writing folder.

blocks.hint: Write Torres's claim in your own words.
Write one piece of evidence from the article. Name its source.

handouts.key:
Claim in the student’s own words: Torres argues that our school should begin at 8:30 a.m. or later because students need enough sleep to learn well and stay healthy.

Look for: A clear position favoring a later school start. Strong answers include the proposed time and the benefits. Accept accurate paraphrases; copying the original sentence does not meet the own-words instruction. Common slip: Writing only that teenagers need sleep, without stating what the school should do.

Evidence with its source named: Accept any one of these accurate paraphrases:
• In Maya Torres’s article, Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later, the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends 8 to 10 hours of sleep each night for ages 13 to 18.
• In Maya Torres’s article, Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later, the American Academy of Pediatrics recommended in 2014 that middle and high schools start at 8:30 a.m. or later.
• In Maya Torres’s article, Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later, University of Washington researchers found that students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights after Seattle public high schools changed their start time from 7:50 a.m. to 8:45 a.m. in 2016. Accept the reported biology-class grade improvement or reduced first-period lateness or absence at one school as alternatives, with the same source named.

Look for: A specific supporting fact, the article named, and the organization or researchers responsible for the evidence identified. Common slips: Confusing the two medical organizations; claiming all Seattle students’ grades improved; claiming lateness and absence fell at every school; or giving a general reason instead of evidence.

ready: Teacher: a copy of "Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later" by Maya Torres for every student
Students bring a pencil or pen, one color, for marking the article
Students bring their writing folder

l_974a557873fe.title: Marking up the against article and comparing the sides
l_974a557873fe.summary: Students annotate Daniel Okafor's article on buses, after-school activities and family schedules, then compare his reasons with Torres's.
readings: Daniel Okafor, "A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems"

segments.title: Where do the two writers part ways?
segments.description:
The teacher tells students that “Preparing to compare the articles” is due now.
A question about the two writers is on the screen. Each student writes one sentence answering it, then tells a partner.
The teacher hears two answers.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: they disagree about whether a later start is the right fix. Torres says yes. Okafor says it creates problems as serious as the sleep problem. Prepare a copy of Okafor’s article for every student.
shown: Maya Torres and Daniel Okafor both say teenagers need 8 to 10 hours of sleep a night. In one sentence: what do they disagree about?

segments.title: Marking up Okafor’s claim and first problem
segments.description:
The teacher hands out a fresh copy of “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems” and shows its opening paragraph.
Each student underlines the sentence they think is Okafor’s claim. They also circle the word that shows he is turning against Torres.
The teacher then underlines the claim and numbers the paragraph that begins “The first problem is transportation” as problem 1, as with Torres last time.
The teacher writes E beside the buses making several trips, and students copy these marks.
segments.teacherNotes: Claim: “But moving the school day later is not the simple answer it sounds like.” Signal word: But. There is no “should” until the last paragraph. Common mistake: underlining “Nobody wants exhausted students.” or the shared 8 to 10 hours fact.
shown: Nobody wants exhausted students. Teenagers need 8 to 10 hours of sleep a night, and many get far less. But moving the school day later is not the simple answer it sounds like. For many families and communities, a later start would create new problems that are just as serious as the one it tries to solve.

segments.title: Mark the second and third problems
segments.description:
Working alone, students reread the paragraphs that begin “The second problem” and “The third problem” and number them 2 and 3.
They mark supporting details and label predictions about what could happen as possible effects. They reserve E for checkable facts.
They bracket the paragraph that begins “Supporters of later start times” and the paragraph that begins “There are also other ways”. In the margin they write what each one does.
Partners compare numbers and brackets and go back to the text on any difference.
segments.teacherNotes: Problem 2: later end of day, less daylight for practice, part-time jobs, caring for siblings. Problem 3: parents leave early, so no drop-off. The Seattle paragraph answers Torres. The other paragraph offers alternatives. Common mistake: numbering these two as problems 4 and 5.

segments.title: Which pairing is a fairer comparison?
segments.description:
The teacher shows two ways of pairing a Torres reason with an Okafor point.
Each student chooses the fairer pairing and writes two sentences saying why.
Students read their choice to a partner and change it if the partner’s reason is better.
The teacher hears three students.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: B gives the more direct comparison because both writers discuss the Seattle result. A can also support a fair comparison of competing concerns: students’ sleep needs and family schedules. Accept A if students explain that tradeoff accurately. Common mistake: choosing A because it uses a numbered problem.

segments.title: Build the two-column chart
segments.description:
The teacher draws a chart on the board with the columns Torres and Okafor and the rows Reason, Support and Source named. Students take out their marked Torres article from last time; the teacher provides spare copies.
Each student copies it and fills it in for one pair where both writers address the same question, using short phrases.
Partners swap charts and check each cell against the articles.
Charts stay in the writing folder.
segments.teacherNotes: Pairs that work: Seattle (Torres’s Second reason, Okafor’s Seattle paragraph) or buses and practices (Torres’s “Some people say” paragraph, Okafor’s problems 1 and 2). Explain that the Reason row can contain a main reason or a response to one; students label which it is. In the Seattle pair, Torres names University of Washington researchers and Okafor names no source.

segments.title: Exit ticket: Okafor’s claim
segments.description:
Each student writes Okafor’s claim in their own words and names his three problems.
Students keep the ticket in the writing folder.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: a later start is not an easy fix because it would create new problems: transportation, after-school activities and jobs, and family schedules.
shown: In one or two sentences, write Okafor’s claim in your own words and name his three problems.

segments.title: What to do before next time
segments.description:
The teacher sets “Getting ready to judge evidence”, a short ungraded step toward Organizer and drafts (25%), due at the start of next time.
The teacher puts on the screen the two articles to read before next time and reminds students to bring their writing folder.
The teacher tells students that next time they judge evidence for relevance and reliability, then practice quoting and paraphrasing with the article named each time.
The short practice quiz on today’s lesson is taken after class and counts toward no grade.
segments.teacherNotes: Read the title and author of each article aloud so students copy them exactly.
shown: Homework: “Getting ready to judge evidence”, an ungraded step toward Organizer and drafts, due at the start of next time
Read before next time: Maya Torres, “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later”; Daniel Okafor, “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems”

keyIdeas: Okafor’s claim is a call for caution: moving the school day later is not the simple answer, because it would create new problems. The marks used last time (underline the claim, number the reasons, put E beside the evidence) work on an article against a change too.
Okafor gives three problems with a later start, introduced by The first, The second and The third: transportation, after-school activities and jobs, and family schedules.
Two paragraphs in Okafor’s article are not numbered problems. One replies to Torres’s Seattle evidence. The other suggests other ways to help students sleep.
Both writers agree that teenagers need 8 to 10 hours of sleep. They disagree about whether a later start is the right fix.
A fair comparison puts one reason from each article side by side on the same question. Torres and Okafor use the Seattle result in different ways, so it is a good place to compare.

vocabulary.definition: The writer or group that argues for the other position. For Torres, Okafor is the opposing side.
To admit that something the other side says is true. Okafor concedes that the Seattle result is real.
Another way to reach the same goal. Okafor offers alternatives such as limits on phones and screens at night.
What a choice takes away or requires, such as money, time, daylight or jobs.
A two-column table that sets a reason from one article beside a reason from the other.

slides.title: Marking up the against article and comparing the sides
bullets: Identify Okafor’s claim and his three problems with a later start
Compare one reason from each article in a two-column chart
slides.notes: Welcome students. Last time they marked up Maya Torres’s article for a later start. Today they do the same with Daniel Okafor’s article, “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems,” and then set the two sides next to each other. Point to the two goals on the screen. Students need their writing folders, their marked-up copy of Torres’s article and the Okafor article they read at home.

slides.title: What does Okafor argue?
bullets: Write one sentence: What does Daniel Okafor argue?
slides.notes: Students take out their writing folders, their marked-up Torres copy and the article they read at home. Have copies of Daniel Okafor, “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems,” ready for anyone without one. Remind them that the short ungraded step toward Organizer and drafts, set last time, is due now. Each student writes one short sentence from memory, then reads it to a partner. Listen to two pairs. Expected: a later start is not an easy fix because it creates new problems for families and the community. Common mistake: writing only that Okafor “disagrees.” Ask what he thinks a later start would cause.

slides.title: Find the claim and the turn
bullets: Marking key: Underline the claim. Write R1, R2, R3 beside each reason. Bracket evidence and write E and its kind. Circle signal words.

Nobody wants exhausted students. Teenagers need 8 to 10 hours of sleep a night, and many get far less. But moving the school day later is not the simple answer it sounds like. For many families and communities, a later start would create new problems that are just as serious as the one it tries to solve.
slides.notes: Read the marking key aloud, then model on the first paragraph. Circle “But.” Underline the claim. Explain that “Nobody wants exhausted students” concedes a point to the other side, and the turn comes after “But.” Students circle and underline on their own copies as you go. Okafor’s claim is a caution, not a flat “should.” Accept: a later start would create problems as serious as the one it solves. Common mistake: underlining “Nobody wants exhausted students” as the claim. Then each student writes the three words they expect to begin his first reason and tells a partner. Listen to two pairs. Expected prediction: “The first problem.” Do not give this away before students have predicted.

slides.title: Mark up the three problems
bullets: Marking key: Underline the claim. Write R1, R2, R3 beside each reason. Bracket evidence and write E and its kind. Circle signal words.
slides.notes: Leave the marking key up while students work. Students work alone for about six minutes, re-reading the three paragraphs that describe the problems. In each one they circle the signal word and write R1, R2 or R3 beside it. In each paragraph they also bracket the one piece of evidence they find strongest and write its kind in two or three words. Then partners compare their three brackets for three minutes. Where they differ, they go back to the text and decide. Accept any reasoned bracket. Likely R1 (buses): several trips per bus, or seven-year-olds in the dark. R2: 4:00 versus 3:00 p.m., less daylight, jobs, siblings. R3: parents leaving early. The evidence is mostly examples and predicted effects. The 4:00 versus 3:00 p.m. example is a possible change, not a reported result. “Many people think” is not an expert.

slides.title: Build Okafor’s map
bullets: Tell your partner his claim and three problems in your own words.
Fix your own marks where the class map differs.
slides.notes: Each student tells a partner Okafor’s claim and his three problems in their own words. Hear different pairs and fill in the table as the class agrees. For each problem, ask the class to name its strongest piece of evidence. Likely strongest: R1, the bus trips for high school, middle school, then elementary; R2, the 4:00 p.m. end and shrinking daylight; R3, parents leaving early. Accept reasoned choices. Students fix their own marks where the class map differs. His Seattle and “other ways” paragraphs answer the other side. Say that is a different job, covered later in the course.

slides.title: Fix Jo’s comparison chart
bullets: A comparison chart sets a reason beside a reason.
It sets evidence beside evidence.
Is Jo’s chart right? Write what is wrong with it.
Rewrite each cell that is wrong, in your own words.
slides.notes: Hand out Jo’s comparison chart. Jo is a fictional student. Explain that a comparison chart sets a reason beside a reason and evidence beside evidence. Students write whether the chart is right, then rewrite both faulty cells in their own words, starting with the row and the writer’s name and writing a reason as a full sentence. Partners compare and you hear two or three. What to look for: Jo swapped Torres’s cells. The American Academy of Pediatrics recommendation is evidence, and “Teenagers need more sleep” is the reason. Okafor’s evidence cell gives a conditional example, not a reported schedule change. Check that the fix names the reason in a full sentence. Common mistake: fixing only the evidence cell.

slides.title: Compare one reason from each side
bullets: Choose one reason from each writer. Use a different pair from Jo’s.
Both writers ______, but Torres ______ while Okafor ______.
slides.notes: Hand out the comparison chart organizer. Each student chooses one reason from Torres and one from Okafor, a different pair from Jo’s. They write each reason as a short phrase and the evidence with its kind in a few words. Then they finish the sentence frame, using “both” for what the writers share and “but” for where they differ, a few words in each blank. Partners read their sentences to each other once, and you hear two. Expected sentence: both writers agree teenagers need 8 to 10 hours of sleep, but Torres says a later start helps students sleep more while Okafor says it creates new problems. One possible pair: Torres’s reason that later starts give students more sleep, supported by the Seattle study, and Okafor’s concern about family schedules, supported by examples of parents leaving early. Stress that the reason row and the evidence row are different jobs. Keep this answer off the screen until students have written their own.

study.overview: Marking up Daniel Okafor’s article and comparing it with Maya Torres’s gave you three tools you will use again when you plan your own essay. You can find a writer’s real claim even when it comes after a concession. You can tell a reason from the evidence that backs it. And you can compare two sides fairly by setting like beside like. This guide explains each tool with a new, made-up example, so you can practice on the articles yourself.

points.heading: The claim often comes after a concession
points.explanation: A writer may agree with the other side first, then turn with a word like “But.” The agreement is a concession. The claim is what the writer argues after the turn. Okafor’s first paragraph works this way: it opens with “Nobody wants exhausted students,” and the turn comes at “But.” Underline what follows the turn, not the opening agreement. Here is a made-up example. Suppose a writer opens: “Nobody likes a heavy backpack. But replacing every textbook with a tablet is not the fix it seems.” The first sentence concedes. The claim is that the tablet plan is not as good a fix as it seems. If you underlined “Nobody likes a heavy backpack,” you marked the concession by mistake. A good test is to ask what the writer wants the reader to believe by the end of the paragraph.

points.heading: Signal words show the reasons, and evidence comes in kinds
points.explanation: Writers often announce their reasons with signal words such as “The first problem,” “The second problem” and “The third problem.” Circle these and label each reason R1, R2 or R3. Then bracket the strongest piece of support in each paragraph and name its kind in two or three words. Common kinds are an expert statement, a study, a real example and a predicted effect. Be careful with a predicted effect. It says what might happen, not what did happen. Also, “Many people think” is not an expert; it is only an opinion. Here is a made-up example. A writer says: “The first problem with tablets is breakage.” Then the writer adds: “Suppose a tablet slips from a desk and cracks; the family may have to pay for it.” The signal phrase marks R1. The bracketed sentence is evidence, and its kind is a predicted effect, because the writer imagines it and does not report it. A strong study or expert statement would carry more weight than an imagined case.

points.heading: Compare reason to reason and evidence to evidence
points.explanation: A two-column comparison chart has a reason row and an evidence row. The reason row holds each writer’s point, written as a short phrase or a full sentence that says what the writer claims. The evidence row holds the support for that point: what it is and its kind. Never swap the rows. If a cell tells you what the writer believes, it is a reason. If a cell tells you what backs that belief up, it is evidence. Always set one reason beside one reason. Then use a sentence frame to name what the writers share and where they differ: “Both writers ___, but one says ___ while the other says ___.” Here is a made-up example about tablets. Writer A’s reason is that tablets would lighten backpacks, backed by an example of a student carrying five books. Writer B’s reason is that tablets would be costly to replace, backed by a predicted effect of cracked screens. A finished sentence could read: “Both writers care about students’ daily school experience, but Writer A says tablets would ease the load while Writer B says they would bring new costs.” Notice that the “both” part names something the two sides actually share.

Fairer pairing: B is the strongest answer because both writers discuss the same Seattle finding.

Two-sentence explanation: Torres uses the extra sleep students got in Seattle to support starting school later. Okafor accepts that finding but questions whether other communities would get the same result because their transportation, budgets and family schedules may differ.

Also accept A if the student clearly explains the tradeoff between teenagers’ sleep needs and families’ morning schedules. Look for an accurate comparison of competing concerns. A common slip is choosing A only because it includes a numbered problem. Another is claiming that Okafor denies the Seattle sleep finding.

Changed choice or new reason: The blank may remain empty if the student keeps the original answer. If completed, look for a revised choice or reason that accurately explains either B’s direct comparison of the Seattle finding or A’s tradeoff between sleep needs and family schedules.

Look for these distinctions: Transportation includes buses making several trips and possible changes to costs or younger children’s schedules. After-school concerns include daylight for sports, part-time jobs and caring for younger siblings. Family schedules include parents leaving early for work and being unable to drop teenagers off at a later time.

Common slips: Giving the shared fact that teenagers need 8 to 10 hours of sleep as his claim; listing sports, jobs and sibling care as the three separate problems; or treating the Seattle discussion and alternative sleep solutions as additional problems.

segments.title: Which evidence would convince you?
segments.description:
The teacher tells students that “Prepare evidence for your organizer” is due now, and students keep it in their writing folders.

segments.teacherNotes: Expected: B. It names researchers, a place, a year and a result that can be checked. A is an informal observation about friends. It does not show whether students sleep more after a later start. Do not teach the two tests yet; the next segment names them.
shown: Reason: Later start times help students sleep more.
A: Lots of my friends seem tired in first period.

B: In 2016, Seattle’s public high schools moved their start time from 7:50 a.m. to 8:45 a.m. Researchers from the University of Washington found that students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights.
Which is more convincing, A or B? Write one reason why.

segments.title: Two tests for strong evidence
segments.description:
The teacher names two tests: is the evidence relevant, and is it reliable?
The teacher tests the American Academy of Pediatrics recommendation against the displayed reason and thinks aloud for both tests.
Each student then tests the second piece on the screen and writes “relevant?” and “reliable?” with a short why. Students tell a partner, and the teacher hears two.
segments.teacherNotes: AAP piece: relevant, since it is the experts’ advice itself, and reliable, since a medical organization with relevant expertise gives advice that readers can check. Second piece is relevant but not reliable: no one is named. Mistake: judging by whether you agree. Strong evidence can back the side you reject.
shown: Reason: Medical experts say middle and high schools should start at 8:30 a.m. or later.
Evidence to test: In 2014, the American Academy of Pediatrics, an organization of tens of thousands of children’s doctors, recommended that middle and high schools start at 8:30 a.m. or later.
Steps: Read the reason → Test 1, relevant: does it back this reason? → Test 2, reliable: who says it, and can it be checked?
Now you test: Everyone knows that doctors want school to start later.

segments.title: Rank the evidence: strong or weak
segments.description:
The teacher hands out fresh copies of both articles. Working alone, students mark each of six pieces of evidence on the screen as strong or weak and write the test it fails, if any.
Students compare rankings with a partner and go back to the article text on any difference.
The teacher hears three students and asks which test decided each answer.
segments.teacherNotes:
Answers (S strong, W weak):
1 S: relevant, named group.
2 S: named researchers, year, numbers.
3 W: relevant, but the article names no medical source or research supporting this statement.
4 W: “many people” is an unnamed opinion.
5 W: relevant, but the example supposes a change in dismissal time rather than documenting one. It would be stronger with information about actual dismissal times and practice schedules.
6 W: true, but backs a different reason (relevance).
Prepare a copy of each article for every student.
shown: 1. Reason (Torres): Teenagers need 8 to 10 hours of sleep a night. Evidence: The American Academy of Sleep Medicine says people from 13 to 18 years old need 8 to 10 hours of sleep every night.

2. Reason (Torres): Later start times help students sleep more. Evidence: After Seattle’s high schools moved from 7:50 a.m. to 8:45 a.m. in 2016, University of Washington scientists found students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights.
3. Reason (Torres): Sleep is about more than grades. Evidence: Sleep helps the body fight illness and helps young athletes recover.
4. Reason (Okafor): A later start would cause problems with buses. Evidence: Many people think it makes little sense to have seven-year-olds waiting at bus stops in the dark.

5. Reason (Okafor): A later end to the school day would hurt after-school activities. Evidence: If school lets out at 4:00 p.m. instead of 3:00 p.m., sports teams have less daylight for practice, especially in the fall and winter.
6. Reason (Torres): Later start times help students sleep more. Evidence: Teenagers who drive to school are safer behind the wheel when they are rested.

segments.title: Quoting and paraphrasing with the author’s name
segments.description:
The teacher shows one sentence from Maya Torres’s article used two ways: as a quotation and as a paraphrase.
The teacher points out the author’s name in both models, the article title and quotation marks in the first, and the changed wording in the second. Students add “In ‘Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later,’” before the paraphrase so it also names the article.
Students write one rule for each in their own words and tell a partner. The teacher reminds them that copying without quotation marks is plagiarism.
segments.teacherNotes: Quote: exact words, quotation marks, author and article named. Paraphrase: new words and new sentence shape, same meaning, author and article named, no quotation marks. Mistake: swapping a few words and calling it a paraphrase. Essay rule: name the article each time.
shown: Side by side: Quotation: In “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later,” Maya Torres writes, “Those problems are real, but they can be solved.” | Paraphrase: Maya Torres admits that bus and sports problems are real, but she argues that districts can find solutions.
Quotation: exact words, quotation marks, author’s name. Paraphrase: your own words, same meaning, author’s name.

segments.title: Find and fix the citation mistake
segments.description:
A student’s sentence is on the screen. Each student finds what is wrong with it and writes two problems.
Students then rewrite the sentence as a paraphrase that names Maya Torres and her article.
Partners swap rewrites and check for her name, the article title, the same meaning, and the student’s own wording and sentence shape. The teacher hears two rewrites.
segments.teacherNotes: Problems: Torres’s words are copied exactly without quotation marks (plagiarism), and no author or article is named. Sample fix: In “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later,” Maya Torres explains that teenage drivers are safer on the road when they have had enough sleep. Require a paraphrase for this task.

keyIdeas: Strong evidence passes two tests. It is relevant, meaning it backs the reason it sits under. It is reliable when a reader can check it and its source has relevant knowledge and gives trustworthy support.
A true fact can still be weak evidence if it backs a different reason. When no source is named, readers need more information to judge its reliability.
Both articles contain strong and weak evidence, so students judge each piece, not the writer or the side.
A quotation uses the author’s exact words inside quotation marks. A paraphrase says the same thing in the student’s own words. Both name the author.
Evidence in the essay comes only from the two unit articles, with the article named each time. Copying sentences without quotation marks is plagiarism.

vocabulary.definition: Backing up the reason it is placed under. Evidence about a different point is not relevant.
Able to be trusted because it can be checked and its source has relevant knowledge and gives trustworthy support.
To tell the reader which author and article an idea or fact came from.
The author’s exact words, placed inside quotation marks.
Saying an author’s idea in your own words and sentence shape, with the same meaning.
Words that introduce a quotation or paraphrase and name the author, such as “Maya Torres writes”.

study.overview: Strong evidence is relevant to the reason it supports, and it comes from a source you can trust and check. In this lesson you judged evidence from Maya Torres and Daniel Okafor, then practiced citing it with the author’s name and the article title, using a quotation or a paraphrase. This guide goes over both skills so you can use them when you build your organizer and write your essay. In the essay, use evidence only from the two unit articles, and name the article each time.

points.heading: Two tests for strong evidence
points.explanation: Ask two questions about every piece of evidence. First, is it relevant? It must back the exact reason it sits under. Second, is it reliable? Ask where the information comes from, whether that source knows the subject, and whether the facts can be checked. Names, numbers, dates and places are clues to look into, but they are not a guarantee. Example: Torres writes, “In 2014, the American Academy of Pediatrics, an organization of tens of thousands of children’s doctors, recommended that middle and high schools start at 8:30 a.m. or later.” Put it under the reason “Teenagers need more sleep than most of them get.” It is strong. It backs that reason, it comes from a named group of doctors, and you can look it up. Now compare Okafor’s line, “Many people think it makes little sense to have seven-year-olds waiting at bus stops in the dark.” It fits the reason that a later start would cause transportation problems, so it is relevant. But it names no one, so it is only opinion and it is weak. Judge the evidence, not whether you agree with the writer’s side.

points.heading: Weak, limited and off-target evidence
points.explanation: Evidence is weak when it is an opinion with no named source, a comparison with nothing to check, or a guess. A careful worry that uses “might” can be reasonable, but it stays limited until something supports it. Example: Okafor says students who care for younger brothers and sisters after school “might not get home in time.” That is a believable concern. Under a reason about students’ duties at home, it is relevant but weakly supported, because the article gives no real case of a student missing those duties after a schedule change. Also remember that one fact can be strong for one reason and off target for another. Torres reports that California passed a law in 2019 requiring most public high schools to start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. That is strong for the reason “a later start can be put into practice.” It does not show that students sleep more, so it is off target for a reason about sleep gains. The Seattle result, a measured increase of about half an hour of sleep on school nights, is strong for sleep gains. Okafor reminds readers that it comes from one city. Always ask which reason the evidence is supporting.

points.heading: Citing with the author’s name
points.explanation: To cite an article, name the author and the article title. Then either quote or paraphrase. For a quotation, copy the exact words and put them inside quotation marks. For a paraphrase, use your own words and your own sentence shape, check that the facts still match, and still name the author. Quotation example: In “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems,” Daniel Okafor warns, “A good solution should not create as many problems as it solves.” Paraphrase example: In “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later,” Maya Torres reports that in 2014 the American Academy of Pediatrics advised starting middle and high schools at 8:30 a.m. or later. Before you move on, check three things. Does the sentence name the author and the title? Do the quotation marks match the article word for word? Does the paraphrase sound like you and not like the article?

points.heading: Why copying is plagiarism, and how to repair a faulty paraphrase
points.explanation: Copying sentences without quotation marks is plagiarism, even if you change a few words. Adding the author’s name or the title does not fix it. Example of a faulty paraphrase: In “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems,” Daniel Okafor says that many school districts do not have enough buses and drivers to take every student to school at the same time. Only the opening was changed. The rest is Okafor’s sentence with no quotation marks. There are two ways to repair it. You can quote it exactly and put the copied words in quotation marks. Or you can rewrite it fully: In “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems,” Daniel Okafor explains that districts reuse buses for separate trips serving different schools. When you replace weak evidence in your own writing, keep the same reason. A strong fact that backs a different reason does not repair the problem.

Strong or weak? A few words on why
rows: Experts say schools should start later.
In 2014, the American Academy of Pediatrics, an organization of tens of thousands of children's doctors, recommended that middle and high schools start at 8:30 a.m. or later. (Maya Torres)
A later start can be put into practice in real schools.
A California law passed in 2019 requires most public high schools there to start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. and most middle schools no earlier than 8:00 a.m. (Maya Torres)
A later start would hurt students who have duties at home.
Students who care for younger brothers and sisters after school might not get home in time. (Daniel Okafor)
A later start helps students sleep more.

blocks.caption: Evidence to rank

handouts.key:
1. Strong. The recommendation directly supports the reason that experts favor later starts. The American Academy of Pediatrics is a named organization with relevant medical expertise, and the date makes the recommendation easier to check. Common slip: calling it strong only because the student agrees with it.
2. Strong for putting later starts into practice. Torres describes a specific California law with a date and start-time requirements. This supports feasibility, but does not establish that every district can change schedules easily. Common slip: treating the law as evidence that students slept more.
3. Relevant but weakly supported. The statement connects directly to students’ caregiving duties, but Okafor gives no documented example or measured result showing missed caregiving after a schedule change. Common slip: treating a plausible prediction as a demonstrated outcome.
4. Strong for increased sleep. Okafor reports a measured sleep gain after Seattle changed its schedule. The place, date, and reported result make the claim checkable. The result does not guarantee the same gain elsewhere. Common slip: dismissing the finding because Okafor opposes changing the schedule.
Accept alternative ratings when students accurately explain relevance, source support, and limitations.

Find a strong piece of evidence in either article that could replace your partner's weak one. It must back the same reason. Write it as a cited sentence that names the author and the article title. Then check it together with your partner.

handouts.key:
Part 1
Label and weak evidence, sample: MADE UP: Everyone at our school would sleep longer if classes started later.
Reason it is meant to support: A later start helps students sleep more.
Test it fails, and why: Reliable. The statement gives no source or measurements and makes an unsupported claim about everyone.
Look for a clearly labeled invented statement, a specific reason, and an accurate explanation of the failed test. Common slip: naming reliability without explaining the missing support.
Part 2
Replacement cited sentence, sample: In “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems,” Daniel Okafor reports that researchers found Seattle students slept about half an hour more on school nights after their high schools moved to a later start.
Accept accurate quotations or paraphrases from either article that support the partner’s stated reason and name both the author and article title. Exact borrowed wording needs quotation marks. Common slip: replacing the weak statement with a reliable fact about a different reason.

study.overview: A thesis is the claim of your whole essay, written as one sentence. It tells the reader where you stand and why, and each of its reasons later gets its own body paragraph. This guide shows what a thesis is made of, what it is not, and how to check yours. Next time, you will learn to follow evidence with reasoning, so reread Maya Torres, “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later,” with a pen before then and keep your writing folder with your thesis in it.

points.heading: A thesis has three parts: position, because, reasons
points.explanation: A strong thesis is one sentence with three parts. The position says what you believe. The word because links the position to the reasons. The three reasons answer the question why. Here is a thesis on a different question: Students should be allowed to use phones at lunch because lunch is free time, phones keep students in touch with family, and a clear rule can keep phones out of class. The position is “students should be allowed to use phones at lunch.” The reasons are “lunch is free time,” “phones keep students in touch with family,” and “a clear rule can keep phones out of class.” Try splitting a sentence into its parts instead of copying it whole. Take this one: Schools should offer free breakfast because hungry students struggle to focus, a morning meal helps families with busy mornings, and free food means no student is left out. The position is “schools should offer free breakfast.” The three reasons are the three phrases after because.

points.heading: A thesis is not a topic, a feeling or a piece of evidence
points.explanation: Three kinds of sentences often look like a thesis but are not. A topic names a subject and takes no side: “Homework and how much we get.” A feeling tells how you react but gives no reason: “Homework is the worst.” A single piece of evidence tells one story but gives no reasons: “Our school should give less homework because Mia stayed up until midnight on Monday.” (Mia is a made-up student, used only as an example.) Having the word because does not make that last sentence strong. It has a position, but it offers one story instead of reasons. Evidence such as the Seattle results belongs in the body paragraphs, where you will cite it and explain it. The thesis states the reason that evidence supports. A fix for the homework sentence is: Our school should give less homework because students need time to sleep, time with family, and time to practice sports or hobbies.

points.heading: Check your thesis by finding the parts
points.explanation: Writers test a thesis by asking one question: could a reader find the position and each reason? Mark your sentence, or have a partner mark it. Circle the position, underline because, and number each reason. If you cannot find all three reasons, the thesis needs work. Use this frame for the start-time question: Our school (should / should not) start later because ___, ___, and ___. You may choose either side. Reasons can come from Torres: teenagers need more sleep, later starts help students sleep more, and sleep supports health and safety. They can come from Daniel Okafor, “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems”: buses, after-school activities and jobs, and family schedules. One example from the against side: Our school should not start later because it would strain bus schedules, cut into after-school activities and jobs, and disrupt family mornings. Notice that it holds no dates or numbers. Those go in the body paragraphs. Keep your revised thesis in your writing folder, because you will use it to build the planning organizer.

handouts.title: Find the weak thesis and fix it

blocks.text: Below are three sentences about a longer lunch period. Sam is a made-up student, not a real person. Work alone. Write strong or weak for each sentence. For a weak one, write a few words on what is missing.

rows: 1. Lunch at our school and how long it lasts.
2. Our school should lengthen lunch to 40 minutes because students need time to eat a full meal, time to rest before afternoon classes, and time to ask teachers for help.
3. Our school needs a longer lunch because Sam only had five minutes to eat on Tuesday and was hungry all afternoon.
blocks.caption: Three sentences about a longer lunch period

blocks.text: Now choose one weak sentence. Rewrite it as a full thesis: a position, then because, then three reasons.

blocks.hint: Write your thesis in one sentence.

handouts.key:
Sentence 1 — Verdict: Weak. What is missing: A position and three reasons. It names a topic but does not say what the school should do.

Sentence 2 — Verdict: Strong. What is missing: Nothing. Position: Our school should lengthen lunch to 40 minutes. Reasons: Students need time to eat a full meal, rest before afternoon classes, and ask teachers for help. The sentence includes because and gives three reasons that answer why.

Sentence 3 — Verdict: Weak. What is missing: Three general reasons supporting the position. The hypothetical story about Sam offers a specific example instead of stating those reasons. Common slip: Calling the sentence strong just because it includes because.

Rewrite — Sample answer for either weak sentence: Our school should lengthen lunch because students need enough time to finish eating, take a break before afternoon classes, and get help from teachers.

Look for one sentence with a clear position, because, and three distinct reasons that answer why. Accept other sensible reasons. Common slips: Naming only the topic, giving fewer than three reasons, or using another story about one student instead of general reasons.

blocks.text: Write one sentence that answers this question: should school start later? Use your marked-up copies of both articles and the reasons you found earlier in the course. You may choose either side.
Frame
Our school (should / should not) start later because ___, ___, and ___.
Checklist

items: My sentence names a position.
It has the word because.
It gives three reasons, and each reason answers why.
It is one sentence.

blocks.hint: My thesis

blocks.text: Partner check
Swap sheets. Your partner marks the position and each reason on your sentence, then copies the words they marked into the table.

blocks.hint: Revised thesis: change your sentence once, then keep this sheet in your writing folder.

handouts.key:
Frame — Sample completion: Our school should not start later because a schedule change could disrupt shared bus routes, interfere with students’ after-school responsibilities, and complicate family transportation plans. These reasons paraphrase Daniel Okafor’s A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems, in its discussions of transportation, after-school schedules, and family schedules.

Checklist — For the sample answer, all four items should be checked: It names a position, includes because, gives three reasons that answer why, and is one sentence. For other answers, each check must match the student’s actual sentence.

My thesis — Accept the completed sample above or another one-sentence thesis supporting either side with three distinct reasons grounded in the articles. A supporting-position sample is: Our school should start later because teenagers’ changing body clocks make early bedtimes difficult, later starts can increase school-night sleep, and adequate sleep supports health and safety. These reasons paraphrase Maya Torres’s Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later, in its discussions of puberty, Seattle’s start-time change, and health and safety.

Partner check — For the completed frame above:
Position: Our school should not start later.
Reason 1: a schedule change could disrupt shared bus routes.
Reason 2: interfere with students’ after-school responsibilities.
Reason 3: complicate family transportation plans.
For another thesis, the table should copy the exact words marked in that student’s sentence and correctly separate the position from each reason.

Revised thesis — Sample revision: Our school should not start later because changing shared bus routes could create transportation problems, a later dismissal could interfere with jobs and sibling care, and a later arrival could conflict with parents’ work schedules. Accept a revision that improves precision or clarity while retaining one sentence, a position, because, and three reasons.

Common slips: Giving a feeling instead of a reason, repeating the same reason in different words, copying the entire thesis into each table cell, or placing a specific piece of evidence, such as Seattle’s 2016 schedule change, where a general reason belongs.
