l_baf250072a26.title: Explaining how evidence supports the claim
l_baf250072a26.summary: Students learn to follow evidence with reasoning, using sentence starters such as "This shows that" to link the Seattle results to a claim.
readings: Maya Torres, "Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later"

segments.title: Evidence alone: so what?
segments.description:
Put the reason and the evidence on the screen. Each student writes one short sentence that tells a reader what this evidence means for the reason.
Students read their sentence to a partner.
The teacher hears two.
segments.teacherNotes: Students read Maya Torres’s article before class. Expect restating (“Students slept more”) or vague lines (“It is good”). Praise any sentence that says what the result means. Keep their sentences to compare with the model.
shown: Reason: Later start times really do give students more sleep.

Evidence: In “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later,” Maya Torres reports that in 2016 Seattle’s public high schools began the school day almost an hour later, and University of Washington scientists found that students got over thirty minutes more sleep on school nights.
Write one sentence: What does this evidence tell a reader about the reason?

segments.title: Evidence plus explanation
segments.description:
Give out the sheet “From claim to explanation: sentence starters”.
The sheet has the chain from claim to reason to evidence to explanation. Reveal the model explanation for the Seattle evidence. Students compare it with their own warm-up sentence and star one thing the model does that theirs did not.
Teach the sentence starters. Students choose the starter they would use after the next piece of evidence and tell a partner why.
segments.teacherNotes: Point out three moves in the model: it uses the writer’s own words, it says what the result means, and it links back to the reason. Mistake: repeating the evidence in new words. Another: “This proves”, which claims too much from one city. Okafor says Seattle is one city; answering that comes later in the course.

segments.title: Add the explanation
segments.description:
Give out the sheet “Add the explanation”.
Students work alone on the two evidence sentences on the sheet. Under each one they write an explanation that starts with a sentence starter and links back to the reason.
Partners swap papers and check that each explanation says what the evidence means, not just the evidence again.
The teacher hears one explanation for each item.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and sample answers:
1. Reason: Doctors support a later start. Evidence: Torres, in “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later,” reports the American Academy of Pediatrics recommended in 2014 that middle and high schools start at 8:30 a.m. or later. Sample: This matters because a recommendation from doctors who care for children gives schools a health-based reason to reconsider an early start.
2. Reason: Transportation is a problem. Evidence: Okafor, in “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems,” explains that the same buses make several trips each morning, for the high school, then the middle school, then the elementary schools. Sample: This means changing the high school start would also require changing other bus trips or spending more on transportation.
Fast finishers: write one for the melatonin evidence.

segments.title: Fix the paragraph that drops evidence
segments.description:
Give out the sheet “Priya's paragraph”.
Show a paragraph by Priya, a made-up student. Students underline each piece of evidence and circle the spot where an explanation is missing.
Each student rewrites the paragraph, adding an explanation after the evidence and a stronger final sentence.
Partners swap rewrites and check that the explanation links back to the reason. The teacher hears two rewrites.
segments.teacherNotes: Common mistake: adding “Sleep is important” as the explanation. That is true but does not say what the Seattle result means. Look for a starter, the writer’s own words, and a link to the reason. Accept different wordings. Priya is made up for this lesson. Allow about two minutes to mark, five to rewrite, one to check and two to hear rewrites.

segments.title: Make your own evidence and explanation pair
segments.description:
Give out the sheet “My evidence and explanation pair”.
Each student picks one reason from either article and one strong piece of evidence for it that was not used in class today. They write two sentences: the evidence with the author and the article named, then an explanation that starts with a sentence starter.
Partners check with the three questions on the sheet. Each writer fixes one thing, then puts the pair in the writing folder.
segments.teacherNotes: Good choices: Torres on the American Academy of Sleep Medicine’s 8 to 10 hours, the California law, safer driving; Okafor on after-school sports, part-time jobs, or family schedules. Mistake: evidence that backs a different reason than the one chosen. Support: start from Torres’s evidence about the American Academy of Sleep Medicine’s recommendation of 8 to 10 hours. Stretch: a second pair on the other side. Keep for the organizer.

segments.title: Exit ticket: explain this evidence
segments.description:
Give out the sheet “Exit ticket: explain this evidence”.
Each student writes one explanation sentence for the evidence on the sheet, alone, on a half sheet. They put the sheet in the writing folder when finished.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: a sentence like This shows that an early bus makes it hard for teenagers to reach the 8 to 10 hours experts recommend, because their bodies are not ready to sleep that early. Check for a starter and a link to the reason. Re-teach this connection at the start of next time if many only restate.

segments.title: Before you leave
segments.description:
Set the homework: a short ungraded step toward Organizer and drafts, due at the start of next time. Students write it in their planners.
Tell students what comes next time: they use or revise their thesis from last time and fill in an organizer with three reasons, cited evidence, explanations and a counterclaim.
Students keep their paragraph fix, evidence and explanation pair, and exit ticket in the writing folder and bring the folder next time.
segments.teacherNotes: Write the homework and its due time on the board before students leave. Remind students that their thesis from last time is in the writing folder, as it is part of the organizer.
shown: Homework: a short ungraded step toward Organizer and drafts. Due at the start of next time.
Next time: choose a side and fill in an organizer.
Bring your writing folder.

keyIdeas: Evidence does not speak for itself. After each piece of evidence, the writer adds an explanation that tells the reader what it means for the claim.
An explanation answers the question “So what?” and links the evidence back to the reason it supports.
Sentence starters such as “This shows that” and “This matters because” help a writer begin an explanation. The explanation is in the writer’s own words and names the point being made.
A paragraph that drops in facts and moves on is weak. A paragraph that pairs each piece of evidence with an explanation is persuasive.

vocabulary.definition: One or more sentences after a piece of evidence that tell the reader what the evidence means for the claim.
The thinking that connects evidence to a reason or claim, so the reader sees why the evidence matters.
A few opening words, such as “This shows that”, that help a writer begin an explanation.
To end an explanation by tying it to the reason or claim it supports.

study.overview: Evidence is a fact from an article. It does not explain itself, so a reader may not see why it matters. In this lesson you practiced adding an explanation after each piece of evidence. The explanation tells the reader what the fact means and links it back to your reason. A paragraph that pairs every fact with an explanation is far more persuasive than one that just lists facts. Keep your work from this lesson in your writing folder and bring the folder to class.

points.heading: Evidence needs an explanation
points.explanation:
A strong body paragraph follows a chain: claim, reason, evidence, explanation. The claim says what you believe. The reason says why. The evidence is a fact from an article, with the author and the article named. The explanation answers the question “So what?” It says what the evidence means for your reason.

Example. Reason: Later start times really do give students more sleep.
Evidence: In “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later,” Maya Torres reports that Seattle’s public high schools moved their start from 7:50 a.m. to 8:45 a.m. in 2016, and students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights.
Explanation: This shows that when the school day begins later, teenagers use the extra time to sleep, not to stay up later.

Without that last sentence, the reader has numbers but no point. The explanation turns the numbers into support for the reason.

points.heading: Sentence starters and the three moves of a good explanation
points.explanation:
A sentence starter helps you begin an explanation. Useful starters are: This shows that ... / This means that ... / This matters because ... / This suggests that ... / In other words, ...

A good explanation makes three moves. It uses your own words. It says what the evidence means. It links back to your reason.

Example. Reason: A later start can help students learn.
Evidence: Torres reports that in the biology classes the researchers studied in Seattle, grades went up.
Weak: “Grades went up in biology.” This only repeats the evidence.
Weak: “Sleep is good for people.” This is true, but it does not say what the grade result means.
Strong: This suggests that extra sleep may help students learn, at least in the classes the researchers studied.

The strong version begins with a starter, uses new words, and ties the result to the reason about learning. It also says “suggests” and “at least in the classes studied,” because one result from one city does not prove everything. Be careful with a starter like “This proves.” It claims more than the evidence can support.

points.heading: Revising a paragraph that drops evidence
points.explanation:
A weak paragraph drops in facts and moves on. To fix it, find each piece of evidence, mark the spot where an explanation is missing, add the explanation, and then check that the last sentence says something specific.

Suppose a student named Marcus wrote this paragraph:
“A later start would help students get to class. Torres reports that at one Seattle school, fewer students were late or absent from first period after the start time moved. School should start later.”

The evidence is the Seattle result. The missing explanation comes right after it, and the last sentence is too general.

Revision: “A later start would help students get to class. In “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later,” Maya Torres reports that at one Seattle school, fewer students were late or absent from first period after the start time moved. This shows that a later bell lets more students arrive in time for their first lesson. When students are in their seats, they can learn, so a later start gives them a better chance to succeed.”

Now the paragraph names the author and the article, adds an explanation that starts with a starter, and ends by linking back to the reason. Before you finish any paragraph, ask: does my explanation say what the evidence means, and does it link back to my reason?

handouts.key:
Explanation cell: This suggests that a later school start can help teenagers get more of the sleep they need, because the Seattle students gained sleep when their school schedule changed.
Accept explanations that interpret the result and connect it to getting enough sleep. Look for a sentence starter, the writer’s own words, a meaning beyond the reported result, and a link to the reason. All four explanation checks should be yes for this model. Common slips: repeating that students slept longer, writing only that sleep is good, or claiming that Seattle proves every school will get the same result.

handouts.key:
Item 1: This matters because advice from doctors who care for children gives schools a health-based reason to reconsider early start times. Look for a connection between the doctors’ expertise and the reason to start later. Common slip: repeating the recommended start time without explaining why the recommendation matters.
Item 2: This means that moving the high school start later would affect the other schools’ bus trips or require more spending on buses and drivers. Look for an explanation of how shared buses connect school schedules. Common slip: saying only that transportation is a problem.
If you finish early: This shows that an early bedtime may be difficult for teenagers because their bodies begin making them sleepy later in the evening. Look for a connection between the later release of melatonin and difficulty falling asleep early. Common slip: treating the biological shift as laziness or claiming that every teenager falls asleep at 11 p.m.
Partner check: Each explanation should interpret the evidence and connect it to its stated reason. Accept other accurate wording.

blocks.text: Priya is a made-up student. Below is her body paragraph. Underline each piece of evidence. Circle the spot where an explanation is missing. Then rewrite the paragraph in the space below. Priya's paragraph

Schools should start later because students need more sleep. According to Maya Torres in "Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later," the public high schools in Seattle moved their start time from 7:50 a.m. to 8:45 a.m. in 2016. Torres says scientists from the University of Washington found that students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights. Torres also reports that grades went up in the biology classes the researchers studied. Sleep is good for everyone. That is why school should start later.

blocks.hint: Your rewrite of the paragraph

handouts.key:
Underlining: Mark the evidence that Seattle public high schools changed their start from 7:50 a.m. to 8:45 a.m. in 2016; that University of Washington researchers found a little more than half an hour of additional sleep on school nights; and that grades rose in the biology classes studied.
Circling: Mark the gap after the additional-sleep result, before the sentence about biology grades. Also accept marking the gap after the biology-grade evidence, before the vague sentence about sleep.
Sample rewrite: Schools should start later because students need more sleep. According to Maya Torres in “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later,” Seattle public high schools changed their start from 7:50 a.m. to 8:45 a.m. in 2016. This change gave students a later school schedule. Torres, in “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later,” reports that researchers found students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights. This suggests that starting later can help students gain needed sleep instead of simply shifting their bedtime later. Torres, in “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later,” also reports higher grades in the biology classes studied. This suggests that the schedule change may support learning as well as sleep, although this result does not establish what would happen at every school. Seattle’s results give our school a reason to consider a start time that better supports students’ sleep needs.
Look for an explanation after the evidence, a clear link to the sleep reason, and a final sentence that draws the paragraph together. The article should be named with each cited piece of evidence. Accept different accurate rewrites, including ones that omit the biology-grade evidence to keep the paragraph focused on sleep. Common slips: adding only that sleep is important, repeating the sleep result, or claiming that extra sleep definitely caused higher grades.
Partner check: The added reasoning should explain how the Seattle result supports the reason that students need more sleep.

My reason: Teenagers need enough sleep to support their health.
Evidence: Torres, in “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later,” reports that the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends 8 to 10 hours of sleep each night for people ages 13 to 18.
Explanation: This matters because a school schedule should give teenagers a realistic chance to get the amount of sleep experts recommend for their age.
Accept other accurate pairs using evidence not already used during class. Suitable choices include California’s start-time requirements, after-school sports and jobs, and family transportation schedules. Look for evidence that fits the chosen reason, names the author and article, and is followed by an explanation in the student’s own words. Common slips: choosing evidence about a different reason, leaving out the article title, or repeating the evidence as the explanation.
Partner check: For the sample, all three answers are yes: the citation identifies the author and article and supports the reason; the explanation uses a starter and original wording; and it interprets the evidence and links to the reason.
One thing I will fix: Accept a specific revision that fits the student’s writing, such as adding the article title or explaining why the recommended sleep range matters. A student whose pair meets all checks may make the connection more precise.

keyIdeas: A planning organizer lays out the whole essay before drafting: a thesis, three reasons, evidence for each reason with its source named, an explanation for each piece of evidence, and a counterclaim.
Each piece of evidence must back the specific reason it sits under. Evidence that fits a different reason is moved or replaced.
Evidence comes only from the two unit articles, with the article and author named each time. A quotation goes inside quotation marks, and a paraphrase is in your own words.
Every piece of evidence is followed by an explanation that starts with a sentence starter and links back to the reason.
A position can still change while you plan. The thesis in your folder is a starting point.

study.overview: Today you turned your marked-up articles into a planning organizer, a map of your whole essay that you make before you draft. It holds a thesis, three reasons, evidence for each reason, an explanation for each piece of evidence, and a counterclaim. This guide goes over how each part works and gives examples so you can finish your own organizer. Finish any rows you did not complete in class. It is part of Organizer and drafts and is due at the start of next time. Read Daniel Okafor’s “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems” before next time, and bring your organizer in your writing folder.

points.heading: The five parts of a planning organizer
points.explanation: The organizer has five parts, in this order: thesis, three reasons, evidence with its source, an explanation, and a counterclaim. The thesis states your side. Each reason answers the question why. Each piece of evidence backs one reason. Each explanation links that evidence back to the reason. The counterclaim box holds the other side’s strongest point. Your thesis from earlier in the course is only a starting point. You may improve it or switch sides while you plan. Here is a model on a different question, whether schools should offer free breakfast. Thesis: Schools should offer free breakfast because hungry students struggle to focus, a morning meal helps busy families, and free food leaves no student out. Reason 1: Hungry students struggle to focus. Evidence: Suppose a survey of our school found that one in three students says they are too hungry to pay attention in first period. This survey is made up, and it is the only made-up evidence here. Your own evidence must come from the unit articles. Explanation: This shows that hunger keeps many students from paying attention in class, so a morning meal could help them focus. Counterclaim: Free breakfast would cost the school money.

points.heading: Evidence must back the reason it sits under
points.explanation: Evidence is not good just because it comes from the right topic. It has to prove the specific reason in its row. Suppose a student writes the reason “A later start would cause transportation problems.” Under it, the student puts Daniel Okafor’s point that students with part-time jobs would earn less. That is a real point from his article, but it backs a different reason, about after-school activities and jobs. Move it to a row with that reason. Then find evidence that fits buses. Okafor explains that the same buses make several trips each morning: one for the high school, then the middle school, then the elementary schools. That backs the transportation reason. Saying “wrong article” is not enough when you check a row. Say what the evidence shows and what the reason needs. Also, do not use one piece of evidence under two reasons. If it fits only one, move it or replace it.

points.heading: Use only the unit articles, and name them
points.explanation: All your evidence comes from the two unit articles: Maya Torres’s “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later” and Daniel Okafor’s “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems.” Name the article and its author every time you use evidence. You can use evidence in two ways. A quotation uses the writer’s exact words inside quotation marks. For example, Torres ends with “It is time to let us sleep.” A paraphrase says the idea in your own words, with no quotation marks. For example, in “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later,” Maya Torres reports that after Seattle high schools started later, students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights. Copying a sentence without quotation marks is plagiarism, even if you name the article. To avoid it, put exact words in quotation marks. Otherwise, rewrite the idea completely in your own words and check it against the article for accuracy.

points.heading: Explanations and the counterclaim box
points.explanation: Every piece of evidence needs an explanation, because evidence does not argue for itself. Write one short sentence that begins with “This shows that” or “This matters because.” It must use your own words and link back to the reason. In the breakfast model, “Hunger is bad” would be too weak. It repeats a feeling and does not connect the survey to the reason. The model explanation works because it ties the survey result to the reason about focus. For the counterclaim box, write the other side’s strongest point in a few words and name Torres or Okafor. A writer on Torres’s side might note Okafor’s point that districts would need more buses and drivers. A writer on Okafor’s side might note Torres’s Seattle result. Today you only name the counterclaim. Next time you learn to state it fairly and answer it.

Seattle's public high schools moved their start time from 7:50 a.m. to 8:45 a.m. in 2016.
Maya Torres, "Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later"

handouts.key:
Row A
Does the evidence back the reason? No. The evidence shows when Seattle changed its school schedule. It does not show how much sleep teenagers need or whether they get enough. Look for an explanation of this mismatch. Common slip: assuming that a later start automatically proves students slept more.

Rewritten row:
Reason: Teenagers need more sleep than they usually get.
Evidence: Torres reports that the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends 8 to 10 hours of sleep each night for ages 13 to 18. She explains that teenagers’ internal clocks shift later during puberty, making an early bedtime difficult.
Source: Maya Torres, “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later.”
Accept an accurate quotation in quotation marks or a faithful paraphrase of relevant evidence from Torres. Look for evidence about sleep needs and the difficulty of getting enough sleep with an early schedule. Common slip: giving only the Seattle schedule change again.

Row B
Does the evidence back the reason? No. The evidence states teenagers’ sleep needs. It does not explain how a later start would affect buses. Look for a link between the evidence’s subject and the reason’s subject. Common slip: saying only that the source is wrong; Okafor also states the sleep recommendation.

Rewritten row:
Reason: A later start would cause problems with school buses.
Evidence: Okafor explains that many districts use the same buses for several morning trips serving different schools. A later high school start would require changes, such as buying more buses and hiring drivers or moving younger children’s schedules earlier.
Source: Daniel Okafor, “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems.”
Accept an accurate quotation in quotation marks or a faithful paraphrase of Okafor’s transportation argument. Look for an explanation of shared buses and the scheduling problem. Common slip: claiming that every district would have to buy more buses.

handouts.title: Planning organizer
handouts.usedIn: Build your organizer: thesis, reasons, evidence

blocks.text: Use your marked-up articles. Choose one side and build your essay plan here. Keep this sheet in your writing folder.
Thesis

blocks.hint: Write one sentence that states your side on whether school should start later. You may copy your earlier thesis or improve it.

blocks.text: Reasons, evidence and explanations

items: Reason: write three reasons that answer the question why. Each reason needs its own row.
Evidence: add one piece of evidence from your marked-up article under each reason. Use a quotation in quotation marks or a paraphrase. Do not use the same piece of evidence under two reasons.
Source: name the article and the author.
Explanation: write one short sentence that links the evidence back to the reason. Begin with This shows that or This matters because.

blocks.text: Counterclaim

blocks.hint: Write the other side's strongest point in a few words. Name Torres or Okafor.

handouts.key:
Answers vary. Accept either side when the thesis, reasons, evidence and explanations fit together. The following models give answers for every blank. All evidence below is paraphrased.

Model supporting a later start

Thesis: Our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later because the schedule would better fit teenagers’ sleep needs, could help students get more sleep and could support their health.

Reason row A
Reason: An early start conflicts with teenagers’ biological sleep schedules.
Evidence: During puberty, the body releases melatonin later in the evening, so many teenagers do not feel sleepy until around 11 p.m.
Source: Maya Torres, “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later.”
Explanation: This shows that an early bedtime can be difficult for teenagers, so a later start would better fit their sleep schedules.

Reason row B
Reason: Later starts can help students sleep longer.
Evidence: After Seattle’s public high schools changed their start time from 7:50 a.m. to 8:45 a.m., researchers found that students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights.
Source: Maya Torres, “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later.”
Explanation: This shows that a later start can give students additional sleep instead of simply leading them to stay up later.

Reason row C
Reason: More sleep can support students’ health and recovery.
Evidence: Torres explains that sleep helps the body fight illness and helps young athletes recover.
Source: Maya Torres, “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later.”
Explanation: This matters because a schedule that helps students sleep enough could also support their physical health.

Counterclaim: Okafor argues that later starts could disrupt shared bus routes and increase transportation costs.

Model opposing a later start

Thesis: Our school should keep its current start time because a later start could disrupt bus transportation, interfere with after-school responsibilities and create problems for working families.

Reason row A
Reason: A later start could disrupt bus transportation.
Evidence: Many districts use the same buses for several morning trips. Okafor explains that changing high school start times could require additional buses and drivers or earlier schedules for younger children.
Source: Daniel Okafor, “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems.”
Explanation: This matters because changing one school’s schedule could increase costs or shift transportation problems to younger students.

Reason row B
Reason: A later dismissal could interfere with students’ responsibilities after school.
Evidence: Okafor argues that students who care for younger siblings might not get home in time after a later dismissal.
Source: Daniel Okafor, “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems.”
Explanation: This shows that a later school day could make it harder for students to provide care their families depend on.

Reason row C
Reason: A later start could conflict with parents’ work schedules.
Evidence: Some parents currently drop teenagers at school on their way to work; a later start could leave those students needing another ride or staying home alone in the morning.
Source: Daniel Okafor, “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems.”
Explanation: This matters because families could lose a transportation arrangement that fits their work schedules.

Counterclaim: Torres reports that Seattle students slept longer after their schools started later.

What to look for
Thesis: One sentence clearly states a side. Accept a thesis without a list of reasons if its position is clear. Common slip: asking the question instead of answering it.
Reasons: Three distinct answers to why the school should adopt the writer’s position. Common slip: repeating the same reason in different words or giving only a feeling about mornings.
Evidence: Each row contains a different, accurate detail from a unit article that supports that row’s reason. Quotations match the article and use quotation marks; paraphrases use the student’s own wording. Common slips: repeating one piece of evidence across rows, copying without quotation marks or treating a possible outcome as an established local fact.
Source: Every row names both the article and its author. Common slip: writing only an author’s last name or only an article title.
Explanation: Each sentence begins with “This shows that” or “This matters because” and explains how the evidence supports the reason. Common slip: repeating the evidence without explaining the connection.
Counterclaim: A brief, accurate opposing point names Torres or Okafor. Common slip: giving another supporting reason or exaggerating the opposing view.

segments.title: The other side’s best point
segments.description:
Say that “Organizer and drafts: Building the planning organizer” is due now.

segments.title: Stating a counterclaim fairly
segments.description:
Show two versions of Okafor’s transportation point. Students decide with a partner which one Okafor would agree with, and why.
Name the counterclaim as the other side’s strongest point. A fair one passes three tests.

It must be the opponent’s real point, as they would state it, including both options Okafor names: more buses and drivers, or an earlier start for younger children. Support: give a starter to copy.
shown: Version A: Some people are silly to worry about buses when students are too tired to learn.

Version B: Daniel Okafor argues that a later high school start would force districts either to spend more on buses and drivers or to start younger children’s school day earlier, because the same buses make several trips each morning.
Three tests of a fair counterclaim: Is it accurate? Is it calm, with no loaded words? Does it name who holds the view?
Starters: Some people argue that... | Daniel Okafor argues that... | Maya Torres argues that... | A common worry is that...

segments.title: Write your counterclaim
segments.description:
Students write their side, Torres or Okafor, in the box on the sheet.
Students on Torres’s side state Okafor’s transportation point. Students on Okafor’s side state Torres’s Seattle point.
Each writes one or two sentences in fair words, naming the writer.
Partners swap and check the three tests from earlier in the lesson. The teacher hears two.
segments.teacherNotes: Sheet item "Your side (Torres or Okafor)": either answer is fine. Sheet item "State the other side’s point in fair words": Torres side: Daniel Okafor argues that using the same buses for several trips means a later high school start would require extra spending or earlier trips for younger children. Okafor side: Maya Torres argues that later starts help, since Seattle students slept over half an hour longer. Watch for loaded words.

segments.title: How a rebuttal answers
segments.description:
Show the two paragraphs from the articles. Using their marked-up article copies, each student underlines three things in the paragraph that answers their counterclaim: where the writer gives in, the evidence, and the line back to the claim.
Partners compare, then the teacher shows the four steps of a rebuttal.
Point out that evidence has to answer the counterclaim itself, and that this is a strong answer, not proof.
segments.teacherNotes: Torres: gives in at “Those problems are real”; evidence is California; link back is “our school can too.” Explain that this is Torres’s inference: the law shows that schedule changes are possible, but does not show how this school’s bus problems would be solved. Okafor: gives in at “That is a real result”; answer is “one city.” Warn: do not copy these sentences. Paraphrase or quote with marks, naming the author and article title each time.
shown: Torres: “Some people say a later start would cause problems with buses, sports and after-school jobs. Those problems are real, but they can be solved. Districts can change bus routes, and teams can adjust practice times. California has already done it: a state law passed in 2019 requires most public high schools there to start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. and most middle schools no earlier than 8:00 a.m. If a whole state can make the change, our school can too.”

Okafor: “Supporters of later start times point to research. In Seattle, for example, high schools moved their start time almost an hour later in 2016, and researchers found that students there slept about half an hour more on school nights. That is a real result. But it comes from one city with its own buses, budgets and families. A change that worked in Seattle might not work the same way somewhere else.”
Steps: State the other side’s point → Give in to what is true → Answer with evidence, naming the article → Link back to your claim

segments.title: Choose the best rebuttal and fix the weak ones
segments.description:
Give out the sheet “Dana's rebuttals to the bus point”.
Dana is a made-up student on Torres’s side. Four of Dana’s rebuttals to Okafor’s bus point are on the sheet.
Alone, each student picks the strongest and writes one reason. Then each rewrites one weaker one so it answers the point.
Partners compare choices and the teacher hears one fix.
segments.teacherNotes: Strongest: C, though it needs Maya Torres and “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later” named. Add an acknowledgment that bus changes may cost money and a cautious link: “California’s law shows that later schedules are possible, so our school should investigate how to adjust its bus routes.” A: dismisses and has no evidence. B: attacks the writer. D: Seattle shows sleep, not buses, so it is off target. Mistake: rejecting D without explaining that its sleep evidence does not answer the transportation concern.

segments.title: Write your own rebuttal
segments.description:
Give out the sheet “Write your own rebuttal”.
Each student writes a short rebuttal to the counterclaim from earlier. It states the point, gives in to what is true, and answers with evidence from one article, naming the author and article title each time. It ends by linking back to the claim.
Partners check with the three questions on the sheet, and each writer fixes one thing.
Students keep the rebuttal in the writing folder.
segments.teacherNotes: Torres side: use the California law as evidence that later schedules are possible, then explain that local transportation still needs planning. Okafor side: cite the Seattle finding as evidence worth acknowledging, then explain Okafor’s caution that a result from one city does not establish the same outcome everywhere. Name the author and article title in either response. Mistake: “This proves.” Support: starters. Stretch: a second rebuttal to a different counterclaim.

A graded quiz from Short quizzes on the terms of argument (15% of the course grade) is taken then, on what has been taught so far. Students bring the writing folder as always, and the teacher announces anything else.
A short practice quiz on today’s lesson may be taken after class. It counts toward no grade.
Before students leave, tell them that next time they take a graded quiz that counts toward “Short quizzes on the terms of argument”.

keyIdeas: A counterclaim is the strongest point the other side makes. State it fairly and accurately, in calm words, and name the writer who makes it.
A rebuttal answers that specific point. It gives in to what is true, answers with evidence from one of the two articles, and links back to your claim.
Maya Torres and Daniel Okafor each answer the other side in their own articles. Torres answers worries about buses with California. Okafor answers the Seattle result by saying it comes from one city.
A weak rebuttal repeats your claim, attacks the writer, or uses evidence that does not answer the point. Check that your evidence answers the counterclaim itself.

study.overview: A good argument does not ignore the other side. It states the opposing view fairly, then answers it. This guide covers how to write a counterclaim in fair words and how to write a rebuttal that uses evidence from one of the two unit articles. You practiced both with Daniel Okafor’s transportation point and Maya Torres’s reply about California. Keep today’s rebuttal in your writing folder. You will use these skills in your own essay.

points.heading: State the counterclaim fairly
points.explanation:
A counterclaim is the strongest point the other side makes. State it the way that writer would, and name the writer. A fair counterclaim passes three tests: Is it accurate? Is it calm, with no loaded words? Does it name who holds the view?

Compare two versions of Okafor’s transportation point. Version A: “Some people are silly to worry about buses when students are too tired to learn.” It uses the loaded word “silly” and names no one. It also does not say what the worry actually is. Version B: “Daniel Okafor argues that a later high school start would force districts either to spend more on buses and drivers or to start younger children’s school day earlier, because the same buses make several trips each morning.” Version B is accurate, calm and names the writer. It also includes both options Okafor gives. A fair counterclaim is not a weak one. It is the opponent’s real point.

Sentence starters that help: “Some people argue that...”, “Daniel Okafor argues that...”, “Maya Torres argues that...”, “A common worry is that...”

points.heading: The four steps of a rebuttal
points.explanation:
A rebuttal answers one specific point. It follows four steps: state the other side’s point, give in to what is true, answer with evidence and name the article, then link back to your claim.

Torres does this in “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later.” She states the worry (“Some people say a later start would cause problems with buses, sports and after-school jobs”). She gives in with “Those problems are real, but they can be solved.” Her evidence is California, where a 2019 state law requires most public high schools to start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. and most middle schools no earlier than 8:00 a.m. She links back with “If a whole state can make the change, our school can too.”

Okafor does the same in “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems.” He gives in with “That is a real result” about Seattle, then answers that it comes from one city with its own buses, budgets and families.

Notice how strong each answer is. California’s law shows that schedule changes are possible. That is Torres’s inference. The law does not show exactly how this school’s bus problems would be solved. So write that evidence “shows” or “suggests” something. Do not write “This proves.”

points.heading: Spot and fix weak rebuttals
points.explanation:
A weak rebuttal does one of three things. It repeats your claim, it attacks the writer, or it uses evidence that does not answer the point. Always check that your evidence answers the counterclaim itself.

Here are three weak answers to Okafor’s bus point, from a made-up student named Dana, who is on Torres’s side.

“Okafor is wrong about the buses. Schools can figure it out, so this is not a real problem.” This dismisses the worry and gives no evidence.

“Daniel Okafor clearly does not care about teenagers’ health, so nobody should listen to what he says about buses.” This attacks the writer and says nothing about buses.

“In Seattle, high schools moved their start from 7:50 a.m. to 8:45 a.m., and students slept about half an hour longer on school nights. So our school should start later.” The facts are accurate, but they are about sleep, not buses. They are off target for this counterclaim.

To fix a weak answer, find what it is missing. Add a fair statement of the point, give in to what is true, and choose evidence that speaks to the worry.

points.heading: Use the articles honestly
points.explanation:
Your essay may use evidence only from the two unit articles, and you must name the article each time. Name both the author and the title, for example: In “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later,” Maya Torres reports that California passed a law in 2019.

Put ideas in your own words, or copy exact words inside quotation marks. Copying sentences without quotation marks is plagiarism. Do not copy the model paragraphs from Torres or Okafor.

When you write your rebuttal, follow these steps:
1. Write the counterclaim and name the writer.
2. Write what is true in it.
3. Give your evidence and name the article.
4. End with a line that links back to your claim.

Then reread it and ask: does my evidence answer their point?

The homework is a short ungraded step toward Organizer and drafts, called “Answering a counterclaim with a rebuttal.” It is due at the start of next time. Next time you also take a graded quiz on the terms of argument, so review the words counterclaim, rebuttal, evidence and claim. Bring your writing folder.

handouts.title: The other side's best point

blocks.text: Think about Daniel Okafor's article, "A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems." Write one sentence: the strongest point someone on the other side would make against your position.

blocks.hint: Write one sentence. Say which problem or which result you mean.

handouts.key:
Accept either position if the sentence states a specific, fair opposing point.
If the student supports later starts: In “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems,” Daniel Okafor argues that later starts could require districts to pay for more buses and drivers or send younger children to school earlier.
If the student opposes later starts: In “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later,” Maya Torres reports that Seattle students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights after high schools moved their start time later.
Look for a point that challenges the student's position and identifies a particular problem or result. Common slip: saying only that later starts cause problems, without naming a problem.

handouts.title: Write your counterclaim

blocks.text: If you are on Maya Torres's side, state Daniel Okafor's transportation point. If you are on Daniel Okafor's side, state Maya Torres's Seattle point. Write one or two sentences and name the writer.

blocks.hint: State the other side's point in fair words, as that writer would state it.

handouts.key:
Your side (Torres or Okafor): Accept either Torres or Okafor.
State the other side's point in fair words:
For Torres: In “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems,” Daniel Okafor explains that districts reuse buses for several morning trips. Moving high school later could require more buses and drivers or earlier starts for younger children.
For Okafor: In “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later,” Maya Torres reports that Seattle students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights after their high schools started later.
Look for the opposing writer's actual point, neutral language, and enough detail to preserve the reasoning or result. For the transportation point, include both options: additional buses and drivers, or earlier starts for younger children. Common slips: stating the student's own side, calling the opposing view silly, or claiming every Seattle student benefited.

handouts.title: Dana's rebuttals to the bus point
handouts.usedIn: Choose the best rebuttal and fix the weak ones

blocks.text: Dana is a made-up student on Maya Torres's side. Below are four rebuttals Dana wrote to Daniel Okafor's point about buses. Read all four. Then work alone.
Four rebuttals by Dana

rows: Okafor is wrong about the buses. Schools can figure it out, so this is not a real problem.
Daniel Okafor clearly does not care about teenagers' health, so nobody should listen to what he says about buses.

Changing bus routes is a concern, but it is one that can be solved. California has a law that requires most public high schools to start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. If a whole state can make this change, our school can too.

Later start times help students sleep. In Seattle, high schools moved their start from 7:50 a.m. to 8:45 a.m., and students slept about half an hour longer on school nights. So our school should start later.

blocks.text: Part 1: Pick the strongest

blocks.label: The strongest rebuttal is (A, B, C or D)

blocks.hint: Write one reason it is the strongest.

blocks.text: Part 2: Fix a weaker one

blocks.label: The rebuttal I am rewriting (A, B or D)

blocks.hint: Rewrite it so it answers Okafor's point about buses.

handouts.key:
Part 1: Pick the strongest
The strongest rebuttal is: C.
Reason: C acknowledges the transportation concern and uses California's law as relevant evidence that later schedules can be put into practice. Its conclusion still needs caution: the law does not establish how this school's transportation problems would be solved. The evidence also needs Maya Torres and “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later” named.
A dismisses the concern without evidence. B attacks Okafor's character instead of answering his transportation argument. D gives evidence about sleep benefits, which does not answer the concern about buses and costs.
Part 2: Fix a weaker one
The rebuttal I am rewriting: Accept A, B, or D.
Possible rewrite for any choice: Daniel Okafor explains in “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems” that a later start could require more buses and drivers or earlier starts for younger children. These changes could cost money or burden families. However, Maya Torres reports in “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later” that California's law requires most public high schools to start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. and most middle schools no earlier than 8:00 a.m. This shows that later schedules are possible, so our school should investigate how to adjust transportation before making the change.
Look for acknowledgment of the bus concern, relevant article evidence, attribution, and an explanation that supports the claim without promising an easy solution. Common slip: adding more Seattle sleep evidence without addressing transportation.

handouts.title: Write your own rebuttal

blocks.text: Write a short rebuttal to the counterclaim you stated earlier. State the other side's point, give in to what is true, and answer with evidence from one article. Name the author and the article title each time you use the article. End by linking back to your claim. Put your own words in your sentences, or use quotation marks for exact words. Keep this sheet in your writing folder.
Sentence starters you may use

items: Some people argue that ___.
It is true that ___.
However, ___ shows that ___.
In "___," ___ reports that ___.
For this reason, our school should ___.

blocks.hint: Write your rebuttal here.

handouts.key:
Accept either position. The completed response should state the counterclaim fairly, acknowledge what is valid, answer it with relevant article evidence, name the author and article title each time an article is used, and connect the answer to the student's claim. The sentence starters are optional.
Possible response supporting Torres: In “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems,” Daniel Okafor argues that later starts could require more buses and drivers or earlier starts for younger children. Those are real costs and scheduling concerns. However, Maya Torres reports in “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later” that California's law requires most public high schools to start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. and most middle schools no earlier than 8:00 a.m. The law shows that later schedules are possible, although it does not solve our school's bus problems. Our school should pursue a later start while planning how to manage transportation.
Possible response supporting Okafor: In “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later,” Maya Torres reports that Seattle students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights after their high schools started later. That benefit deserves serious attention. However, Daniel Okafor explains in “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems” that Seattle's result comes from one city with its own buses, budgets, and families. The finding supports a possible benefit, but it does not establish that our school would have the same outcome. Our school should examine local transportation and family needs before changing its schedule.
Look for reasoning that answers the specific counterclaim. For the Okafor position, acknowledge the Seattle finding accurately and explain the limit on applying it elsewhere. Common slips: saying California proves local bus problems are solved, saying Seattle's result is worthless, using unrelated evidence, or copying article wording without quotation marks.

segments.title: Anatomy of a model body paragraph
segments.description:
Say once that the survey in today’s models is made up for practice. Show the unlabeled breakfast paragraph and read it aloud.
In pairs, students jot the job of each sentence in a few words. Then the teacher shows the four parts and labels each sentence.
Point out that the source is named in the evidence sentence and that the last sentence links back to the reason.
segments.teacherNotes: Answers: sentence 1 topic sentence (the reason); 2 evidence with source named; 3 explanation (reasoning); 4 link back. Common mistake: calling sentence 1 evidence. segments.teacherNotes: Answers: 1 topic sentence (given); 2 evidence (teacher survey named); 3 explanation; 4 link back. Mistake: labeling sentence 3 as evidence because it mentions focus. Ask which sentence tells what the survey means. Support: sentence starters can mark the explanation.

segments.title: Choose the better topic sentence, then make your own
segments.description:
Give out the sheet “Choose the better topic sentence, then make your own”.
Show a library paragraph with its evidence and explanation and two possible topic sentences. Alone, each student picks the better one and writes one sentence on why.
Partners compare, and the teacher hears one reason for the choice.
Then each student writes their own topic sentence and one made-up line of evidence (starting “Suppose”) for the recess paragraph, on a reason different from concentration.
segments.teacherNotes: Answer: B. A repeats the claim and names no reason; B states one reason the evidence backs. Mistake: picking A because it sounds strong. Sample own answer: “Third, recess would lift students’ mood.” Evidence must back that reason. Stretch: write the explanation too.

A short practice quiz on today’s lesson may be taken after class. It counts toward no grade.

keyIdeas: A body paragraph proves one reason. It is built from a topic sentence, evidence with its source named, an explanation, and a line that links back to the claim.

Reasoning is the explanation that tells the reader what the evidence means for the claim, in the writer’s own words.

study.overview: A strong body paragraph proves one reason for your claim, and every sentence in it has a job. This guide goes back over the four parts of a model body paragraph, the difference between a topic sentence and evidence, what reasoning is, and how a counterclaim and a rebuttal work. The examples use a made-up claim about free breakfast at school. The survey in them is invented for practice and is not real data. When you write your own essay, your evidence comes only from the two unit articles, with the article named each time.

points.heading: A body paragraph has four parts
points.explanation:
A body paragraph proves one reason. It is built from a topic sentence, evidence with its source named, an explanation, and a link back to the claim. Here is the model paragraph again, with each sentence labeled.

Topic sentence: First, free breakfast would help students pay attention in class.
Evidence with source named: In the Student Council survey, 40 of 100 students who skipped breakfast said they felt too hungry to focus before lunch.
Explanation: This matters because a student who cannot focus in first period misses the lesson that later classes build on.
Link back: For this reason, free breakfast would make learning easier for hungry students.

Notice that the evidence sentence names where the information came from. Notice too that the last sentence returns to the reason from the first sentence. When you label a paragraph, ask what job each sentence does. Do not label by topic words alone.

points.heading: The topic sentence states the reason
points.explanation:
The topic sentence tells the reader the one reason this paragraph will prove. It does not repeat the whole claim, and it is not a piece of evidence. Suppose the claim is that the school should offer free breakfast.

Too broad: Our school should definitely offer free breakfast because it is a great idea. This repeats the claim and names no reason.
A piece of evidence: 40 of 100 students who skipped breakfast felt too hungry to focus. This is information, not a reason.
A topic sentence: First, free breakfast would help students pay attention in class. This states one reason, and evidence can back it.

A quick test is to ask whether the sentence says why the claim is true or only supplies a fact. If it says why, it is the topic sentence. If it supplies a fact, it is evidence.

points.heading: Reasoning explains what the evidence means
points.explanation:
Reasoning is the explanation that tells the reader what the evidence means for the claim, in your own words. Evidence alone does not finish the job, because the reader still has to guess why it matters. In the breakfast paragraph, the explanation sentence is the reasoning: it says that a student who cannot focus in first period misses the lesson that later classes build on.

A weak explanation only repeats the evidence: Many students said they felt too hungry to focus. A strong explanation answers the question so what? It connects the fact to the reason. Try starting with This matters because or This shows that, then finish the thought in your own words.

points.heading: A counterclaim and its rebuttal
points.explanation:
A counterclaim is the other side’s strongest point, stated fairly. A rebuttal answers it with evidence and links back to your claim. Do not make the other side sound silly, because a fair counterclaim makes your rebuttal more convincing.

Example for the breakfast claim:
Counterclaim: Some people worry that serving breakfast would take time away from class.
Rebuttal: Suppose the cafeteria staff found that breakfast can be served in the ten minutes before the first bell. Then no class time would be lost, and students could still eat before learning begins. Free breakfast remains a good choice for our school.

The example evidence starts with Suppose because it is made up. Real evidence in your essay will come from the unit articles. The rebuttal does three things. It names the worry, answers it with evidence, and ends by returning to the claim.

blocks.text: Read the paragraph below. Sentence 1 is already labeled. Label sentences 2, 3 and 4 on your own. Use only the four labels shown. The survey in this paragraph is made up for practice.
The four labels

items: Topic sentence
Evidence
Explanation
Link back

rows: Second, a short break between classes would help students focus.
Suppose a survey of teachers at our school found that 18 of 24 teachers said students seemed more alert after a five-minute break.
When students move and rest for a few minutes, their minds reset, so they can pay attention to the next lesson.
A short break between classes therefore helps students focus.
blocks.caption: A body paragraph on the claim that students need a short break between classes

handouts.key:
Sentence 1: Topic sentence (already given). It states the reason: a short break would help students focus.
Sentence 2: Evidence. The hypothetical teacher survey supplies information supporting the reason and names its source.
Sentence 3: Explanation. It explains how movement and rest could help students pay attention. Common slip: calling this evidence because it mentions focus. It interprets the evidence rather than reporting another survey result.
Sentence 4: Link back. It connects the paragraph to the reason that short breaks help students focus.

blocks.text: Part 1. Read the library paragraph. Its topic sentence is missing. The evidence is a made-up survey, used for practice.
Library paragraph

items: Topic sentence: A or B, see below.
Suppose a survey of students at our school found that 40 of the 60 students who use the library after school finished their homework there.
This shows that a quiet room with books and computers lets students finish work they might not finish at home.

blocks.text: Two possible topic sentences

items: A: Our school library should definitely stay open after school because it is a great idea.
B: Keeping the library open after school would give students a quiet place to finish their homework.

blocks.hint: Which topic sentence is better, A or B? Write one sentence on why.

blocks.text: Part 2. Your own paragraph

Claim: Our school should add a daily recess for eighth graders. The first reason, that recess helps students concentrate, is already taken. Choose a different reason. Write a topic sentence for it, then one made-up line of evidence that backs your reason. Start the evidence with the word Suppose.

blocks.hint: Your topic sentence
One made-up line of evidence, starting Suppose

handouts.key:
Part 1: B. Sample explanation: B gives a specific reason for keeping the library open—a quiet place to finish homework—and the survey supports that reason. Accept answers that connect B's reason to students finishing homework in the library. Common slip: choosing A because it sounds confident; A repeats the claim without a specific supporting reason.
Part 2, topic sentence: Answers vary. Sample: Third, daily recess would give eighth graders more chances to build friendships. Look for a clear reason supporting daily recess that differs from concentration.
Part 2, evidence: Answers vary. Sample: Suppose a survey of eighth graders at our school found that 36 of 48 students said playing games during recess helped them get to know classmates. Look for a hypothetical statement beginning with Suppose that supplies specific evidence for the student's chosen reason. Common slips: repeating the reason without supporting information, using concentration again, or giving evidence about a different benefit.

l_1fe7b4080db6.title: Introductions and conclusions that work
l_1fe7b4080db6.summary: Students study model introductions and conclusions, then practice a hook, background sentences, a thesis, and a closing that goes beyond repeating the claim.

segments.title: Which opening keeps you reading?
segments.description:
Say that last time students labeled the parts of a body paragraph, and today they build the first and last paragraphs.
Show two openings for a made-up essay. Each student picks one and writes a few words on why, in about one minute.
Partners tell each other their pick, one minute each way. The teacher hears two picks.
segments.teacherNotes: Expect B: it puts the reader in a scene, while A only announces the topic. Accept a short phrase such as “it puts me in a scene”. Do not name the word hook yet; the next segment does. Students have their writing folders out.
shown: A: This essay is about lunch at Maple Street Middle School.
B: The bell rings, and you have taken only two bites of your sandwich.
Which opening makes you want to keep reading? Write a few words on why.

segments.title: Anatomy of a model introduction
segments.description:
Give out the sheet “Model introduction and conclusion: a longer lunch at Maple Street Middle School”.
Say once that Maple Street Middle School is made up. Show its model introduction unlabeled and read it aloud.
In pairs, students jot the job of each sentence in a few words.
The teacher labels the sentences as hook, background and thesis, and shows the three steps.
Show how Maya Torres and Daniel Okafor open their articles. Name three kinds of hook: a scene, a question and a bold statement.
segments.teacherNotes: Answers: sentence 1 hook; 2 and 3 background; 4 thesis with position, because and three reasons. Mistakes: calling the thesis the hook, or developing a full evidence-and-explanation argument in the background. Hooks use no invented numbers. Prepare copies of “Model introduction and conclusion: a longer lunch at Maple Street Middle School”, which holds both models.

segments.title: A conclusion that does more than repeat
segments.description:
Ask: besides saying the claim again, what else should a last paragraph do? Each student writes a guess and tells a partner.
Show the Maple Street conclusion and label its three jobs.
Show how Torres and Okafor end their articles. Set the rule: no new evidence in a conclusion.
segments.teacherNotes: Answers: sentence 1 restates the claim in new words; 2 says why it matters; 3 is a call to act naming who and what. Torres ends with a call to act; Okafor ends with a standard for a good solution. Mistake: copying the thesis word for word.
shown: What else should a last paragraph do besides say the claim again?
1. In short, a longer lunch would give Maple Street students time to eat well, to rest and to be with friends.
2. Students who are fed and rested are ready to learn, and that helps the whole school.
3. The principal should add 15 minutes to lunch before the next school year begins.
Steps: restate the claim in new words → say why it matters → call to act: who should do what
Torres ends “Let Us Sleep”: “It is time to let us sleep.”
Okafor ends “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems”: “A good solution should not create as many problems as it solves.”

segments.title: Fix Riley’s introduction and conclusion
segments.description:
Give out the sheet “Fix Riley’s introduction and conclusion”.
Riley is a made-up student who wrote about the same lunch topic. Show Riley’s introduction and conclusion.
Alone, each student finds the biggest problem in each paragraph and rewrites one sentence in each to fix it.
Partners compare their fixes. The teacher hears one fix for each paragraph.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and answers:
Intro 1: announces the topic, no hook. Open with a scene or question.
Intro 2: a definition says nothing useful. Name the issue.
Intro 3: position, but no because or reasons. Add three reasons.
Conclusion 1: copies the claim. Restate in new words.
Conclusion 2: vague, repeats. Say why it matters.
Conclusion 3: an unsupported survey claim and new evidence. Cut it; moving it to a body paragraph would not make it valid evidence.
Conclusion 4: no call to act. Say who should do what.
Mistake: fixing only wording, not the job.

vocabulary.definition: The first paragraph of an essay. It has a hook, background sentences and a thesis.
The opening sentence that grabs the reader, such as a scene, a question or a bold statement.
One or two sentences after the hook that tell the reader what the issue is and why it matters.
The last paragraph of an essay. It restates the claim, says why it matters and ends with a call to act.
To say your claim again in new words, not copied from your thesis.
A closing sentence that says who should do what, so the reader knows the next step.
