study.overview: The first and last paragraphs of an argumentative essay each have clear jobs. An introduction pulls the reader in, explains the issue and states your position with its reasons. A conclusion says the claim again in new words, tells the reader why it matters and asks someone to act. This guide uses the made-up Maple Street Middle School lunch essay and a made-up student, Riley, so you can see each job done well and done badly.

points.heading: An introduction has three jobs
points.explanation:
Every introduction needs a hook, background sentences and a thesis, in that order. The hook grabs the reader. The background tells the reader what the issue is and why it matters, and it leads to the thesis. The thesis gives your position, the word because, and your three reasons.

Example from the Maple Street model (the school is made up). Sentence 1, the hook: “When the lunch bell rings, Dani has taken one bite of her sandwich, and the line for the microwave still stretches out the cafeteria door.” Sentences 2 and 3, the background: “At Maple Street Middle School, lunch is 20 minutes long, and that includes the time spent waiting in line. Many students end up eating in a rush or leaving food on their trays.” Sentence 4, the thesis: “Maple Street Middle School should lengthen lunch to 30 minutes because a longer lunch lets students finish a full meal, gives their minds a break, and helps them focus in afternoon classes.” The position is the first part, because comes next, and then come three reasons.

Keep the background short. Save detailed evidence and its explanation for the body paragraphs. One brief fact is fine if you name where it comes from. For the start-time essay, you could write that Daniel Okafor, in “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems,” says teenagers need 8 to 10 hours of sleep a night and many get far less.

points.heading: Choose a hook that puts the reader in the moment
points.explanation:
A hook can be a scene, a question or a bold statement. It should never announce the topic. A sentence like “In this essay, I am going to write about lunch at our school” tells the reader nothing to care about. Compare it with the Dani scene above, which makes you picture the problem.

Three kinds, with examples about the Maple Street topic:
- Scene: a small moment the reader can picture, like Dani and her one bite of sandwich.
- Question: “Have you ever stood in a lunch line so long that the bell rang before you sat down?”
- Bold statement: “A rushed lunch is a wasted lunch.”

Professional writers use the same moves. Maya Torres opens “Let Us Sleep” with a scene: “Every school morning, millions of teenagers drag themselves out of bed before the sun is up.” Okafor opens with a bold statement: “Nobody wants exhausted students.”

A hook should not use invented numbers or claims about your own school. If you are stuck, start with “Imagine…” or “Have you ever…?” Try two hooks of different kinds and keep the stronger one.

points.heading: A conclusion does more than repeat
points.explanation:
A strong conclusion does three things: it restates the claim in new words, says why the issue matters, and ends with a call to act that names who should do what. It adds no new evidence. A new fact at the end has no explanation behind it, and it belongs in a body paragraph if it belongs anywhere.

The Maple Street conclusion shows all three jobs:
1. “A 30-minute lunch would give Maple Street students the time they need to eat well and recharge.” This restates the claim in new words. It does not copy the thesis.
2. “Students who are fed and rested can give their full attention to every class that follows.” This says why it matters.
3. “The principal and the student council should work together to add ten minutes to the lunch period starting next semester.” This is a call to act. It names who (the principal and the student council) and what (add ten minutes to lunch).

The articles end in different ways. Torres closes with a call to act: “It is time to let us sleep.” Okafor closes with a standard for a good solution: “A good solution should not create as many problems as it solves.” For your own essay, make the ending name who should do what.

points.heading: Fix the job, not just the wording
points.explanation:
When you revise an opening or an ending, ask which job is missing. Changing a few words will not fix a paragraph that skips a job.

Riley, a made-up student, wrote about the same lunch topic. Riley’s introduction begins “In this essay, I am going to write about lunch at our school.” That sentence announces the topic and has no hook. A better first sentence puts the reader in a scene or asks a question. Riley’s thesis, “Maple Street Middle School should make lunch longer,” gives a position but no because and no reasons. The fix is to add three reasons.

Riley’s conclusion has its own problems. It says “A survey found that most students at Maple Street skip lunch because it is too short.” That is new evidence, and nothing supports it. The fix is to cut it. Moving it to a body paragraph would not make it valid evidence, because essays use evidence only from the two unit articles. Riley’s last sentence, “That is why I think lunch should be longer,” also never says who should act. Replace it with a sentence that names who should do what.

Before you finish, check your opening for a hook, background and a thesis with a position, because and three reasons. Check your ending for new wording, why it matters, a call to act and no new evidence.

handouts.title: Model introduction and conclusion: a longer lunch at Maple Street Middle School

blocks.text: Maple Street Middle School is made up. This essay argues that its lunch period should be longer. Read the introduction and the conclusion. Each is one paragraph, and each sentence is listed in order.
Introduction

items: When the lunch bell rings, Dani has taken one bite of her sandwich, and the line for the microwave still stretches out the cafeteria door.
At Maple Street Middle School, lunch is 20 minutes long, and that includes the time spent waiting in line.
Many students end up eating in a rush or leaving food on their trays.
Maple Street Middle School should lengthen lunch to 30 minutes because a longer lunch lets students finish a full meal, gives their minds a break, and helps them focus in afternoon classes.

blocks.text: Conclusion

items: A 30-minute lunch would give Maple Street students the time they need to eat well and recharge.
Students who are fed and rested can give their full attention to every class that follows.
The principal and the student council should work together to add ten minutes to the lunch period starting next semester.

handouts.title: Fix Riley’s introduction and conclusion

blocks.text: Riley is a made-up student who wrote about the same lunch topic as the Maple Street models. Read each of Riley's paragraphs. Work alone.
Riley's introduction

items: In this essay, I am going to write about lunch at our school.
Lunch is the meal that people eat in the middle of the day.
Maple Street Middle School should make lunch longer.

blocks.hint: What is the biggest problem in this introduction? Answer in a sentence.
Rewrite one sentence of the introduction to fix that problem.

blocks.text: Riley's conclusion

items: Maple Street Middle School should make lunch longer.
A longer lunch is a good idea, and it would be good for everyone.
A survey found that most students at Maple Street skip lunch because it is too short.
That is why I think lunch should be longer.

blocks.hint: What is the biggest problem in this conclusion? Answer in a sentence.
Rewrite one sentence of the conclusion to fix that problem.

handouts.key:
Introduction—biggest problem: Accept a specific problem with a sentence’s job: the opening announces the topic instead of drawing readers in; the definition gives no useful background; or the claim lacks reasons. Sample answer: “The introduction states a position but gives no reasons for it.”
Introduction—rewrite: Match the revision to the problem identified. Sample: “Maple Street Middle School should lengthen lunch to 30 minutes because students need time to finish their meals, rest their minds, and prepare for afternoon classes.” For the opening, accept a scene or question such as “Have you ever had to stop eating because the lunch bell rang?” For background, accept “Maple Street’s lunch period lasts 20 minutes, including time spent waiting in line.” Look for a sentence that performs its intended job. Common slip: changing a few words without fixing the missing job.
Conclusion—biggest problem: The survey claim is unsupported and introduces new evidence. Sample answer: “Riley introduces a survey without support, and a conclusion should not add new evidence.” Also accept a precise explanation that the paragraph repeats the claim, gives only a vague statement of importance, or lacks a call to act.
Conclusion—rewrite: Match the revision to the problem identified. To replace the survey sentence, accept “The principal and student council should work together to extend lunch to 30 minutes.” This removes the unsupported claim and supplies a call to act. To restate the claim, accept “Students at Maple Street need more time to eat and recharge.” To explain importance, accept “Time to eat and take a break helps students return to class ready to focus.” To replace the final sentence, accept a call naming the principal and student council and a specific action. Look for a substantive fix. Common slips: treating the survey as established evidence, moving it to a body paragraph, or saying “Something should change” without naming who should act.

handouts.title: Write your hook, background and thesis
handouts.usedIn: Write your hook, background and thesis

blocks.text: You are writing the opening of your start-time essay. You may change your side or your reasons from the organizer. Use no made-up numbers and make no claims about our school.
Two hooks
Write two hooks of different kinds: a scene, a question or a bold statement. Name the kind, then write the hook. If you need a start, try "Imagine…" or "Have you ever…?". Then circle the better hook.

blocks.hint: Hook 1: kind and sentence
Hook 2: kind and sentence

blocks.text: Background

blocks.hint: Write one or two sentences. Any fact must come from one of the two articles, and you must name that article.

blocks.text: Thesis
Take your thesis from your writing folder. Check that it has all three parts below. Then write an improved thesis.

items: A position on whether school should start later
The word because
Three reasons

blocks.hint: My improved thesis

blocks.text: Partner check
Trade sheets. Your partner reads your opening and points to the hook, the position and each reason.

handouts.key:
Hook 1—kind and sentence: Sample: “Scene: Imagine trying to follow a classroom discussion while struggling to keep your eyes open.” Look for a clear imagined scene, a relevant question, or a supportable bold statement, correctly labeled. Common slip: presenting an invented event at our school as fact.
Hook 2—kind and sentence: Sample: “Question: How can students focus on learning when they struggle to stay awake?” The kind must differ from the first hook. Accept either hook being circled if it draws readers into the start-time issue. Common slip: writing two questions and labeling one a scene.
Background: Sample: “In Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later, Maya Torres explains that teenagers need 8 to 10 hours of sleep each night. Daniel Okafor’s A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems raises concerns about transportation and family schedules.” Look for one or two relevant sentences that name the article supporting each fact. Accept background drawn from either article. Common slips: omitting the article’s title, inventing local facts, or developing a full body-paragraph argument.
My improved thesis: Sample supporting a later start: “Our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later because the change could help teenagers get enough sleep, improve their learning, and support their health.” Sample opposing a change: “Our school should keep its current start time because a later start could complicate bus schedules, interfere with after-school responsibilities, and disrupt family routines.” Look for a clear position, the word because, and three identifiable reasons supported by the unit articles. Common slips: giving only a topic, listing fewer than three reasons, or making unsupported guarantees.
Partner check: In the supporting sample, the position is that school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later; the reasons concern sleep, learning, and health. In the opposing sample, the position is to keep the current start time; the reasons concern buses, after-school responsibilities, and family routines. The hook is the selected scene or question. Accept accurate identification of these parts in the student’s own opening.

handouts.title: Write your conclusion

blocks.text: Write a three-sentence conclusion for your start-time essay. Write it without looking at the Maple Street model.

blocks.hint: Sentence 1: restate your claim in new words.
Sentence 2: say why it matters.
Sentence 3: end with a call to act.

blocks.text: Partner check
Trade sheets. Your partner checks two things and tells you what they find.

items: The conclusion adds no new evidence.
The call to act names who should do what.

handouts.key:
Sentence 1—restate the claim: Supporting sample: “A later first bell would give students a schedule that better supports their need for sleep.” Opposing sample: “Keeping the current start time while addressing sleep habits is the better choice for our school.” Look for the essay’s position expressed in fresh wording. Common slip: copying the thesis word for word.
Sentence 2—say why it matters: Supporting sample: “Helping students arrive rested supports their ability to learn and stay healthy.” Opposing sample: “Students need support for healthy sleep that also respects their families’ daily responsibilities.” Look for the significance of reasons already developed in the essay. Common slip: introducing a new fact or repeating that the proposal is a good idea without explaining why.
Sentence 3—call to act: Supporting sample: “The school board should set the first bell at 8:30 a.m. or later.” Opposing sample: “Before changing the schedule, school leaders should provide sleep lessons, teachers should limit late-night homework, and families should set nighttime screen limits.” Look for a named person or group and a concrete action consistent with the claim. Common slip: “We should do something” without a specific action.
Partner check—no new evidence: The conclusion should contain no new statistics, studies, survey claims, or other supporting evidence. Statements about importance should build on the essay’s existing reasoning.
Partner check—who should do what: In the supporting sample, the school board should set the first bell at 8:30 a.m. or later. In the opposing sample, school leaders should provide sleep lessons, teachers should limit late-night homework, and families should set nighttime screen limits before a schedule change. Accept other clear, relevant calls to act supported by the student’s argument.

ready: Teacher: the two unit articles, "Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later" by Maya Torres and "A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems" by Daniel Okafor, to show how each opens and ends
Students: the writing folder, with the organizer and the thesis in it

l_0fd524224099.title: Drafting the body paragraphs in class
l_0fd524224099.summary: Students use their organizers to draft three reason paragraphs and the counterclaim paragraph, and the final essay is set.

segments.title: Folders out: your introduction and conclusion practice is due now
segments.description:
Say that “Introduction and conclusion practice” is due now.
Students take out their writing folders and put that practice on the desk beside their organizer.
Each student reads the thesis in the folder and writes its three reasons as short labels, in the order they will draft them.
Each student tells a partner in one sentence which reason has the strongest evidence, and the teacher hears one.
segments.teacherNotes: Do not collect or grade anything now. Expect labels such as sleep, learning and health, or buses, after-school activities and family schedules. A student without the organizer drafts from the thesis and the articles.
shown: Write the three reasons from your thesis as short labels, in the order you will draft them. Then tell a partner in one sentence which reason has your strongest evidence.

segments.title: Draft the three reason paragraphs
segments.description:
Hand out copies of “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later” by Maya Torres and “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems” by Daniel Okafor, and the “Reason paragraph draft” sheet.
The sheet has the four parts of a reason paragraph. Using the organizer, each student drafts reasons 1 and 2 on the sheet, then reason 3 on their own paper with the same four parts.
Copied words go inside quotation marks, and every piece of evidence names its article and author.
Call time at about five minutes for each paragraph. Walk the room, and have each student answer the three check questions on the sheet before moving on.
segments.teacherNotes: Check questions, each answered yes: 1 article and author named in the evidence; 2 copied words inside quotation marks; 3 explanation follows the evidence and ties it to the reason. Mistakes: topic sentence repeating the whole thesis; no article named; no explanation. Support: “This shows that”, “This matters because”. Stretch: a second piece of evidence. Unfinished paragraphs wait until next time.

segments.title: Anatomy of a counterclaim paragraph
segments.description:
Say once that the Maple Street paragraph, its writers and its articles are made up for practice.
Show the paragraph and read it aloud.
In pairs, students jot the job of each of the five sentences in a few words.
Label the sentences on the board, and point to the writer’s name, the place where the writer gives in, and the evidence.
segments.teacherNotes: Answers: 1 counterclaim with the writer named; 2 gives in to what is true; 3 rebuttal evidence with its source; 4 explanation; 5 link back. Mistakes: thinking the give-in weakens the essay; stating the other side unfairly. Point out that the evidence measures the effect of a longer lunch, and that sentence 4 compares time lost and regained across the same day.
shown: 1. Dana Ruiz, in her made-up article “Keep the Bell Schedule,” argues that a longer lunch would take five minutes of class time from the school day.
2. That concern is fair, because less class time means less time to practice.

3. However, Marcus Bell reports in his made-up article “Lost in the Lunch Line” that when one school added five minutes to its lunch, the time teachers spent settling hungry, restless students fell from about ten minutes to about four minutes in each of the two afternoon classes.
4. This shows that a longer lunch can win back class time: the two afternoon classes together regained about twelve minutes, which is more than the five minutes the lunch takes from the day.
5. Five minutes of class time is a small price for a lunch that sets students up to learn.

segments.title: Turn the case around
segments.description:
Give out the sheet “Turn the case around”.
The Maple Street essay now argues against a longer lunch, so Marcus Bell’s point becomes its counterclaim.
The sheet has the prompt. Alone, each student writes two sentences: one that states Bell’s point fairly, naming him and his article, and one that gives in to what is true.
Partners read each other’s sentences and check that Bell and his article are named and that the concession acknowledges his point fairly.
The teacher hears two pairs.
segments.teacherNotes: Sample: “Marcus Bell, in his made-up article “Lost in the Lunch Line,” argues that teachers spend about ten minutes of each afternoon class settling hungry, restless students. That is true, and hungry students cannot focus.” Mistakes: loaded words like “complains”; no give-in; naming Ruiz. Possible answer: Ruiz’s evidence suggests that a second serving window could reduce the wait. Maple Street should investigate whether that change would give students enough time to eat before taking time from classes.

segments.title: Draft your counterclaim paragraph
segments.description:
Give out the sheet “Counterclaim paragraph steps”.
The sheet has the four steps of the paragraph.
Each student takes the counterclaim box from the organizer and drafts it as the closing part of the reason paragraph it fits best, so the essay keeps three body paragraphs.
The rebuttal uses evidence from one of the two articles, named with its author, and the last sentence links back to the student’s claim.
Partners read each other’s counterclaim and rebuttal and point to the writer’s name, the give-in, the evidence and the link back.
segments.teacherNotes: Mistakes: a rebuttal that repeats the claim; evidence that does not answer the counterclaim; a loaded word for the other writer. Support: start with “Daniel Okafor argues that” or “Maya Torres argues that”. Check that every student explains how the rebuttal evidence answers the counterclaim before linking back to the claim. Students who finish may mark where the counterclaim sits in the reason paragraph.

segments.title: Before you leave: the final essay is set
segments.description:
Set the homework: “Final essay”, worth 60% of the course grade. Write its name and due time on the board: due at the start of the class on Review of argument terms and a final quiz; essays handed in.
Tell students what to expect next time: they finish a full draft in class and add transitions such as “First,” “In addition,” and “However,” between paragraphs.
Students keep their paragraphs, organizer and articles in the writing folder and bring the folder.
A short practice quiz on today’s lesson may be taken after class. It counts toward no grade.
segments.teacherNotes: Say the deadline in the words on the board. Remind students that the introduction and conclusion from earlier in the course go in the folder too, so the full draft can be put together next time.

keyIdeas: A reason paragraph proves one reason from the thesis. It has a topic sentence, evidence with the article and author named, an explanation, and a line that links back to the claim.

slides.title: Drafting the body paragraphs
bullets: Three reason paragraphs and a counterclaim paragraph
slides.notes: Welcome students. Today they turn the organizer into sentences: three reason paragraphs, then the counterclaim and rebuttal. Near the end the final essay is set. Students need their writing folders, which hold the organizer, drafts and articles.

slides.title: Folders out
bullets: Write the three reasons from your thesis as short labels, in the order you will draft them. Then tell a partner in one sentence which reason has your strongest evidence.
slides.notes: Say that “Introduction and conclusion practice” is due now. Students take out their writing folders and put that practice on the desk beside their organizer. Do not collect or grade anything now. Each student reads the thesis in the folder and writes its three reasons as short labels. Then each tells a partner in one sentence which reason has the strongest evidence. Hear one answer from the room. Expect labels such as sleep, learning and health, or buses, after-school activities and family schedules. A student without the organizer drafts from the thesis and the articles.

slides.title: Four parts of a reason paragraph
bullets: Does the evidence name its article and author?
Are all copied words inside quotation marks?
Does it explain how the evidence supports the reason?
slides.notes: Hand out copies of “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later” by Maya Torres and “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems” by Daniel Okafor, and the “Reason paragraph draft” sheet. Using the organizer, each student drafts reasons 1 and 2 on the sheet, then reason 3 on their own paper with the same four parts. Call time at about five minutes for each paragraph. Walk the room. Each student answers the three check questions before moving on; each answer should be yes. Common mistakes: a topic sentence that repeats the whole thesis, no article named, no explanation. Support: sentence starters “This shows that” and “This matters because”. Stretch: a second piece of evidence. Unfinished paragraphs wait until next time. Remind students that the organizer is a starting point: a row can change if the new evidence still backs its reason.

steps.title: Topic sentence
steps.detail: One sentence that states this reason.

steps.title: Evidence
steps.detail: From one of the two unit articles.

steps.title: Explanation
steps.detail: Show how the evidence supports the reason.

steps.title: Closing sentence

slides.title: Maple Street counterclaim paragraph (made up for practice)
bullets: 1. Dana Ruiz, in her made-up article “Keep the Bell Schedule,” argues that a longer lunch would take five minutes of class time from the school day.
2. That concern is fair, because less class time means less time to practice.

3. However, Marcus Bell reports in his made-up article “Lost in the Lunch Line” that when one school added five minutes to its lunch, the time teachers spent settling hungry, restless students fell from about ten minutes to about four minutes in each of the two afternoon classes.
4. This shows that a longer lunch can win back class time: the two afternoon classes together regained about twelve minutes, which is more than the five minutes the lunch takes from the day.
5. Five minutes of class time is a small price for a lunch that sets students up to learn.
slides.notes: Say once that the Maple Street paragraph, its writers and its articles are made up for practice. Read the paragraph aloud. In pairs, students jot the job of each of the five sentences in a few words. Then label the sentences on the board and point to the writer’s name, the place where the writer gives in, and the evidence. Answers: 1 counterclaim with the writer named; 2 gives in to what is true; 3 rebuttal evidence with its source; 4 explanation; 5 link back. Point out that the evidence measures the effect of a longer lunch, and that sentence 4 compares time lost and regained across the same day: about ten minutes down to about four is six minutes regained in each class, so about twelve in the two classes, against five minutes lost. Common mistakes: thinking the give-in weakens the essay; stating the other side unfairly.

slides.title: Turn the case around
bullets: Maple Street Middle School, its essay, Marcus Bell and his article are made up for practice.
The Maple Street essay now argues against a longer lunch, so Marcus Bell’s point becomes its counterclaim.
In his article “Lost in the Lunch Line,” Bell argues that when lunch is short, hungry and restless students cost teachers about ten minutes of each afternoon class.
slides.notes: Give out the sheet “Turn the case around”. Students work alone and write two sentences. Partners then read each other’s sentences and run the partner check. Hear two pairs. A sample to keep for after students have written: “Marcus Bell, in his made-up article “Lost in the Lunch Line,” argues that teachers spend about ten minutes of each afternoon class settling hungry, restless students. That is true, and hungry students cannot focus.” Common mistakes: loaded words like “complains”; no give-in; naming Ruiz instead of Bell. The point of the task is that the same counterclaim moves work from either side of a question.

slides.title: Turn the case around (continued)

Sentence 2: give in to what is true in his point.
Partner check: Are Bell and his article named? Does the second sentence acknowledge his point fairly?

slides.title: Draft your counterclaim paragraph
bullets: Take the counterclaim box from your organizer.
Close the reason paragraph it fits best, so the essay keeps three body paragraphs.
Partner check: point to the writer’s name, the give-in, the evidence and the link back.
slides.notes: Give out the sheet “Counterclaim paragraph steps”. Each student drafts the counterclaim as the closing part of the reason paragraph it fits best. The rebuttal uses evidence from one of the two articles, named with its author, and the last sentence links back to the student’s claim. Check that every student explains how the rebuttal evidence answers the counterclaim before linking back. Support: start with “Daniel Okafor argues that” or “Maya Torres argues that”. Common mistakes: a rebuttal that repeats the claim; evidence that does not answer the counterclaim; a loaded word for the other writer. Partners read each other’s counterclaim and rebuttal and point to each part. Students who finish may mark where the counterclaim sits in the reason paragraph.

points.heading: A reason paragraph has four parts
points.explanation:
Each reason paragraph proves one reason from your thesis. Part 1 is a topic sentence that states the reason. It should not repeat the whole thesis. Part 2 is evidence, with the article and author named. Part 3 is an explanation of how the evidence supports the reason. Part 4 is a closing line that links back to your claim. The organizer is a starting point, so you may swap a detail if the new evidence still backs the same reason.

Example for a pro-later-start essay:
1. A later start gives students more time to sleep.
2. Maya Torres reports in “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later” that after Seattle’s public high schools moved from 7:50 a.m. to 8:45 a.m. in 2016, University of Washington scientists found students “slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights.”
3. This shows that students used the extra morning time for sleep and did not just stay up later.
4. A schedule that helps students sleep more supports the claim that our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later.

If you get stuck on part 3, start with “This shows that” or “This matters because.” Then ask: does my explanation tie the evidence to the reason?

points.heading: Cite every piece of evidence the same way
points.explanation:
Evidence comes only from the two unit articles: “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later” by Maya Torres and “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems” by Daniel Okafor. Name the article and its author each time you use evidence. Put exact words inside quotation marks. If you paraphrase, still name the author. Copying sentences without quotation marks is plagiarism.

Weak: Most schools start too early.

Stronger: Maya Torres reports in “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later” that a Centers for Disease Control and Prevention report found “fewer than one in five American middle and high schools started that late.”

The stronger version names the article and author and puts the copied words in quotation marks. After it, you still need an explanation sentence. Before you move on, check three things: the article and author are named, copied words are in quotation marks, and an explanation follows the evidence.

points.heading: A counterclaim paragraph states, gives in, answers and links back
points.explanation:
A counterclaim paragraph names the other writer and states that writer’s point fairly. It gives in to what is true, answers with evidence from an article, explains how that evidence answers the point, and links back to your claim. Giving in does not weaken your essay. It shows you understand the other side. Avoid loaded words such as “complains.”

Practice paragraph from class. Maple Street, its writers and their articles are made up for practice:
1. Dana Ruiz, in her made-up article “Keep the Bell Schedule,” argues that a longer lunch would take five minutes of class time from the school day.
2. That concern is fair, because less class time means less time to practice.
3. However, Marcus Bell reports in his made-up article “Lost in the Lunch Line” that when one school added five minutes to its lunch, the time teachers spent settling hungry, restless students fell from about ten minutes to about four minutes in each of the two afternoon classes.
4. This shows that a longer lunch can win back class time: the two afternoon classes together regained about twelve minutes, which is more than the five minutes the lunch takes from the day.
5. Five minutes of class time is a small price for a lunch that sets students up to learn.

The jobs are: 1 counterclaim with the writer named, 2 giving in, 3 rebuttal evidence with its source, 4 explanation, 5 link back. In your own essay, place this at the end of the reason paragraph where it fits best.

points.heading: The same moves work from either side
points.explanation:
Whether you argue for or against a later start, you use the same four steps, and the evidence still comes from the two unit articles. Make sure your rebuttal answers the counterclaim. A rebuttal that only repeats your claim does not.

Example for a pro-later-start essay:
1. Counterclaim: Daniel Okafor argues in “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems” that schools and families can help students sleep in other ways, such as limiting phones and screens at night.
2. Give in: Screens can make it harder to fall asleep, so those limits could help.
3. Rebuttal: However, Maya Torres explains in “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later” that during puberty the brain releases melatonin later in the evening, so many teenagers do not feel tired until around 11 p.m.
4. Explanation: This matters because a phone limit cannot change a body clock that runs later, so an early bell still cuts sleep short.
5. Link back: A later start fits how teenagers’ bodies work, which supports the claim that our school should start later.

Writing against a later start, you would flip the roles. You would name Maya Torres in your counterclaim and answer with evidence from Daniel Okafor’s article.

items: Does the evidence name its article and its author?
Are all copied words inside quotation marks?

handouts.key:
Accept either position when the reasons support the student's claim and the evidence accurately represents the articles. The following sample supports a later start.

Reason 1
My reason in a few words: Enough sleep.
Part 1: topic sentence: A later school start would help teenagers get the sleep they need.
Part 2: evidence: In “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later,” Maya Torres explains that teenagers need 8 to 10 hours of sleep each night and that puberty shifts their internal clocks later.
Part 3: explanation: This matters because teenagers may struggle to fall asleep early even when they try. Starting school later could give them more time to sleep in the morning.
Part 4: closing sentence: Our school should adjust its schedule to better match teenagers' sleep needs.
Look for a specific reason, accurate evidence, the article's title and author, an explanation of the connection, and a return to the claim. Common slip: treating teenagers' later internal clocks as proof that every teenager falls asleep at the same time.

Reason 2
My reason in a few words: Learning.
Part 1: topic sentence: A later start could help students do better in class.
Part 2: evidence: In “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later,” Maya Torres reports that after Seattle high schools moved their start time from 7:50 a.m. to 8:45 a.m., students slept a little more than half an hour longer, and grades increased in the biology classes studied.
Part 3: explanation: This shows that a later start can be followed by both more sleep and better classroom results. The findings support trying a schedule that helps students arrive rested, although they do not guarantee the same results at every school.
Part 4: closing sentence: Giving students a better chance to arrive ready to learn supports starting school later.
Look for a reason distinct from getting enough sleep and an explanation focused on learning. Common slips: saying all Seattle students' grades rose or claiming that the study proves sleep alone caused the improvement.

Reason 3, on the student's own paper
My reason in a few words: Health.
Part 1: topic sentence: A later start could also support students' health.
Part 2: evidence: In “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later,” Maya Torres explains that sleep helps the body fight illness and helps young athletes recover.
Part 3: explanation: This matters because students need rest for their bodies as well as their schoolwork. A schedule that allows more sleep could help students recover from physical activity and stay well.
Part 4: closing sentence: Supporting students' health gives our school another reason to start later.
Look for cautious wording that connects an opportunity for more sleep with the benefits Torres describes. Common slip: promising that a later start will prevent illness.

Check each paragraph before you move on
Does the evidence name its article and its author? Yes: each sample names “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later” and Maya Torres. Students should identify both in each paragraph.
Are all copied words inside quotation marks? Yes: the sample evidence is paraphrased. Any student who copies source wording must put that wording inside quotation marks. Common slip: changing only a few words while retaining the article's sentence structure.
Does the paragraph explain how the evidence supports the reason? Yes: each explanation connects the evidence to sleep, learning, or health. Common slip: repeating the evidence instead of explaining its importance.

handouts.key:
Sentence 1: In the made-up article “Lost in the Lunch Line,” Marcus Bell argues that a short lunch leaves students hungry and restless, so teachers lose about ten minutes of each afternoon class settling them down.
Sentence 2: Bell has a fair point that students who are hungry and restless can have trouble focusing, which takes time away from learning.

Look for Bell's name, his article's title, and a fair statement of his point in the first sentence. The second sentence should acknowledge the concern without accepting that a longer lunch is the only solution. Students may acknowledge the general concern without accepting the exact time estimate. Common slips: naming Ruiz, using a loaded verb such as complains, or giving a rebuttal instead of a concession.

Partner check
Are Bell and his article named? Yes: Marcus Bell and “Lost in the Lunch Line.” Both must appear.
Does the second sentence acknowledge his point fairly? Yes: it recognizes that hunger and restlessness can interfere with learning. Common slip: a sentence that dismisses Bell's concern instead of recognizing what is reasonable about it.

handouts.title: Counterclaim paragraph steps

blocks.text: Take the counterclaim box from your organizer. Draft it as the closing part of the reason paragraph it fits best, so that your essay keeps three body paragraphs. The rebuttal uses evidence from one of the two articles, named with its author.
Step 1: state the counterclaim

blocks.hint: Name the writer and state the other side's point fairly. You may start with "Daniel Okafor argues that" or "Maya Torres argues that".

blocks.text: Step 2: give in

blocks.hint: Say what is true in the other side's point.

blocks.text: Step 3: rebuttal

blocks.hint: Give evidence from one article, naming the article and its author. Then explain how it answers the counterclaim.

blocks.text: Step 4: link back

blocks.hint: End by linking back to your claim.

blocks.text: Partner check: point to each of these

items: The writer's name
The place where the writer gives in
The evidence
The link back to the claim

handouts.key:
Accept other accurate counterclaims and rebuttals that fit the student's position. This sample supports a later start.

The reason paragraph this closes: Learning.
Look for a paragraph whose reason connects directly to the counterclaim and rebuttal. Common slip: attaching the response to an unrelated reason.

Step 1: state the counterclaim
In “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems,” Daniel Okafor argues that Seattle's results may not apply to communities with different buses, budgets, and family needs.
Look for a named writer and a fair account of the objection. Common slip: claiming that Okafor denies that Seattle students gained sleep.

Step 2: give in
He is right that one city's experience cannot guarantee the same results at our school.
Look for a specific acknowledgment of the objection's merit. Common slip: immediately dismissing the objection without acknowledging anything true.

Step 3: rebuttal
However, in “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later,” Maya Torres reports that Seattle students slept a little more than half an hour longer after the change, and grades increased in the biology classes studied. These results show that a later start can bring benefits. Differences between communities are a reason to plan carefully, but they do not erase that evidence of possible benefits for learning.
Look for evidence from a unit article, its title and author, and an explanation that answers the objection. Common slips: repeating the claim without evidence, guaranteeing better grades locally, or treating the Seattle findings as proof that transportation problems have been solved.

Step 4: link back
Our school should start later, with careful planning to help students gain sleep and arrive ready to learn.
Look for a clear return to the student's claim that follows from the response. Common slip: introducing an unrelated reason.

Partner check: point to each of these
The writer's name: Daniel Okafor in the counterclaim; Maya Torres introduces the rebuttal evidence.
The place where the writer gives in: The sentence acknowledging that Seattle's experience cannot guarantee the same results locally.
The evidence: Torres's report of increased sleep and higher grades in the biology classes studied in Seattle.
The link back to the claim: The final sentence supporting a later start with careful planning.
Look for all four features in the closing part of an existing reason paragraph, preserving three body paragraphs. Common slip: making the counterclaim a separate additional body paragraph.

Students should state and concede that measured benefit before considering the serving-window alternative. Update the prompt and sample answer to preserve Bell’s actual evidence.

l_0c74f2cbf0f6.title: Completing the full draft with transitions
l_0c74f2cbf0f6.summary: Students finish a full five-paragraph draft in class, adding transitions such as "First," "In addition," and "However," between paragraphs.

segments.title: Folders out: lay out your draft
segments.description:
Students take out their writing folders and lay out the introduction, the three reason paragraphs, the counterclaim paragraph and the conclusion.
Each student numbers the pieces in the order a reader should meet them and marks any piece not yet written, in about one minute.
Each student reads the last sentence of the introduction and the first sentence of the next piece to a partner, one minute each way, and says whether the join feels like a jump.
The teacher hears two pairs.
segments.teacherNotes: Collect nothing. Have spare copies of both articles ready. Expect jumps such as a thesis followed straight by evidence. Other joins are checked later in the lesson. A student missing a piece starts it in the finishing segment.

segments.title: Transitions: the bridge between paragraphs
segments.description:
Show three paragraph openings from Maya Torres in “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later”. Then show three from Daniel Okafor in “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems”.
Ask: what do these openings do for the reader? Each student writes a guess and tells a partner, and the teacher hears two.
Show the four jobs of a transition, then the five-paragraph shape with the joins marked. Show one join with a transition word only and the same join with a link phrase added.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected guess: they count the reasons so the reader knows where they are. Point out that Okafor orders his points without “First,” and the job is the same. The counterclaim and rebuttal follow reason 3 inside the same paragraph, so students fold their counterclaim paragraph under it. Mistake: stacking three transitions on one join.
shown: Torres: “First, teenagers need more sleep than most of them get.”
Torres: “Second, when schools do start later, students really do sleep more.”
Torres: “Third, sleep is about more than grades.”
Okafor: “The first problem is transportation.”
Okafor: “The second problem is what happens after school.”
Okafor: “The third problem is family schedules.”

Table: Job | Transition words | Where it goes / Order | First, Second, Third, Finally | Opening each reason paragraph / Add | In addition, Also, Another reason | Adding a new reason / Contrast | However, On the other hand | Opening the counterclaim / Ending | For these reasons, In conclusion | Opening the conclusion
Steps: Introduction → Reason paragraph 1 (First,) → Reason paragraph 2 (In addition,) → Reason paragraph 3 (Finally,) with the counterclaim (However,) and rebuttal → Conclusion (For these reasons,)
Side by side: Word only: In addition, students need time to rest. | Link phrase added: Besides needing time to eat, students also need time to rest.

segments.title: Choose the better transition and say why
segments.description:
Give out the sheet “Choose the better transition: Maple Street lunch”.
The sheet has five joins from a made-up essay on a longer lunch at Maple Street Middle School. Each has a blank and two choices.
Alone, each student picks A or B for every join and writes a few words naming the job: order, add, contrast or ending.
Partners compare answers and settle any difference by naming the job.
The teacher hears one join and the reason for it.
segments.teacherNotes: Items and answers: 1 A, order opens the first reason. 2 B, adds a second reason; However would turn to the other side. 3 A, last reason. 4 A, contrast opens the counterclaim. 5 A, ending. Mistakes: choosing However because it sounds formal; using First twice.

segments.title: Finish the full draft
segments.description:
Students put their pieces in order and write any piece still missing, starting with the shortest.
They fold the counterclaim and rebuttal under the end of reason paragraph 3.
They circle the article and author named in each reason paragraph and put quotation marks around any copied words.
The teacher walks the room and asks each student which paragraph is still unfinished.
segments.teacherNotes: Mistakes: new evidence in the conclusion; a conclusion copied from the thesis. Support: a student with several pieces missing uses the organizer and sentence starters to complete each missing paragraph, including cited evidence and explanation in each reason paragraph and the counterclaim with rebuttal within the third. Stretch: add a second piece of evidence. A draft not finished today is finished before peer review so the partner has something to read.

segments.title: Add transitions to your draft
segments.description:
Give out the sheet “Transition table”.
Students write a transition at the start of each reason paragraph, the counterclaim and the conclusion, using the table on the sheet.
They underline each transition.
They turn at least one join into a link phrase that names the idea just finished.
segments.teacherNotes: Support: copy the order words from the table in sequence. Stretch: replace each plain transition with a link phrase. Mistakes: First on two paragraphs; However opening a reason that agrees with the claim. Writers may add a sentence to smooth a join, but nothing new as evidence.

segments.title: Read the joins aloud
segments.description:
Partners swap folders. Each reads aloud the last sentence of one paragraph and the first sentence of the next, at one join the writer has starred, about 30 seconds each.
The partner says “jump” or “smooth” in a few words, about 30 seconds each.
Each writer changes a few words at that join if it needs it, in about one minute.
segments.teacherNotes: Keep this to one join each. Writers star the join before swapping. The full read with the checklist comes next time. Listen for joins where the transition names the wrong job.

segments.title: Before you leave
segments.description:
Set the homework: “Organizer and drafts”, a graded assignment that counts toward Organizer and drafts (25% of the course grade). Write its name and due time on the board: due at the start of next time.
Tell students what to expect next time: partners read each other’s drafts and give written feedback on claim, evidence, explanation, counterclaim and organization using a checklist.
Students keep the full draft, organizer and articles in the writing folder and bring the folder.
A short practice quiz on today’s lesson may be taken after class. It counts toward no grade.
segments.teacherNotes: Say the due time in the words on the board. Remind students that the final essay’s due time is still on the board from last time.

keyIdeas: A transition is a word or phrase that shows how one idea connects to the next. It tells the reader whether the essay is putting reasons in order, adding one, turning to the other side or ending.
Pick a transition by its job. “First,” “Second,” and “Finally,” put reasons in order. “In addition,” adds a reason. “However,” turns to the other side. “For these reasons,” opens the ending.
A transition word alone can leave a jump. A link phrase that names the idea just finished makes the join smooth.

A full draft has five paragraphs: the introduction, three reason paragraphs and the conclusion. The counterclaim and rebuttal close the third reason paragraph. Every reason paragraph still names its article and author.

vocabulary.definition: A word or phrase that shows how one idea or paragraph connects to the next.
A transition that puts reasons in a sequence, such as First, Second and Finally.
A transition that adds another reason or point, such as In addition or Also.
A transition that turns to a different or opposing idea, such as However or On the other hand.
A short phrase that names the idea just finished and leads into the next one, such as Besides needing time to eat.
How smoothly a reader moves from one sentence or paragraph to the next without a jump.

study.overview: A strong essay does more than list its parts. It also shows the reader how the parts fit together. In this lesson you put your five paragraphs in order, finished the missing pieces, and added transitions at the joins. This guide reviews what a transition does, how to choose one, and how to check that your whole draft holds together before partners read it next time.

points.heading: A transition shows the reader how two ideas connect
points.explanation:
A transition is a word or phrase that tells the reader what is happening next. It has one of four jobs. Order puts reasons in line (First, Second, Finally). Add brings in another reason that points the same way (In addition, Also, Another reason is). Contrast turns to the other side (However, On the other hand). Ending wraps up the essay (In conclusion, In short, Overall).

Example: Maya Torres, in “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later,” opens her three reasons with “First, teenagers need more sleep than most of them get,” then “Second, when schools do start later, students really do sleep more,” then “Third, sleep is about more than grades.” The reader always knows where they are. Daniel Okafor, in “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems,” does the same job without “First”: “The first problem is transportation,” then “The second problem is what happens after school.” Different words, same job. Pick a transition by its job, not by how formal it sounds.

points.heading: A link phrase makes a join smooth
points.explanation:
A transition word alone can still leave a jump. A link phrase fixes this by naming the idea you just finished, so the reader sees how the two paragraphs connect.

Example, using a made-up essay about lunch: “In addition, students need time to rest.” This works, but it is a plain word and a new idea. Now add a link phrase: “Besides needing time to eat, students also need time to rest.” The opening phrase points back to the last paragraph (eating) and forward to the new one (resting). Try this at least once in your draft.

Three mistakes to avoid. Do not stack three transitions on one join. Do not use “First” on two paragraphs. Do not open a reason that agrees with your claim with “However,” because “However” turns to the other side. You may add a sentence to smooth a join, but do not add new evidence.

points.heading: Check the whole shape and the joins in your draft
points.explanation:
A full draft has five paragraphs: the introduction, three reason paragraphs and the conclusion. The counterclaim and rebuttal do not get a paragraph of their own. They close the third reason paragraph, and “However,” or “Some people argue” opens the counterclaim. Check your joins in order: introduction to reason 1 (order), reason 1 to reason 2 (order or add), reason 2 to reason 3 (order or add), reason 3 to the counterclaim (contrast), and the rebuttal to the conclusion (ending).

Also check what is inside each paragraph. Every reason paragraph names its article and author. For example: In “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later,” Maya Torres reports that the American Academy of Sleep Medicine says people from 13 to 18 years old need 8 to 10 hours of sleep. Any copied words need quotation marks, and evidence comes only from the two unit articles. Keep the conclusion free of new evidence, and do not copy your thesis word for word.

To test a join, read the last sentence of one paragraph and the first sentence of the next. If it feels like a jump, check which job the transition does and whether a link phrase would help. If any piece is still unfinished, finish it before peer review, so your partner has a full draft to read. Next time, partners read each other’s drafts with a checklist. Bring your writing folder, with your full draft, organizer and both articles.

handouts.key:
Join 1: A. First, — order. It introduces the first supporting reason. Common slip: choosing However, even though the writer has not turned to an opposing view.

Join 2: B. In addition, — add. It introduces another reason supporting a longer lunch. Common slip: choosing However because it sounds formal, although the ideas agree.

Join 3: A. Finally, — order. It introduces the last supporting reason. Common slip: choosing First and restarting the sequence.

Join 4: A. However, — contrast. It introduces the opposing concern that a longer lunch would reduce class time. This turn occurs within the same paragraph. Common slip: treating the counterclaim as another supporting reason and choosing In addition.

Join 5: A. In conclusion, — ending. It brings the reasons together and restates the position. Common slip: choosing For example, which signals an example rather than a conclusion.

handouts.title: Sentence starters for unfinished paragraphs

blocks.text: Use these starters only for a paragraph you have not yet written. Look at your organizer for your claim, reasons, evidence and counterclaim. Fill each ___ with your own words. Evidence must come from the two unit articles, and you must name the article each time. If you copy words exactly, put quotation marks around them.
A reason paragraph

items: One reason I hold this position is that ___.
In the article ___ by ___, the writer explains that ___.
This evidence shows that ___ because ___.
This matters because ___.

blocks.text: The counterclaim and rebuttal, at the end of reason paragraph 3

items: Some people argue that ___.
This view misses an important point, because ___.
In the article ___ by ___, the writer shows that ___.
So the concern can be answered by ___.

blocks.text: The conclusion

items: Put another way, my claim is that ___.
My reasons were ___, ___ and ___.
The most important point for our school is ___.

blocks.text: Keep the conclusion free of new evidence, and do not copy your thesis word for word.

handouts.key:
Answers will vary. The following completions support starting school at 8:30 a.m. or later.

A reason paragraph, blanks in order:
1. Later school starts can help teenagers get more sleep.
2. Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later; Maya Torres; students in the Seattle study slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights after their schools moved the start time from 7:50 a.m. to 8:45 a.m.
3. A later start can increase students’ sleep; the students studied gained sleep instead of simply staying awake later.
4. A school schedule should help teenagers get the rest they need.
Look for a reason that supports the student’s claim, accurate evidence from a named article, and an explanation connecting that evidence to the reason. Common slips: omitting the article title, repeating evidence instead of explaining it, or claiming that every school would get Seattle’s results.

The counterclaim and rebuttal, blanks in order:
1. Later starts could disrupt bus routes and family schedules.
2. Scheduling difficulties deserve planning, but they do not erase the possible benefits of more sleep.
3. Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later; Maya Torres; California’s law requires most public high schools to start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. and most public middle schools no earlier than 8:00 a.m.
4. Considering changes to bus routes and practice schedules while checking how those changes would affect local families.
Look for a fair opposing concern, a response that addresses it, accurately attributed evidence, and an explanation of how the response supports the claim. The California example shows that a broad schedule change is possible; it does not prove that every local transportation problem is solved. Common slips: dismissing the concern, claiming all California schools start at 8:30 a.m., or placing the counterclaim in a separate paragraph instead of at the end of the third reason paragraph.

The conclusion, blanks in order:
1. Our school should begin at 8:30 a.m. or later to better support teenagers’ needs.
2. More opportunity for sleep; better conditions for learning; support for students’ health.
3. Choosing a schedule that helps students arrive rested and ready to learn.
Look for the same position expressed in fresh words, a summary of the reasons actually developed in the draft, and a closing thought about their importance. Common slips: introducing new evidence, adding an undeveloped reason, or copying the thesis word for word. Students arguing against a later start should use reasons, evidence, a rebuttal, and a conclusion that consistently support that position.

segments.title: What a helpful comment sounds like
segments.description:
Show the Peer review checklist and read its five questions aloud.
Say once that the Maple Street draft, its writers and its articles are made up for practice. Show two comments on one sentence from that draft.
Each student writes what makes the second comment more useful and tells a partner. The teacher hears two, then shows the pattern: name what works, point to the place, suggest one next step.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected answer: the second comment is kind, names the place and gives a next step. Mistake: thinking kind means only praise. Stress that a next step is also kind. Review the writer’s draft, not the writer.
shown: Table: Area | Ask yourself / Claim | Can I find the position and each reason? / Evidence | Does each piece of evidence name its article and author? / Explanation | Does each piece of evidence get a “So what?” / Counterclaim | Is the other side stated fairly, with a writer named and a rebuttal? / Organization | Are there five paragraphs, with transitions that fit?
Sentence from the draft: Marcus Bell, in his article “Lost in the Lunch Line,” says students lose ten minutes waiting to be served.

Side by side: Comment A: “Good job, I liked it.”; no place named; no next step | Comment B: “Marcus Bell is named with his article, so I know where the evidence comes from. Next, add a sentence that starts ‘This matters because’ to tell me what ten minutes means for a student’s lunch.”
Steps: name what works → point to the place → suggest one next step

segments.title: Fix the unhelpful comments
segments.description:
Give out the sheet “Maple Street paragraph and comments”.
Show the whole made-up Maple Street paragraph and three unhelpful comments on it.
Each student reads the paragraph, then rewrites two of the three comments so each is kind, specific and names a checklist area.
Partners swap and check each other’s rewrites for a place in the draft and a next step. The teacher hears two rewrites.
segments.teacherNotes:
Items and sample rewrites:
A. “Nice. Nothing to fix.” (evidence): Marcus Bell and his article are named, with the title in quotation marks. Next, add a sentence on what ten minutes means for a student’s lunch.
B. “Your explanation is bad.”: Your sentence after the evidence, “A longer lunch is good for students,” does not say why. Try “This shows that” and connect the ten minutes to eating enough.
C. “Your counterclaim is lame.”: You include the other side, which is fair. Next, name who says it and add a rebuttal with evidence from an article.
Mistakes: kind but vague; harsh; rewriting the writer’s sentence. Stretch: rewrite all three.

segments.title: Read your partner’s draft and use the checklist
segments.description:
Partners swap folders, with the full draft on top. The sheet has the three steps.
The reviewer reads the whole draft silently, then marks Claim, Evidence, Explanation, Counterclaim and Organization “yes” or “not yet” in the Mark column of the Peer review checklist. The Evidence mark covers every check in its question.
The reviewer writes Comment 1 (one thing that works) and Comment 2 (one next step) on the sheet, not on the draft. Each comment names a place, such as the paragraph and the sentence.
The teacher walks the room and asks each reviewer which paragraph a comment points to.
segments.teacherNotes: Evidence is “yes” only if the article and author are named, the details match the article, they support the paragraph’s reason, and copied words have quotation marks. Mistakes: marking “yes” everywhere; commenting on spelling only; writing on the draft. Support: use the pattern. Stretch: say which “not yet” matters most.

segments.title: Talk through the feedback
segments.description:
Partners sit side by side with both checklists. Each reviewer reads their two comments aloud while the writer listens.
The writer may ask “Where exactly?” and writes down anything unclear. Each direction takes about two minutes.
The teacher hears one comment a writer found useful and why.
segments.teacherNotes: Writers listen first and do not argue. A writer who disagrees says so after, with a reason. Remind reviewers to read the comment as written, not add harsher words.
shown: Reviewer reads two comments aloud. Writer listens, then asks: “Where exactly?”

segments.title: Choose three changes
segments.description:
Alone, each writer reads the comments and checklist marks, then picks three changes to make to the draft. If the feedback suggests fewer than three useful changes, the writer checks the draft against the checklist to identify the remaining changes.
For each change the writer writes the paragraph it goes in and the checklist area it helps.
Each writer tells their partner which change comes first and why. The teacher hears two.
segments.teacherNotes: Accept a rejected comment if the writer gives a reason. Push students past only spelling fixes toward evidence, explanation or the counterclaim. Sheets stay in the writing folder with the draft.

segments.title: Before you leave
segments.description:
Set the homework: write “Final essay: a short ungraded step, due at the start of the next class” on the board. Say that this prepares students for Final essay, which counts for 60% of the course grade.
Tell students what to expect next time: they revise their drafts in class, strengthening weak evidence, adding missing explanations and tightening sentences, then proofread for spelling and punctuation.
Students keep the draft, the completed checklist and the articles in the writing folder and bring the folder.
A short practice quiz on today’s lesson may be taken after class. It counts toward no grade.

study.overview: Peer review gives you a fresh reader for your draft. Your partner reads the whole draft, marks five areas on a checklist, and writes two comments on the checklist sheet: one thing that works and one next step. Then you decide which changes will make your essay stronger. This guide covers the checklist, what a helpful comment sounds like, how to take feedback, and how to turn it into a plan of three changes.

points.heading: The checklist covers five areas
points.explanation: The Peer review checklist asks one question about each area. Claim: can I find the position and each reason? Evidence: does each piece name its article and author, match that article, support the paragraph’s reason, and put copied words in quotation marks? Explanation: does a sentence after each piece of evidence say how it supports the claim? Counterclaim: is the other side named, with a rebuttal? Organization: are there five paragraphs in a clear order, with transitions that connect them? The reviewer reads the whole draft silently before marking anything, then writes yes or not yet for each area. Evidence is yes only if every check in its question is met. Example: suppose a draft says, “California passed a law in 2019 about school start times,” and names no article or author. Evidence is not yet, because the reader cannot tell where the fact comes from. Marking yes everywhere is not kind. It leaves the writer with nothing to improve.

points.heading: A helpful comment is kind and specific
points.explanation: Kind does not mean only praise. A helpful comment does three things: it names what works, it points to a place in the draft, and it suggests one next step. A next step is a kindness, because it shows the writer how to improve. Compare two comments on the sentence “Maya Torres, in “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later,” says California passed a law in 2019 about start times.” The first says, “Looks fine.” It names no place and gives no next step. The second says, “In paragraph three, your first sentence names Maya Torres and her article, so I know where the California law comes from. Next, add a sentence starting ‘This shows that’ to tell me why a law in another state matters for our school.” Write comments about the draft, not the writer, and write them on the checklist sheet, not on the draft.

points.heading: Feedback is advice, and you decide
points.explanation: When your partner reads two comments aloud, listen first and do not argue. If something is unclear, ask, “Where exactly?” and write down the answer. If you disagree, say so afterward and give a reason. A comment you reject for a good reason is allowed, because you are the writer and the final choice is yours. Reviewers have a job here too: read the comment as written, and do not add harsher words. Example: a partner says, “In paragraph two, add a rebuttal.” You may answer, “My rebuttal is in paragraph four, but I can add a transition so it is easier to find.” That is a useful reply, because it turns the comment into a clear change.

points.heading: Turn feedback into three changes
points.explanation: Choosing three changes makes a plan. On the My three changes sheet, write each change, the paragraph it goes in, and the checklist area it helps. Choose changes that make the claim, evidence and explanation clearer. Fixing spelling alone is not enough. If your partner’s feedback gives you fewer than three useful changes, check your own draft against the checklist to find the rest. Then pick the change you will make first and be ready to say why. Example: Change: add a “This shows that” sentence after the California evidence. Paragraph: 3. Area: Explanation. Keep the checklist, the comments and your plan in your writing folder with the draft, ready for revising next time.

handouts.title: Peer review checklist
handouts.usedIn: Read your partner’s draft and use the checklist

blocks.text: Read your partner’s whole draft silently. Then mark each area below. Write your marks and comments on this sheet, not on the draft. Each comment must name a place in the draft, such as the paragraph and the sentence.

rows: Does the draft state a clear claim about whether school should start later?
Does each piece of evidence name its article and author, match that article, support the paragraph’s reason, and put any copied words in quotation marks?
Does a sentence after each piece of evidence say how it supports the claim?
Does the draft name the other side and answer it with a rebuttal?
Are there five paragraphs in a clear order, with transitions that connect them?
blocks.caption: Write yes or not yet in the Mark column.

blocks.text: Your two comments

blocks.hint: Comment 1: one thing that works. Name the place.
Comment 2: one next step. Name the place.

handouts.key:
Marks depend on the partner’s draft. Look for the following, in sheet order:

Claim: Mark yes if the draft clearly states whether school should start later. Mark not yet if it only introduces the question or leaves the writer’s position unclear. Common slip: treating the topic as a claim.

Evidence: Mark yes only if every piece of evidence names its article and author, accurately represents the article, supports the paragraph’s reason, and uses quotation marks around copied words. Otherwise, mark not yet. For example, Maya Torres’s “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later” reports that Seattle students slept a little more than half an hour longer after the schedule changed. Daniel Okafor’s “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems” explains concerns about shared buses and family schedules. Common slips: naming only the author, treating a possible consequence as a measured result, or overlooking copied words without quotation marks.

Explanation: Mark yes if a sentence after each piece of evidence explains how it supports the claim. Otherwise, mark not yet. An explanation should connect the detail to the writer’s reasoning. Common slip: repeating the evidence without explaining its importance.

Counterclaim: Mark yes if the draft identifies an opposing position and answers it with a rebuttal. Otherwise, mark not yet. Common slip: mentioning the opposing position but giving no answer to it.

Organization: Mark yes if the draft has five paragraphs in a clear order and transitions connect the ideas. Otherwise, mark not yet. Look for an introduction, body paragraphs and a conclusion. Common slip: counting paragraphs without checking their order or connections.

Comment 1: Answers vary. Look for a kind, specific comment identifying something that works and naming its location. Example, if it matches the draft: In paragraph two, your sentence about Seattle names Torres and her article and gives a specific sleep benefit. That evidence supports your reason about getting enough sleep. Common slip: writing only that the paragraph is good.

Comment 2: Answers vary. Look for a respectful, useful next step tied to a specific location. Example, if it matches the draft: In paragraph four, you recognize the concern about shared buses. After that sentence, explain how your proposed schedule would address that concern. Common slips: giving vague advice, criticizing the writer, or rewriting the paragraph for the writer.

handouts.title: Maple Street paragraph and comments

blocks.text: This paragraph, its writer, its article and its author are made up for practice. Read the paragraph. Then read the three comments a reviewer wrote on it.
Maple Street body paragraph

Maple Street Middle School should make lunch ten minutes longer because students need enough time to eat. Marcus Bell, in his article “Twenty Minutes Is Not Enough,” reports that students at his school ate more of their meals after lunch was lengthened by ten minutes. A longer lunch is good for students. Some people say a longer lunch would make the school day end later. Lunch is still important.
Three unhelpful comments

items: A (evidence): “Nice. Nothing to fix.”
B: “Your explanation is bad.”
C: “Your counterclaim is lame.”

blocks.text: Choose two of the comments. Rewrite each one so it is kind, specific and names a checklist area. Point to a place in the paragraph and give one next step.

blocks.hint: Rewrite 1. Start with the letter of the comment you chose.
Rewrite 2. Start with the letter of the comment you chose.

handouts.key:
Rewrite 1: Accept a rewrite of A, B or C that begins with the chosen letter, names a checklist area, points to a specific place and gives a kind, useful next step.

Rewrite 2: Accept a rewrite of a different comment using the same criteria. Suitable answers for each choice follow:

A — Evidence: In the second sentence, you name Marcus Bell and “Twenty Minutes Is Not Enough,” so readers can identify your source. Next, explain how the detail about students eating more supports your reason that students need enough time to eat. Look for recognition that the evidence names an author and article. Common slip: claiming that naming a source alone proves the evidence is accurate.

B — Explanation: After the evidence, your sentence “A longer lunch is good for students” stays focused on lunch. Next, explain how eating more of their meals would help students and support your claim. Look for a connection between the reported detail and the reason. Common slip: replacing the vague sentence with another general statement that lunch is helpful.

C — Counterclaim: Your fourth sentence recognizes the concern that a longer lunch could make dismissal later. Next, answer that concern with a reason supported by evidence from the practice article. Look for recognition that “Lunch is still important” does not answer the scheduling concern. Common slips: insulting the opposing view, repeating the claim, or inventing evidence.

For either rewrite, accept other wording that meets the criteria. Students should comment on the writing rather than judge the writer.

handouts.title: My three changes

blocks.text: Read your partner’s comments and checklist marks. Pick three changes to make to your draft. If the feedback gives you fewer than three useful changes, check your draft against the checklist to find the rest. For each change, write the paragraph it goes in and the checklist area it helps.

blocks.label: The change I will make first

handouts.key:
Answers depend on the writer’s draft and feedback. Each row must identify a concrete revision, its actual paragraph and the checklist area it improves. Accept changes found through the writer’s own checklist review when partner feedback offers fewer than three useful changes.

Row 1 — Change: A specific revision supported by the feedback or checklist. Paragraph: The paragraph where that revision belongs. Area: Claim, Evidence, Explanation, Counterclaim or Organization, matching the revision. Example, if appropriate: Add the article title beside Torres’s name in the Seattle evidence sentence | Paragraph two | Evidence.

Row 2 — Change: Another specific revision. Paragraph: Its actual location. Area: The matching checklist area. Example, if appropriate: Explain how the extra sleep supports readiness to learn after the Seattle evidence | Paragraph two | Explanation.

Row 3 — Change: A third specific revision. Paragraph: Its actual location. Area: The matching checklist area. Example, if appropriate: Answer the shared-bus concern instead of only stating it | Paragraph four | Counterclaim.

The change I will make first: Accept one of the listed revisions. Look for a priority that improves the argument, such as clarifying the claim, correcting evidence or adding a missing rebuttal. In the partner discussion, the writer should explain why that change matters.

Common slips: writing only improve evidence, omitting paragraph locations, choosing an area that does not match the change, or listing only spelling fixes.
