segments.title: Weak evidence and the three tests
segments.description:
Say that revising fixes what the draft says and proofreading fixes how it is written, so revising comes first.
Say once that Maple Street Middle School, Marcus Bell and his lunch article are made up for practice. Apply the matching, specificity and source-naming tests to this example; students’ own essays must use only the two unit articles.
Show the Maple Street reason and its evidence. Each student writes one sentence on what is wrong with it and tells a partner, and the teacher hears two.
Then show the three tests for evidence.
segments.teacherNotes: Expected: “Lots of kids” is vague and names no article or author. Mistake: thinking evidence is weak only when it is untrue. A true fact can still be weak if it is vague, unsourced or fits another reason.
shown: Reason: A longer lunch helps students eat enough.
Evidence in the draft: “Lots of kids say they are hungry at lunch, so lunch should be longer.”
What is wrong with this evidence? Write one sentence.

Table: Test | Question to ask / Matches | Does it back the reason it sits under? / Specific | Does it give a fact, number or event, not “lots” or “studies show”? / Sourced | Does it name the article and author, from the two unit articles?

segments.title: Choose the stronger replacement and say why
segments.description:
Give out the sheet “Choose the stronger replacement”.
Show two possible replacements for the weak Maple Street sentence, with the title of Marcus Bell’s made-up article.
Alone, each student picks A or B and writes one sentence on why, naming the test that decides it.
Then each student writes the replacement as a full sentence that names the author and the article.
Partners compare choices, and the teacher hears one choice and its reason.
segments.teacherNotes: Answer: B. A is specific and named but backs a different reason (bus rides). Mistake: picking A because it has a number. Sample: In his article “Give Us Time to Eat,” Marcus Bell writes that students at Maple Street have 20 minutes for lunch and spend about 12 of them waiting in line. Stretch: adjust the explanation to fit.

segments.title: Replace one weak piece of evidence in your draft
segments.description:
Each student rereads the evidence in each reason paragraph using the three tests and stars the weakest piece.
They find a stronger fact in one of the two articles that backs the same reason and use it to replace the starred evidence.
They rewrite the sentence with the article and author named and quotation marks around any exact words.
Then they rewrite the explanation after it to fit the new evidence. The teacher asks each student which test the old evidence failed.
segments.teacherNotes: Mistakes: a fact that fits another reason; keeping the old explanation; exact words without quotation marks. Support: start from a “not yet” on the evidence line of the checklist. Stretch: replace a second piece. Evidence in the rebuttal may come from either article.

segments.title: Add a missing explanation and tighten
segments.description:
Give out the sheet “Add a missing explanation and tighten”.
The sheet has a wordy Maple Street sentence. Each student cuts it to one clear sentence and tells a partner, and the teacher hears one.
The sheet has two sentence starters for explanations.
In their draft, each student finds one piece of evidence with no explanation, or a thin one, and writes one clear sentence.
Then they tighten one other sentence by cutting words that add nothing.
segments.teacherNotes: Sample tightening: A longer lunch would help students. The cut keeps the original meaning and drops the filler. Mistakes: cutting the article name or the explanation instead of filler; “This shows that” followed by a repeat of the evidence. Support: copy a starter and finish it.

segments.title: Proofread: find and fix the errors
segments.description:
Say that proofreading comes last and checks spelling, punctuation and quotation marks.
Show a short made-up Maple Street passage with errors in it, and the made-up source wording from Marcus Bell’s article to compare with sentence 1.
Each student underlines the error in each sentence and writes a short fix silently, about two minutes, then compares with a partner for one minute.
The teacher takes one fix aloud, from a sentence chosen at random.
segments.teacherNotes:
Mistake: missing the exact words that need quotation marks while hunting for spelling. Spell-check can miss a wrong word that is spelled correctly. Items and answers:
1. Marcus Bell writes, “A longer lunch is a simple fix, not a costly one.”
2. recieve should be receive.
3. Comma splice: use a period, or add “and.”
shown: Table: Check | Look for / Spelling | words spelled wrong, or the wrong word that sounds the same / Punctuation | commas, periods, capital letters / Quotation marks | exact words from an article
Made-up source wording from Marcus Bell’s article “Give Us Time to Eat” (for practice): “A longer lunch is a simple fix, not a costly one.”
1. Marcus Bell writes that a longer lunch is a simple fix, not a costly one.
2. This shows that students recieve only eight minutes to eat.
3. A longer lunch would give students time to eat, it would also help them focus.

segments.title: Proofread your own draft
segments.description:
Each student checks every quoted phrase in the draft against the article and adds quotation marks where exact words are copied.
Then they read each paragraph slowly for spelling and punctuation, fixing what they find.
The teacher walks the room and asks students to point to one quotation or paraphrase and its matching wording in the article.
segments.teacherNotes: Mistakes: changing a word inside quotation marks; leaving copied words with no marks, which is plagiarism under the class policy. Support: check only the reason paragraphs first. Stretch: read the draft last sentence first to catch spelling.

segments.title: Before you leave
segments.description:
Write “Final essay: a short ungraded step” on the board with its due time: the start of next time.
Tell students that next time they review the terms of argument and take a quiz on what has been taught so far. It belongs to Short quizzes on the terms of argument (15%).
Tell them to bring their writing folder.
A short practice quiz on today’s lesson may be taken after class. It counts toward no grade.
segments.teacherNotes: Say the due time in the words on the board. Remind students that the final essay’s due time is still on the board from earlier in the course. Announce what else students may use for the quiz.

keyIdeas: Revising changes what a draft says. Proofreading fixes how it is written and comes last.

Weak evidence is vague, has no named source, or fits a different reason than the one it sits under. Replace it with a specific fact from one of the two unit articles, with the article and author named.
When evidence changes, its explanation changes too. Each explanation tells the reader what this evidence shows for the reason.
Tightening a sentence means cutting words that add nothing, so the idea comes through faster.
Proofread for spelling, punctuation and quotation marks. Exact words from an article go inside quotation marks.

vocabulary.definition: To change a draft so that what it says is stronger, such as replacing weak evidence or adding an explanation.
To read a draft closely for mistakes in spelling, punctuation and quotation marks, after the revising is done.
To cut words that add nothing so a sentence says its idea in fewer, clearer words.
Using more words than the idea needs.
Two complete sentences joined by only a comma. Fix it with a period or by adding a joining word such as “and.”

study.overview: A first draft is rarely finished. In revising, you change what the draft says. In proofreading, you fix how it is written, and you do it last. After this lesson you can spot weak evidence, replace it with a specific fact from one of the two unit articles, and rewrite the explanation so it fits. You can also tighten wordy sentences and check spelling, punctuation and quotation marks. The practice examples come from a made-up school, Maple Street Middle School, and a made-up writer, Marcus Bell, who wrote the made-up article “Give Us Time to Eat.” They are only for practice. Your own essay uses evidence from the two unit articles only.

points.heading: Revise first, proofread last
points.explanation: Revising changes ideas: the evidence, the explanations and the wording that makes a sentence clear. Proofreading fixes small errors in spelling, punctuation and quotation marks. Do revising first. If you proofread a sentence and then replace it, the proofreading was wasted. Example: you fix a comma in an evidence sentence, then decide the evidence is weak and swap it for a better fact. The comma work is gone. So make the evidence and explanations final, and then proofread.

points.heading: Test your evidence three ways
points.explanation: Evidence is weak when it is vague, has no named source, or backs a different reason than the one it sits under. A true fact can still be weak. Ask three questions. Matching: does it back the reason it sits under? Specific: does it give a fact, number or event, not a word like “lots”? Sourced: does it name the article and author? Practice example. Reason: A longer lunch helps students eat enough. Weak evidence: “Lots of kids say they are hungry at lunch, so lunch should be longer.” It is vague and names no article or author. Now compare two facts from Marcus Bell’s made-up article. A says students ride the bus for an average of 35 minutes each morning. B says students have 20 minutes for lunch and spend about 12 of them waiting in line. A has a number and a named source, but it backs a different reason, bus rides. B matches the reason. A strong replacement reads: In his article “Give Us Time to Eat,” Marcus Bell writes that students at Maple Street have 20 minutes for lunch and spend about 12 of them waiting in line. In your own essay, find the replacement fact in one of the two unit articles, under the same reason. Evidence in your rebuttal may come from either article.

points.heading: Change the explanation and tighten the sentence
points.explanation: When you change the evidence, change the explanation too. An explanation tells the reader what this evidence shows for the reason. Suppose the new evidence is the 20-minute lunch with 12 minutes in line. A fitting explanation is: This matters because students are left with only about eight minutes to eat. A weak one is: This shows that students wait in line. It only repeats the evidence. Two starters help: “This matters because ...” and “This supports my claim because ...” Tightening means cutting words that add nothing, so the idea comes through faster. Wordy: “It is the case that, in my opinion, a longer lunch would really and truly help students quite a lot.” Tight: “A longer lunch would help students.” Cut filler only. Keep the article name and the explanation.

points.heading: Proofread quotation marks, spelling and punctuation
points.explanation: Start with quotation marks. Exact words from an article go inside quotation marks, and you never change a word inside them. Suppose Marcus Bell’s article says, “A longer lunch is a simple fix, not a costly one.” If you copy those words, write: Marcus Bell writes, “A longer lunch is a simple fix, not a costly one.” If you change the words, it is a paraphrase. Keep it in your own words and still name the article and author. Copied words with no quotation marks are plagiarism, even when you name the article. Next check spelling. Spell-check can miss a wrong word that is spelled correctly, such as their and there. Last check punctuation. Look for two complete sentences joined by only a comma. “A longer lunch would give students time to eat, it would also help them focus.” Fix it with a period: “A longer lunch would give students time to eat. It would also help them focus.” You could also add “and.” Reading your draft from the last sentence up can make spelling mistakes stand out.

1. B. Matching decides the choice: the lunch and waiting times support the reason that students lack time to eat. A gives a specific bus-ride time but does not support that reason. Common slip: choosing A just because it contains a number.
2. Sample: In his article “Give Us Time to Eat,” Marcus Bell reports that Maple Street students have 20 minutes for lunch and spend about 12 minutes waiting in line. Look for the correct fact, the author’s name and the article’s title. Students may add that this leaves about 8 minutes to eat. Common slip: leaving out the article title or author.

handouts.title: Replace one weak piece of evidence in your draft
handouts.usedIn: Replace one weak piece of evidence in your draft

blocks.text: Use the three tests on the evidence in each reason paragraph of your draft. Star the weakest piece. Then find a stronger fact in one of the two unit articles that backs the same reason, and use it to replace the starred evidence. Evidence in your rebuttal may come from either article.
The three tests

items: Matching: the fact backs the reason it sits under.
Specificity: the fact gives a number, a name or a detail, not a word like "lots."
Source-naming: the sentence names the article and its author.

blocks.hint: Which test did your old evidence fail? Say how.
Rewrite the evidence sentence with the new fact. Name the article and the author. Put quotation marks around any exact words.
Rewrite the explanation that comes after it so that it fits the new evidence.

handouts.key:
1. Answers depend on the draft. Look for a named test and a specific explanation of the weakness. Sample: My evidence failed specificity because “students sleep more” does not say how much more. Accept matching when the evidence supports a different reason, or source-naming when the sentence omits the article or author. Common slip: naming a test without explaining how the old evidence fails it.
2. Sample for a reason about getting more sleep: In “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later,” Maya Torres reports that students in the Seattle study slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights after their schools changed the start time from 7:50 a.m. to 8:45 a.m. Look for an accurate fact from either unit article that supports the same reason, with the author and title named. Exact copied wording needs quotation marks. Common slip: selecting a detailed fact that supports a different reason.
3. Sample: The extra sleep supports a later start because the schedule change helped students get more rest on school nights. Look for an explanation connecting the replacement evidence to the student’s reason and claim. Common slips: repeating the fact without explaining its importance, keeping an explanation that fits only the old evidence, or claiming that one city’s results guarantee the same outcome everywhere.

handouts.title: Add a missing explanation and tighten
handouts.usedIn: Add a missing explanation and tighten

blocks.text: First practice on a made-up Maple Street sentence. Then work on your own draft.

blocks.label: Wordy sentence
blocks.value: It is the case that, in my opinion, a longer lunch would really and truly help students quite a lot.

blocks.hint: Cut it to one clear sentence. Keep the meaning.

blocks.text: Two sentence starters for explanations

items: This matters because ...
This supports my claim because ...

blocks.hint: Find one piece of evidence in your draft with no explanation, or a thin one. Write one clear explanation sentence for it. You may copy a starter and finish it.
Choose one other sentence in your draft. Write it again here, cutting words that add nothing. Keep the article name and the explanation.

handouts.key:
1. Sample: A longer lunch would help students. Accept a clear sentence that preserves the original meaning and removes filler. Common slip: adding a new claim about grades or health.
2. Answers depend on the draft. Sample following evidence about teenagers’ later internal clocks: This matters because an early school schedule can require teenagers to wake before they have had enough sleep. Look for a clear connection between the selected evidence and the reason or claim. Common slip: using “This shows that” to repeat the evidence without explaining it.
3. Answers depend on the draft. Look for fewer unnecessary words, the same meaning, and retained source information and reasoning. Sample original: In “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later,” Maya Torres explains the fact that teenagers need 8 to 10 hours of sleep every night. Sample revision: In “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later,” Maya Torres explains that teenagers need 8 to 10 hours of sleep each night. Common slip: cutting the article title, author or explanation instead of filler.

blocks.text: Proofread last, after your evidence and explanations are final. Work through the steps in order, one paragraph at a time.
Step 1: quotation marks

items: Find every phrase in your draft that you took from an article.
Put the article beside it and compare the words, one by one.
If the words are exactly the same, they need quotation marks around them.
Never change a word inside quotation marks.
If you changed the words, it is a paraphrase. Keep it in your own words and still name the article and the author.
Copied words with no quotation marks are plagiarism, even when you name the article.

blocks.text: Step 2: spelling and punctuation

items: Read each paragraph slowly, a sentence at a time.
Check spelling. Spell-check can miss a wrong word that is spelled correctly, such as their and there.
Check that each sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a period, question mark or exclamation point.
Look for two complete sentences joined by only a comma. Fix them with a period or with a word such as "and."
Check the commas and periods around your quotation marks.

blocks.text: If you have time

items: Check only your reason paragraphs first.
Read your draft starting from the last sentence and moving up. Spelling mistakes stand out when the sentences are out of order.

keyIdeas: An argument is built from five parts with different jobs: a claim, evidence, reasoning, a counterclaim and a rebuttal.
Evidence is a fact from a source. Reasoning is the writer’s own explanation of what that fact means for the claim.
A counterclaim is the other side’s strongest point, stated fairly. A rebuttal answers that point with evidence and links back to the claim.
You know a term when you can use it on a new topic, not only on the start-time articles.
Looking back at a draft shows which changes made the argument clearer, and that is how a writer gets better.

vocabulary.definition: To look back at your own work and say what changed, why it changed and what you would do next time.

study.overview: A strong argument works because each part has its own job. This guide goes over the five parts: claim, evidence, reasoning, counterclaim and rebuttal. It shows how to tell them apart, how to use them on a topic that is not about school start times, and how to look back at your own draft to see what made it clearer. Use the examples below to check your understanding, then try the same moves in your own words.

points.heading: Five parts, five different jobs
points.explanation: A claim is the position the writer takes. Evidence is a fact, number or example from a source. Reasoning is the writer’s own explanation of how the evidence supports the claim. A counterclaim is the other side’s strongest point, stated fairly. A rebuttal answers that point and leads back to the claim. Example from “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later”: Maya Torres writes, “Our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later.” That is her claim. She reports that when Seattle’s public high schools moved from 7:50 a.m. to 8:45 a.m. in 2016, students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights. That is evidence, because it comes from a source and has dates and numbers. A reasoning sentence would be your own: “Half an hour a night adds up to about two and a half hours over a school week, so a later bell gives students real time to catch up on sleep.” Each part does something the others cannot.

points.heading: Evidence is the fact; reasoning is what you say about it
points.explanation: Evidence can be traced to a source. Reasoning cannot, because it is your thinking. Clue words such as “this shows that” or “this matters because” often signal reasoning. Two mistakes are common. The first is calling a reasoning sentence evidence because it sounds factual. The second is writing reasoning that only repeats the evidence. Example from “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems”: Daniel Okafor explains that the same buses make several trips each morning, one for the high school, then the middle school, then the elementary schools. That is evidence. Weak reasoning: “The buses make several trips, so there are several trips.” Stronger reasoning: “This shows that moving one school’s start time can force other schools to change theirs, so the cost reaches more than just the high school.” The stronger version tells the reader what the fact means for the claim.

points.heading: A counterclaim is stated fairly; a rebuttal answers it and returns to the claim
points.explanation: A good counterclaim names the other side’s strongest worry in a way the other side would accept. A good rebuttal then answers that worry, usually with evidence, and ends by pointing back to your claim. Example: Okafor’s counterclaim is that a later high school start would force the district to buy more buses and hire more drivers, or send younger children to school earlier. Torres answers that districts can change bus routes. She adds that a 2019 California law requires most public high schools there to start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. Then she returns to her claim: if a whole state can make the change, our school can too. A sentence that only mentions buses is not automatically a counterclaim. Ask who is speaking and what the sentence does. If it answers a worry and leads back to the writer’s position, it is a rebuttal.

points.heading: Use the terms on a new topic, then on your own draft
points.explanation: You know a term when you can use it on a topic you have not studied. Try this one. Suppose a survey of our school found that 70% of eighth graders feel tired by 11 a.m. This is made up for practice and is not real data. Claim: Our school should add a 20-minute break in the middle of the morning. Evidence: the survey figure of 70%. Reasoning: a break gives tired students time to move and eat a snack, so they can focus in the classes that follow. Counterclaim: Some people say a break would take time away from classes. Rebuttal: Suppose a trial week at our school kept every class and only shortened the passing periods, and teachers reported that students were more alert afterward. The break costs very little class time, so our school should add it. Then do the same with your essay. Put your draft and your final essay side by side. Find the change that matters most, such as a new explanation after a quotation or a fairer counterclaim, and say why it helps a reader. That habit is how a writer gets better.

The facts below are made up for practice. They are not real data.

items: Shared claim: Teachers should assign no homework on weekends.
Shared counterclaim: Some people say students need the weekend to finish long projects.
Suppose a survey of our school found that 60% of eighth graders spend three hours or more on homework over a weekend.

Draw a term card. Write one sentence that is an example of that term on this topic. Use what is shown above. Do not write the name of the term.

handouts.key:
Round 1 — My sentence: Answers depend on the card drawn. Accept sentences such as these: Claim: Teachers should keep weekends free of homework so students have more time for other activities. Evidence: In the hypothetical school survey, 60% of eighth graders spent at least three hours on homework over a weekend. Reasoning: Spending at least three hours on homework leaves students with less weekend time for rest and family activities. Counterclaim: Supporters of weekend homework argue that students need that time to finish long projects. Rebuttal: Although long projects take time, students in the hypothetical trial finished them on time with Friday class work time and weekly progress checks, which supports keeping weekends free of homework. Look for a sentence that performs the assigned role. Common slips: presenting an opinion as evidence, repeating evidence without explaining it, or repeating the claim without answering the counterclaim.

Round 1 — My partner's term, and the words that gave it away: The term must match the role of the partner's sentence. Accept clues such as “should keep weekends free” for claim; “60%” with attribution to the hypothetical survey for evidence; “leaves students with less weekend time” for reasoning; “students need that time to finish long projects” for counterclaim; and the trial results used to answer the project concern for rebuttal. Judge the sentence's meaning, not just a signal word. A common slip is labeling a sentence rebuttal merely because it begins with “although.”

Round 2 — My second sentence: Apply the same criteria to the new card received from the partner. Accept a different sentence that accurately models the assigned term and uses the shared information. Evidence must preserve the hypothetical facts: 60% spent three hours or more on weekend homework, or students finished long projects on time during the trial with Friday class work time and weekly progress checks. A common slip is changing “three hours or more” to “exactly three hours.”

Round 2 — My partner's term, and the words that gave it away: Accept the correct term for the partner's new sentence plus specific words that show its role. Use the same criteria as in Round 1. A common slip is naming the term on the card even when the sentence actually performs a different role.

handouts.key: Two sentences: Answers vary. Look for a specific change from draft to final and an explanation of how it helps the reader. Example: In my draft, I mentioned the Seattle sleep results without explaining them, so I added reasoning that connects the extra sleep to my claim for a later start. This helps readers understand why the evidence supports my position. Accept other concrete changes involving evidence, source attribution, explanation, organization, counterclaim, rebuttal, or clarity. Students may describe changes they remember making. A common slip is saying only “My essay got better” or listing an edit without explaining why it matters.

t_e17c39ded0b3.prompt: Maya Torres and Daniel Okafor both say that teenagers need 8 to 10 hours of sleep a night. If they agree on that fact, why might they still disagree about whether our school should start later?
followUps: Does a true fact by itself tell a school what it should do? Why or why not?
What worry could make a person hesitate even after agreeing that students need sleep?
How could the fact about 8 to 10 hours of sleep become a reason in the claim “Our school should start at 8:30 a.m. or later”?

t_14ad067d198f.prompt: Which statement is a claim about school start times?

choices.text: Some parents leave for work early.
Our school should start later.
I feel tired on school mornings.
Teenagers need 8 to 10 hours of sleep.

t_14ad067d198f.explanation: “Our school should start later” takes a side that people could disagree with. “Some parents leave for work early” and “Teenagers need 8 to 10 hours of sleep” are checkable facts. “I feel tired on school mornings” expresses a personal feeling.

t_3d7ecb1aafe7.prompt: Daniel Okafor’s article says that some parents leave for work early. How could this fact help support an argument against a later school start?

choices.text: It proves that every family would oppose a later start.
It shows that a personal feeling cannot be part of a discussion.
It could support a concern about changes to family transportation.
It states a claim that the school must keep its schedule.

t_3d7ecb1aafe7.explanation: The fact can support a claim that a later start may make transportation harder for some families. “It proves that every family would oppose a later start” goes beyond what the fact shows. “It shows that a personal feeling cannot be part of a discussion” confuses a fact with a feeling. “It states a claim that the school must keep its schedule” treats a checkable statement as a claim.

t_a43c31578dad.prompt: The statement “I feel nervous about riding the bus in the dark” expresses a personal feeling.

choices.text: True
False

t_a43c31578dad.explanation: The statement describes how one person feels. It does not take a side on what the school should do.

t_3c13317cbe78.prompt: A student says that “The public high schools in Seattle moved their start time later in 2016” is a claim because it is about school schedules. Is the student right? Explain why, then rewrite the idea as a claim about what our school should do, using the Seattle fact as a reason.
t_3c13317cbe78.answer: The student is not right. The statement is a fact because it can be checked; it does not take a side. A possible claim is: Our school should consider starting later because Seattle’s public high schools moved their start time later in 2016.
t_3c13317cbe78.explanation: A topic alone does not make a statement a claim. The original reports a checkable event. The rewrite takes a side about our school and uses the event as a reason.

t_31849cb81147.prompt: State your first position on whether our school should start later. Give one reason using “because,” and name one thing you still want to find out.
t_31849cb81147.answer: Possible answer: Our school should consider starting later because students may have more time to sleep. I want to find out how a later start would affect bus schedules.
t_31849cb81147.explanation: The first sentence takes a side and gives a reason. The second identifies a question to investigate. A supported position against a later start is also acceptable.

t_1f41786399f0.prompt: Torres writes: “In 2014, the American Academy of Pediatrics, an organization of tens of thousands of children’s doctors, recommended that middle and high schools start at 8:30 a.m. or later.” Does this sentence take a stand, or can it be checked and does it back up a reason?
followUps: The doctors’ number, 8:30 a.m., is the same as the number in Torres’s claim. Why does that match not make this sentence her claim?
Who is the sentence about: the doctors, or our school? How does that help you decide?
Which of Torres’s reasons does this sentence back up, and which kind of evidence is it: expert, study, number or example?

t_0b31adb8f407.prompt: For her second reason, Torres has the Seattle study, where high schools moved from 7:50 a.m. to 8:45 a.m. and students slept a little over half an hour more. For her third reason, she says tired students struggle to pay attention, control their moods and make safe choices, and that rested students are safer drivers. Is her third reason backed up as well as her second? Why or why not?
followUps: If you wanted stronger evidence for the third reason, which kind would you look for: expert, study, number or example?
Does a reason stop being a reason when it has weak evidence, or does it only become easier to argue against? What do you think?
If Torres could keep only one of her three reasons, which would you tell her to keep, and what evidence from her article would you point to?

Okafor writes that nobody wants exhausted students and that teenagers need 8 to 10 hours of sleep. Does that mean he disagrees with Maya Torres about sleep? Where in his first paragraph does he turn, and which word shows it?
Is it enough to say that Okafor disagrees? What does he say a later start would cause, and for whom?
Is Okafor’s claim a flat “school should not start later,” or is it a caution? What words in his first paragraph make you think so?

t_45d687627e0f.prompt: Okafor gives three problems with a later start: buses, after-school activities and jobs, and family schedules. Which one is his strongest reason, and what piece of evidence makes it the strongest?
followUps: His example of school ending at 4:00 p.m. instead of 3:00 p.m. is a change that might happen, not a result someone reported. Does that make it weaker evidence than Torres’s Seattle study? Why or why not?

Okafor writes that many people think it makes little sense to have seven-year-olds waiting at bus stops in the dark. Is that the same kind of evidence as a statement from a doctors’ organization? Explain.
Torres says that problems with buses, sports and jobs are real but can be solved. Does her answer weaken the reason you chose, or does your reason still stand?

t_ba09c9d1ba0e.prompt: Should our school start later? Answer in one sentence that includes one reason.
followUps: Does your reason explain why, or does it only say how you feel about mornings?
What is a reason someone on the other side could give for the opposite answer?
If you could keep only one reason for your answer, would this be the one? Why?

t_95003ce7ae6b.prompt: Maya Torres gives reasons about how much sleep teenagers need, how later starts help students sleep more, and how sleep supports health and safety. Daniel Okafor gives reasons about buses, after-school sports and jobs, and family schedules. Which side’s three reasons would make the stronger thesis, and why?
followUps: Which one of that side’s reasons could the other side answer most easily?
If you had to cut one reason from that side and keep only two, which would you cut?
Which reason would you save for a body paragraph because it needs evidence to back it up?

t_e2be713b23cf.prompt: Which sentence is a complete thesis for an essay about adding a school garden?

choices.text: Our school should add a garden because it supports learning, improves the grounds, and is a good idea.
Our school should add a garden because it supports learning, improves the grounds, and encourages teamwork.
A school garden could support learning, improve the grounds, and encourage students to work together.
Our school should add a garden because one class grew tomatoes, beans, and lettuce in containers.

t_e2be713b23cf.explanation: The correct sentence states a position and gives three reasons after because. “Our school should add a garden because it supports learning, improves the grounds, and is a good idea” gives only two reasons; calling the garden a good idea restates the position. “A school garden could support learning, improve the grounds, and encourage students to work together” gives possible benefits but does not state a position. “Our school should add a garden because one class grew tomatoes, beans, and lettuce in containers” offers an example instead of three reasons.

t_1d7540cdddf4.prompt: A student writes, “Our school should add more water fountains because a student once waited in a long line for a drink.” Explain why this is a weak thesis. Then rewrite it as a one-sentence thesis with a position and three reasons.
t_1d7540cdddf4.answer: The sentence states a position, but it offers one example instead of three reasons. A possible revision is: Our school should add more water fountains because students could get water more easily, spend less time waiting in line, and return to class sooner.
t_1d7540cdddf4.explanation: A strong thesis names the writer’s position and gives three reasons that answer why. The story about one student could serve as evidence, but it does not provide three reasons.

t_89805003620b.prompt: In “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later,” Maya Torres describes a change in Seattle high schools. What role does the description of students sleeping longer play in an argument for later starts?

choices.text: It is evidence supporting a reason for later starts.
It is the claim that schools should start later.
It is the source where the article was published.
It is a counterclaim against later start times.

t_89805003620b.explanation: The Seattle result is evidence that supports the reason that later starts can help students sleep more. “It is the claim that schools should start later” confuses a result with the writer’s position. “It is the source where the article was published” confuses information with its source. “It is a counterclaim against later start times” misreads a supporting result as an opposing position.

t_6ccd1c2e8c02.prompt: In an essay, the title of an article can identify the source of a fact the writer uses.

choices.text: True
False

t_6ccd1c2e8c02.explanation: A source is where information comes from. Naming the article tells the reader where the writer found the fact.

t_204ec256e357.prompt: A student argues that school should not start later because a later schedule could make family transportation harder. What is the reason in this argument?

choices.text: School should not start later.
The article “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems.”
A later schedule could make family transportation harder.
Some parents may no longer be able to drop off teenagers on their way to work.

t_204ec256e357.explanation: The transportation concern explains why the student holds the position, so it is the reason. “School should not start later” is the claim. “The article ‘A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems’” names a source. “Some parents may no longer be able to drop off teenagers on their way to work” is a specific detail that can support the reason.

t_a5a07a9655fd.prompt: Which one piece of evidence in either article convinced you most? Write the first few words of that sentence. Then tell your partner in one sentence why.
followUps: Is “it sounds true” or “I agree with that side” a reason to call evidence strong? Why or why not?
Would your piece of evidence still convince a reader who disagrees with the side you chose?
Where does your evidence come from, and could a reader check it?

t_81918ad2ec5c.prompt: Maya Torres uses the Seattle result as evidence that a later start helps students sleep more: after the high schools moved their start time from 7:50 a.m. to 8:45 a.m. in 2016, students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights. Daniel Okafor reports the same result, but he says it came from one city with its own buses, budgets and families. Is the Seattle result strong evidence for a later start at our school, or does Okafor’s point make it weak?
followUps: Does Okafor’s point change whether the Seattle result is relevant to the reason about sleep, or only whether it applies to our school?
What would we need to find out about our school to decide if Seattle is a fair comparison?
Can the same fact be strong for one reason and off target for another? Which reasons in these articles could the Seattle result back, and which could it not?

t_2796f61dc4be.title: Short quizzes on the terms of argument 1
t_2796f61dc4be.prompt: Time allowed: 10 minutes. Your teacher will announce what you may use. This quiz is on what has been taught so far. Work alone and in silence. Write your answers clearly. For questions that ask you to explain, use complete sentences. When time is called, stop writing.
steps:
Which sentence is a claim? (1 point)
A. Our library has three shelves of graphic novels.
B. Our school should keep the library open during lunch.
C. I feel happy when I read.
D. The library opens at 8:00 a.m.
A student argues that the school should add bike racks because more students could ride to school. What is the reason in this argument? (1 point)

A student wants to support the reason that a later start gives teenagers more time to sleep. Which would be evidence for that reason? (1 point)
A. A student says later starts sound nice.
B. A writer claims that mornings are unpleasant.
C. A report measures students’ sleep before and after a school’s start time changes.
D. A student guesses that everyone would be happier.
What is a source in an argument? Give one example of a source students may use for their school start-time essay. (2 points)

A student writes that school should start later because teenagers need enough sleep. The student wants to support that reason with information from Maya Torres’s article. Explain why a recommendation from a named group of sleep experts would be more reliable than an unnamed person’s guess. (2 points)
t_2796f61dc4be.answerKey:
1. B. Award 1 point for selecting B. (1 point)
2. More students could ride to school. Award 1 point for identifying this reason. (1 point)
3. C. Award 1 point for selecting C. (1 point)
4. A source is where information or evidence comes from. An example is Maya Torres’s article, “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later,” or Daniel Okafor’s article, “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems.” Award 1 point for a correct definition and 1 point for either article. (2 points)
5. The named group has expertise in sleep, so readers can identify who made the recommendation and consider their knowledge. The unnamed person’s expertise and basis for the guess cannot be checked. Award 1 point for identifying the experts’ relevant knowledge and 1 point for explaining a limitation of the unnamed guess. (2 points)
Total: 7 points
t_2796f61dc4be.toward: Short quizzes on the terms of argument

t_fdbd8339d6ac.prompt: Which side are you on today? Write your side, then one reason from the articles that you could use.
followUps: Is that a reason from an article, or a feeling like “mornings are awful”? Why do you think so?
Which article and which author does your reason come from?
Does your reason answer why school should or should not start later, or does it only repeat your side?

t_16733685e3e6.prompt: Torres reports that after Seattle’s public high schools moved their start from 7:50 a.m. to 8:45 a.m. in 2016, students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights. Okafor agrees that this is a real result, but says it comes from one city and might not work the same way somewhere else. Is the Seattle result strong evidence for what our school should do?
followUps: What would you want to know about our school’s buses, budgets and families before you trusted the Seattle result?
Which reason does the Seattle result back best: that teenagers need more sleep than most get, or that students sleep more after a later start? Why?
If you are on Okafor’s side, how could you use the Seattle result in your counterclaim box?

t_827b73a0fa4f.prompt: A student’s reason is: “A later school day could make after-school responsibilities harder.” Which evidence from “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems” best supports that reason?

choices.text: Some parents leave for work early in the morning.
Some students care for younger siblings after school.
Some buses make several trips each school morning.
Some teenagers get less than the sleep they need.

t_827b73a0fa4f.explanation: Caring for younger siblings is an after-school responsibility that a later end time could affect. “Some parents leave for work early” concerns morning family schedules; “some buses make several trips” concerns transportation; and “some teenagers get less than the sleep they need” concerns sleep needs.

t_fbdead522d32.prompt: Jordan writes this organizer row: Reason: Later starts can help students sleep more. Evidence: In “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later,” Maya Torres reports that the American Academy of Pediatrics recommended a start time of 8:30 a.m. or later. Explain why the evidence does not directly support the reason. Then replace it with better evidence from Torres’s article and name the article and author.
t_fbdead522d32.answer: The recommendation tells schools when to start; it does not show that students slept more. In “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later,” Maya Torres reports that Seattle students slept a little more than half an hour longer on school nights after their high schools started later.
t_fbdead522d32.explanation: The recommendation supports a claim about what doctors advise. The Seattle result directly reports a change in students’ sleep after a later start, so it fits Jordan’s reason.

t_263106e23720.prompt: A writer who plans to argue for a later start can name Okafor’s concern about family schedules as a counterclaim.

choices.text: True
False

t_263106e23720.explanation: Okafor’s concern gives a point from the opposing side. Naming it in the counterclaim box helps the writer plan for that view.

t_6d8a37b2a639.prompt: A student’s reason is that a later start could affect family schedules. The evidence says that, in “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems,” Daniel Okafor explains that some parents drop teenagers off on their way to work. Which explanation best links the evidence to the reason?

choices.text: This shows that some families already have a routine for getting to school.
This matters because parents and students both have morning responsibilities.
This shows that a later start could make some families change their morning routines.
This matters because teenagers need enough sleep to pay attention at school.

t_6d8a37b2a639.explanation: The correct explanation connects the drop-off evidence to the effect on family schedules. “Some families already have a routine” restates the evidence without explaining the effect of a later start; “parents and students both have morning responsibilities” is too general; and “teenagers need enough sleep” shifts to a different reason.

t_a716e0ecdd4b.prompt: Which thesis gives a clear position and three reasons for an organizer about school start times?

choices.text: School should keep its current start time because a later start could disrupt buses, after-school responsibilities, and family schedules.
School should keep its current start time because changing it would be a bad idea for many people in the community.
School start times affect students, buses, after-school responsibilities, and family schedules in several ways.
School should start later because students need sleep, and the school should keep its current start time because buses matter.

t_a716e0ecdd4b.explanation: The correct thesis takes one position and names three reasons. “Changing it would be a bad idea” gives a position but no three specific reasons; “school start times affect students” names topics without a position; and “school should start later” paired with “keep its current start time” gives conflicting positions.

t_a90b9b9e4eef.prompt: Here is a reason and a piece of evidence. Reason: Later start times really do give students more sleep. Evidence: In “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later,” Maya Torres reports that in 2016 Seattle’s public high schools began the school day almost an hour later, and University of Washington scientists found that students got over thirty minutes more sleep on school nights. What does this evidence tell a reader about the reason?
followUps: Which words in your sentence say what the result means, and which words only repeat the result?
Which sentence starter did you use, and why did you choose it over the others?
Does your sentence link back to the reason about students getting more sleep, or does it stand on its own?

t_ac287ca83c10.prompt: Priya’s paragraph gives the Seattle results and then says, “Sleep is good for everyone.” Is that a good explanation of the evidence, or is it true but not enough? Take a side and give a reason.
followUps: What does the Seattle result tell a reader that “Sleep is good for everyone” does not?
Which sentence starter would you use to begin a stronger explanation, and how would your sentence go?
Would a reader who disagrees with Priya be more persuaded by her sentence or by yours? Why?

t_e0aac5b884d3.prompt: Reason: Teenagers need enough sleep to stay healthy. Evidence: In “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later,” Maya Torres reports that the American Academy of Sleep Medicine recommends 8 to 10 hours of sleep each night for people ages 13 to 18. Which sentence best explains how the evidence supports the reason?

choices.text: This shows that teenagers need 8 to 10 hours of sleep.
This shows that all teenagers get enough sleep each night.
This shows that every school must start at 8:30 a.m.
This shows that enough sleep is a health need for teenagers.

t_e0aac5b884d3.explanation: The correct sentence connects the experts’ recommendation to the reason about health. “Teenagers need 8 to 10 hours of sleep” repeats the evidence. “All teenagers get enough sleep” is not supported by the recommendation. “Every school must start at 8:30 a.m.” claims more than this evidence establishes.

t_323c33e03f31.prompt: A writer follows evidence about California’s school start-time law with “This shows that California has a school start-time law.” This sentence explains why the evidence supports a reason.

choices.text: True
False

t_323c33e03f31.explanation: The sentence repeats the evidence but does not explain what the law means for a reason or claim.

t_3970d9120292.prompt: A paragraph argues that later starts can make after-school activities harder. It cites Daniel Okafor’s point in “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems” that teams may have less daylight for practice if school ends later. Which sentence should follow the evidence?

choices.text: This matters because teams could have less daylight after school.
This matters because teams could have less time to practice outdoors.
This matters because all teams would have to cancel their games.
This matters because students need more sleep on school nights.

t_3970d9120292.explanation: The correct sentence explains how reduced daylight can make practice harder. “Less daylight after school” restates the evidence. “Cancel their games” makes a claim the evidence does not establish. “More sleep on school nights” shifts to a different reason.

t_4163277c3495.prompt: A student writes: “Later starts can affect family schedules. In ‘A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems,’ Daniel Okafor explains that some parents now drop their teenagers off on their way to work. Family schedules are important.” Identify the problem with the final sentence. Then replace it with an explanation that links the evidence to the reason.
t_4163277c3495.answer: The final sentence is too general; it does not explain the evidence. Replacement: “This matters because a later start could make a family’s usual ride to school harder to arrange.”
t_4163277c3495.explanation: The replacement explains what the evidence means for the reason about family schedules. Other wording is acceptable if it makes that connection without simply repeating the evidence.

t_42dbab2ca35a.prompt: Reason: Schools can help students sleep without changing the start time. A paragraph cites Daniel Okafor’s suggestion in “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems” that teachers make sure homework does not keep students up past midnight. Which revision best explains the evidence?

choices.text: This shows that reducing late homework could leave students more time to sleep.
This shows that homework should not keep students up past midnight.
This shows that changing the start time would never help students sleep.
This shows that every student stays up past midnight doing homework.

t_42dbab2ca35a.explanation: The correct sentence connects the homework suggestion to the reason about helping students sleep. “Homework should not keep students up” repeats the suggestion. “Changing the start time would never help” makes an unsupported claim. “Every student stays up past midnight” overstates the evidence.

t_37b2814010dc.title: Explain evidence for your organizer
t_37b2814010dc.prompt: This short, ungraded step prepares you for Organizer and drafts (25%). Complete it at home by the start of next time.
steps: Choose a reason you may use in your essay and a piece of evidence you prepared earlier that supports it.
Write the evidence in your own words, naming its author and article.
Add an explanation beginning with a sentence starter such as “This suggests that.” Explain what the evidence means and how it supports your reason.
Check that your explanation does more than repeat the evidence.

t_ef1136f1ccf1.title: Organizer and drafts: Building the planning organizer
t_ef1136f1ccf1.prompt: Complete your planning organizer for your own five-paragraph argumentative essay. Use evidence only from the two unit articles. Name the article and author each time you use evidence. Put any exact words from an article in quotation marks; write paraphrases in your own words. Keep your organizer in your writing folder. This assignment counts toward Organizer and drafts (25% of the course grade) and is due at the start of next time. Your work will be scored using the rubric below.
steps: Review your thesis and revise it if needed. Write one sentence that states your position on whether school should start later.

Complete three reason rows. For each reason, add a different piece of evidence from a unit article and name its title and author. Check that the evidence supports the reason in that row; move or replace evidence that does not fit.
Under each piece of evidence, write one short explanation beginning with “This shows that” or “This matters because.” Explain how the evidence supports that row’s reason.
In the counterclaim box, name the other side’s strongest point in a few words and identify Torres or Okafor. Then reread your plan and improve one reason, evidence choice or explanation.
t_ef1136f1ccf1.answerKey:
1. A strong thesis clearly takes either position on a later school start. Watch for a question, a vague preference or a statement that does not take a side.
2. A strong plan gives three distinct reasons and matches each with different, relevant evidence, naming the article and author each time. For example, a student arguing against a later start could pair concern about daylight for sports with Okafor’s discussion of later dismissal and practice time in “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems.” Watch for repeated evidence, evidence that supports a different reason, missing source names, copied words without quotation marks or inaccurate paraphrases.
3. Each explanation begins with “This shows that” or “This matters because” and connects its evidence to the specific reason. Watch for explanations that merely repeat evidence or make a broad statement without explaining the connection.
4. A strong counterclaim fairly names an opposing point and identifies Torres or Okafor. The student also improves a reason, evidence choice or explanation. Watch for a counterclaim that supports the writer’s own position or misrepresents the other side, and for a plan with no apparent improvement.

t_58b526d103f8.prompt: Here are two versions of Daniel Okafor’s transportation point. Version A: “Some people are silly to worry about buses when students are too tired to learn.” Version B: “Daniel Okafor argues that a later high school start would force districts either to spend more on buses and drivers or to start younger children’s school day earlier, because the same buses make several trips each morning.” Which version would Okafor agree with, and why?
followUps: Which word in Version A would make Okafor feel he was not being heard fairly?
Version B names two things a district might have to do. Why does it matter that both are in the sentence?
Can a counterclaim be fair to the other side and still be a strong point? What would that look like?

t_8fffcba32f05.prompt: Maya Torres ends her answer about buses with this line: “If a whole state can make the change, our school can too.” California passed a law in 2019 that requires most public high schools there to start no earlier than 8:30 a.m. Does that law show that our school can solve its own bus problem, or only that a later schedule is possible? Explain your thinking.
followUps: Okafor says a result from one city might not work the same way somewhere else. Does his worry also apply to California’s law?
What would our school need to find out about its own buses before you felt sure?
How could Torres word her last line so it is honest about what the law shows and still links back to her claim?

t_15851cc2373a.prompt: A student supports later school starts. Which sentence fairly states Daniel Okafor’s concern about family schedules in “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems”?

choices.text: Daniel Okafor argues that parents should stop taking teenagers to school.
Daniel Okafor argues that teenagers should always stay home alone in the morning.
Daniel Okafor argues that families’ morning routines matter more than sleep.
Daniel Okafor argues that a later start could disrupt some families’ morning routines.

t_15851cc2373a.explanation: The correct sentence states Okafor’s concern calmly and names him. “Parents should stop taking teenagers to school” changes his concern into a recommendation. “Teenagers should always stay home alone in the morning” turns a possible result into a rule. “Families’ morning routines matter more than sleep” makes a comparison Okafor does not make.

t_55bc658d9dd4.prompt: A student answers Okafor’s concern about family schedules by saying that his opinion is foolish. This is a fair counterclaim.

choices.text: True
False

t_55bc658d9dd4.explanation: Calling Okafor’s opinion foolish uses a loaded word instead of stating his concern calmly and accurately.

t_82103dc2fe33.prompt: A student argues that a school should start later. A counterclaim says a later end to the school day could disrupt sports practices. Which evidence from “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later” most directly answers that concern?

choices.text: Maya Torres says teams can adjust practice times.
Maya Torres says teenagers need 8 to 10 hours of sleep.
Maya Torres says rested students can pay attention better.
Maya Torres says teenagers’ internal clocks shift later.

t_82103dc2fe33.explanation: Adjusting practice times addresses the concern about sports directly. “Teenagers need 8 to 10 hours of sleep” supports the need for sleep but does not answer the practice concern. “Rested students can pay attention better” concerns learning, not practice schedules. “Teenagers’ internal clocks shift later” explains sleep patterns, not how teams could adjust.

t_f2c02a55d2c8.prompt: A student argues that the school should start later. Daniel Okafor says in “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems” that a later end to the school day could leave sports teams with less daylight for practice. Write a short rebuttal. State his point fairly, acknowledge what is true, use evidence from Maya Torres’s article, and link back to the student’s claim.
t_f2c02a55d2c8.answer: Daniel Okafor argues that a later school day could leave sports teams with less daylight for practice. This scheduling problem is real. In “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later,” Maya Torres says teams can adjust practice times. The school should consider those adjustments as it plans a later start, although teams would still need a workable schedule.
t_f2c02a55d2c8.explanation: The response states Okafor’s concern accurately and acknowledges it. It names Torres and her article, uses her suggestion about practice times to answer the sports concern, and links the answer to the claim without pretending the adjustment is guaranteed to work.

t_147869e50fd3.prompt: A student argues against a later start. A counterclaim says students need more sleep. The student replies, “School should not start later because a later start is a bad idea.” What is the main problem with this rebuttal?

choices.text: It acknowledges the sleep concern without naming its writer.
It repeats the claim without answering the sleep concern.
It uses sleep evidence without explaining its connection.
It answers the sleep concern but uses loaded language.

t_147869e50fd3.explanation: The reply restates the student’s position and gives no answer or evidence about sleep. “It acknowledges the sleep concern without naming its writer” is wrong because the reply does not acknowledge the concern. “It uses sleep evidence without explaining its connection” is wrong because it gives no evidence. “It answers the sleep concern but uses loaded language” is wrong because it does not answer the concern.

t_65313f164f26.title: Answering a counterclaim with a rebuttal
t_65313f164f26.prompt: This short, ungraded step prepares you for Organizer and drafts (25% of the course grade). Complete it at home by the start of next time.
steps: Review the counterclaim in your planning organizer. Make sure it states the other side’s point fairly and names the writer.
Add a short rebuttal that acknowledges what is true about that point and answers it with evidence from one of the two unit articles. Name the author and article title.
Explain how the evidence answers the counterclaim and connects to your claim. Use your own words, or put exact words from the article in quotation marks.

t_8e9da8e4b9d4.prompt: Look at the library paragraph. Its evidence is a made-up survey: 40 of the 60 students who use the library after school finished their homework there. Its explanation says a quiet room with books and computers lets students finish work they might not finish at home. Which topic sentence is better, A or B? A: “Our school library should definitely stay open after school because it is a great idea.” B: “Keeping the library open after school would give students a quiet place to finish their homework.” Why?
followUps: Which exact words in each sentence tell the reader the reason? Point to them.
Which topic sentence do the survey and the explanation back up more closely, and how can you tell?
Could sentence A work somewhere else in the essay? Where, and what would it do there?

t_3b2d0932cfd9.prompt: In the made-up Student Council survey, 40 of 100 students who skipped breakfast said they felt too hungry to focus before lunch. Is that enough evidence to say free breakfast would help students pay attention in class? Defend your answer.
followUps: Does the explanation sentence make the evidence stronger, or does it only restate it? What in the sentence shows that?
What second piece of evidence would make this paragraph more convincing?
If 60 of 100 students had said they were too hungry to focus, would your answer change? Why or why not?

t_8a569c0d22ea.prompt: A writer claims that the school should start later. What is the job of this sentence in a body paragraph? “Later start times could help students get more sleep.”

choices.text: It supplies evidence for the claim.
It states a reason for the claim.
It answers an opposing claim.
It names the source of evidence.

t_8a569c0d22ea.explanation: The sentence states a reason that a later start could help students. “It supplies evidence for the claim” confuses a reason with information that supports it. “It answers an opposing claim” describes a rebuttal. “It names the source of evidence” describes a citation.

t_a0700673ff48.prompt: A writer argues for a later start. The writer uses evidence from “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later” that Seattle students slept longer after the schedule changed. Which sentence is reasoning?

choices.text: Seattle students slept longer after the schedule changed.
The article describes a change in Seattle schools.
More sleep could help students arrive ready to learn.
Later start times can create transportation problems.

t_a0700673ff48.explanation: “More sleep could help students arrive ready to learn” explains what the evidence means for the argument. “Seattle students slept longer after the schedule changed” restates the evidence. “The article describes a change in Seattle schools” identifies its subject without explaining its meaning. “Later start times can create transportation problems” introduces an opposing concern.

t_1e301fbe5415.prompt: In an essay arguing against a later start, a fair counterclaim could state that a later start may help teenagers get more sleep.

choices.text: True
False

t_1e301fbe5415.explanation: A counterclaim states a point from the other side fairly. More sleep is a reason offered by supporters of a later start.

t_ff30ee2b6ab0.prompt: A writer argues for a later start. A counterclaim says that changing bus schedules could be difficult. What is the job of a rebuttal?

choices.text: Repeat that concern as the essay’s main claim.
Name the concern without responding to it.
Replace the concern with a different reason.
Answer that concern with evidence tied to the claim.

t_ff30ee2b6ab0.explanation: A rebuttal responds to the opposing point with evidence and connects the answer to the writer’s claim. “Repeat that concern as the essay’s main claim” changes the writer’s position. “Name the concern without responding to it” states a counterclaim but does not answer it. “Replace the concern with a different reason” avoids the opposing point.

t_8306869226b8.prompt: A writer claims that the school should start later. A body paragraph will use evidence from “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later” that Seattle students slept longer after their schools changed the start time. Which is the better topic sentence, and why? “Our school should start later.” “A later start could give students more time to sleep.”
t_8306869226b8.answer: “A later start could give students more time to sleep” is better because it states one reason that the Seattle evidence supports. The other sentence repeats the claim without giving a reason.
t_8306869226b8.explanation: A topic sentence should state the paragraph’s reason. The Seattle evidence supports the reason about sleep; repeating the overall claim does not identify that reason.

t_ac78e15bc746.title: Short quizzes on the terms of argument 2
t_ac78e15bc746.prompt: Time allowed: 12 minutes. Your teacher will announce what you may use. This graded quiz is on what has been taught so far. Answer each question and explain your thinking where asked. The quiz is marked in points.
steps: What is reasoning in an argument? (1 point)

A student argues that a community center should stay open on Saturdays because it gives families a place to exercise. A report from the center says that 75 people used its gym on a recent Saturday. Explain how this evidence supports the student’s reason. (2 points)
What is a counterclaim? (1 point)

A student argues that a park should add more trees. Someone on the other side argues that planting trees would cost money that the park needs for repairs. What should a rebuttal do in response? (2 points)

A writer argues that a community pool should extend its evening hours. An opponent says that extra hours would require paying staff for more time. Which response is the fairest counterclaim? (1 point)
A. Anyone against longer hours is selfish.
B. The pool is a great place to swim.
C. Longer hours would require more staff pay, which could strain the pool’s budget.
D. The pool must stay open later because everyone deserves it.
t_ac78e15bc746.answerKey:
1. 1 point: Reasoning explains, in the writer’s own words, what the evidence means for the claim or how it supports a reason. (1 point)
2. 1 point for explaining that people used the gym on Saturday; 1 point for connecting that use to the reason that the center gives people a place to exercise. For example: The gym use shows that people have a place to exercise at the center on Saturdays. (2 points)
3. 1 point: A counterclaim is a point made by the opposing side of an argument, stated fairly. (1 point)
4. 1 point for explaining that a rebuttal answers the concern about repair costs; 1 point for explaining that it uses relevant evidence and links the answer back to the claim. (2 points)
5. C. 1 point for choosing C. (1 point)
Total: 7 points
t_ac78e15bc746.toward: Short quizzes on the terms of argument

t_15f94f929b25.prompt: Here are two openings for a made-up essay about lunch at Maple Street Middle School. Opening A: “This essay is about lunch at Maple Street Middle School.” Opening B: “The bell rings, and you have taken only two bites of your sandwich.” Which opening makes you want to keep reading? Tell your partner your pick and why.
followUps: What does opening B let you see or feel that opening A does not?
How could you rewrite opening A so that a reader wants to keep going?
Can you think of a reader or a situation where opening A would be the better choice? Why?

t_b72034b84fb6.prompt: Maya Torres ends “Let Us Sleep” with “It is time to let us sleep.” Daniel Okafor ends “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems” with “A good solution should not create as many problems as it solves.” Which ending would make a reader more ready to act, and why?
followUps: Who is Torres asking to act, and what does she want them to do?
What would Okafor need to add so that his ending names who should do what?
Would your own ending be stronger as a call to act or as a standard for a good solution? Explain your choice.

t_f004597e0815.prompt: Which opening uses a scene as a hook for an essay about starting school later?

choices.text: Your alarm rings while the sky is still dark.
In this essay, I will discuss school schedules.
A school schedule lists the times classes meet.
Schools should start later for three reasons.

t_f004597e0815.explanation: “Your alarm rings while the sky is still dark” puts the reader in a scene. “In this essay, I will discuss school schedules” only announces the topic. “A school schedule lists the times classes meet” gives a definition. “Schools should start later for three reasons” states a position but does not give the reasons.

t_fa8853775961.prompt: Which sentence is the strongest thesis for an essay arguing that school should start later?

choices.text: Schools should start later because the school day begins too early for many students.
Schools should start later because students need more sleep, better focus and healthier routines.
School start times affect students, families, teachers and the wider community.
Should schools change their schedules to give students a different start time?

t_fa8853775961.explanation: The correct thesis states a position and gives three reasons. “Schools should start later because the school day begins too early for many students” gives a position but does not offer three distinct reasons. “School start times affect students, families, teachers and the wider community” introduces the issue without taking a position. “Should schools change their schedules to give students a different start time?” asks a question without stating a position.

t_07e694ec34e1.prompt: A conclusion about school start times should introduce a new fact from an article to make its final point stronger.

choices.text: True
False

t_07e694ec34e1.explanation: A conclusion restates the claim in new words, explains why it matters and ends with a call to act. New evidence belongs in a body paragraph.

t_2824efc1a9c5.prompt: A student argues that school should keep its current start time because a later schedule could complicate transportation, after-school responsibilities and family routines. The student ends with: “School should keep its current start time because a later schedule could complicate transportation, after-school responsibilities and family routines.” Identify two problems with this conclusion and rewrite it as three sentences.
t_2824efc1a9c5.answer: The conclusion copies the thesis and does not explain why the issue matters or call anyone to act. One possible revision: “Keeping the current start time would avoid disrupting buses, after-school responsibilities and family routines. School schedules affect the whole community, so leaders should consider families as well as students. Before changing the schedule, school leaders should offer sleep lessons, teachers should limit late-night homework, and families should set nighttime screen limits.”
t_2824efc1a9c5.explanation: The revision restates the position in new words, explains its importance and names actions for school leaders, teachers and families. It adds no new evidence.

t_9220bc782a47.prompt: Which final sentence is the clearest call to act for an essay supporting later school start times?

choices.text: A later school start is an issue that matters to many people.
Students need enough sleep to feel ready for their school day.
The school board should set the first bell at 8:30 a.m. or later.
The question of school schedules deserves more discussion.

t_9220bc782a47.explanation: The correct sentence names who should act and what they should do. “A later school start is an issue that matters to many people” says the issue matters but requests no action. “Students need enough sleep to feel ready for their school day” states a reason but requests no action. “The question of school schedules deserves more discussion” suggests discussion without naming who should act.

t_5abc22d001bb.title: Introduction and conclusion practice
t_5abc22d001bb.prompt: This short, ungraded step prepares you for Organizer and drafts (25% of the course grade). Complete it at home by the start of next time. Work on your own.
steps: Read the introduction and conclusion you wrote for your school start-time essay. Check that the background explains the issue and leads to your thesis.
Revise your introduction so its hook draws the reader in and its thesis states your position and three reasons.
Revise your conclusion so it restates your claim in new words, says why the issue matters, and ends by naming who should act and what they should do. Add no new evidence.
Keep your revised writing in your writing folder.

t_bff3f59c6d2b.prompt: Which of your three reasons has your strongest evidence? Tell your partner in one sentence.
followUps: What makes that evidence strong: a number, a named expert, or a real place such as Seattle?
Which article and which author would you name when you cite it?
Does the evidence fit this reason only, or could it also back a different one?

t_44ecb71559d7.prompt: Suppose the Maple Street essay argues against a longer lunch, and Marcus Bell, in his made-up article “Lost in the Lunch Line,” reports that after one school added five minutes to lunch, settling time fell from about ten minutes to about four minutes in each of two afternoon classes. If you were the Maple Street writer, would saying “That is true” to Bell’s point make your essay stronger or weaker?
followUps: What would a reader think of a writer who never mentions Bell’s point at all?
Which words would make Bell sound unfair, and which words would state his point fairly?
After you give in, what could the Maple Street writer say to keep the claim against a longer lunch?

t_6f2d92eb8ad7.prompt: A student paraphrases a sleep recommendation from Maya Torres’s article, “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later.” Which citation names both the article and its author?

choices.text: Torres, “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems”
Okafor, “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later”
Torres, “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later”
Okafor, “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems”

t_6f2d92eb8ad7.explanation: Torres wrote “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later.” “Torres, ‘A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems’” gives the wrong title; “Okafor, ‘Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later’” gives the wrong author; and “Okafor, ‘A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems’” names the other article and its author.

t_b80a4883e2f6.prompt: A student argues against a later start because it could disrupt family schedules. The student paraphrases Daniel Okafor’s point in “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems” that some parents drop teenagers off on their way to work, but a later start could make that difficult. Which explanation best connects this evidence to the reason?

choices.text: This matters because teenagers need more sleep than younger children.
This matters because school buses make several trips each morning.
This matters because every parent would have to change work hours.
This matters because families might need a different way to get students to school.

t_b80a4883e2f6.explanation: The correct explanation connects the evidence to a possible disruption in family transportation. “This matters because teenagers need more sleep than younger children” shifts to sleep needs; “This matters because school buses make several trips each morning” shifts to bus scheduling; and “This matters because every parent would have to change work hours” makes a claim the evidence does not support.

t_7f07f3d15328.prompt: A student drafting a paragraph about learning may replace a detail from the organizer with new evidence from a unit article if that evidence supports the paragraph’s reason.

choices.text: True
False

t_7f07f3d15328.explanation: The organizer is a starting point. New evidence can replace an earlier choice when it still supports the paragraph’s reason.

t_e2c846aca120.prompt: A student argues that school should start later. The student writes: Daniel Okafor argues in “A Later Start Is Not the Easy Fix It Seems” that a later start could make transportation harder for families. That is a fair concern. However, teenagers need sleep, so school should start later. What is missing from the rebuttal? Explain how the student could improve it using evidence from one unit article.
t_e2c846aca120.answer: The rebuttal repeats the claim without giving evidence that answers the transportation concern. The student could name Maya Torres and “Let Us Sleep: Why School Should Start Later,” then paraphrase her suggestion that districts can change bus routes. The student should explain how changing routes could help address transportation before linking back to the claim.
t_e2c846aca120.explanation: A useful rebuttal responds to the other side’s specific point with cited evidence and explains the connection. A link back to the claim can follow that explanation.

t_60d8ae92855f.prompt: A student’s five-paragraph essay argues against a later start. Where should the student place a counterclaim and rebuttal about the sleep benefits of a later start?

choices.text: In the closing part of the body paragraph where that counterclaim fits best.
In a separate fourth body paragraph after the three reason paragraphs.
In the introduction before the essay states its claim and reasons.
In the conclusion after the essay has finished its body paragraphs.

t_60d8ae92855f.explanation: Placing the counterclaim and rebuttal in the body paragraph where they fit keeps the essay’s three body paragraphs. “In a separate fourth body paragraph after the three reason paragraphs” adds a body paragraph; “In the introduction before the essay states its claim and reasons” puts the response before the argument is developed; and “In the conclusion after the essay has finished its body paragraphs” leaves the response outside the body.

t_2dc685900713.title: Final essay
t_2dc685900713.prompt: Write your own five-paragraph argumentative essay answering: Should school start later? Take a clear position and support it using only the two unit articles. Final essay is worth 60% of your course grade. It is due at the start of the class on Review of argument terms and a final quiz; essays handed in.
steps: Write an introduction with a hook, background on the start-time question, and a thesis that states your position and three reasons.

Write three body paragraphs, one for each reason. Give each paragraph a topic sentence, evidence from a unit article, an explanation of how the evidence supports the reason, and a link back to your claim. Name the article and author each time you use evidence. Put exact words inside quotation marks; name the article and author when you paraphrase, too.
